packs.title: PDP Scenario Deck — 15 Layouts and a Blank Key Frame
packs.summary: Fifteen hose-layout scenario cards — lengths, diameters, appliances, elevation, standpipe, relay — with the pressure answer left blank on every one, plus the structured friction-loss key frame the operator fills from their own department's hose, coefficients, and appliance losses. The scenarios are universal; every number is yours.
packs.removes_prep: The drill opens with the operator building a reference key covering every hose diameter and length their apparatus carries, at the flows they actually pump, plus appliance and elevation adjustments — and then writing one scenario per card. That is the better part of an hour of paperwork before a single rep, and the scenarios a tired operator invents are the ones they already know how to solve.
packs.local_fill_note: This pack contains no pressures, no coefficients, and no appliance losses, deliberately. DrillGround is not a hydraulics authority and a wrong coefficient here would be pumped at a real fire. Fill the key frame from your department's own hydraulic reference and your apparatus's actual hose complement — then the cards become scoreable.

components.label: Friction-loss key frame — fill before the first rep
components.instructions: One row per hose diameter and length your apparatus actually carries. Get the coefficients and appliance losses from your department's hydraulic reference or your training division, not from memory and not from the internet. Where your department mandates a flat pump pressure for a preconnect, write that instead of the calculation and note that it is a mandated figure.

items.text: Hose on my apparatus — one row per size and length carried
fields: Diameter
Length carried
Target flow at the nozzle we use
Friction loss at that flow, per my department's reference
Nozzle pressure required
Source of these figures and date
items.teaching_focus: Building the key from the apparatus rather than from a textbook, so the numbers match the hose that is actually in the bed.

items.text: Appliances on my apparatus
fields: Appliance — gated wye, siamese, master device, standpipe
Loss per my department's reference
Flow at which that loss applies
items.teaching_focus: Appliance loss is the term operators most often drop entirely.

items.text: Elevation
fields: Gain or loss per story used by my department
Per foot figure if used
How my department handles below-grade
items.teaching_focus: Sign errors on elevation are the most common arithmetic failure in the deck.

items.text: Mandated pump pressures, if my department sets them
fields: Preconnect and its mandated PDP
Any layout where policy overrides calculation
Policy reference
items.teaching_focus: Where policy overrides arithmetic, policy wins, and the operator should know which is which.

components.label: Layout scenario cards
components.instructions: One layout per card. Front is the layout; the back is where you write your own answer from your key, once, in pen. Draw, state the pump discharge pressure out loud with the terms named — nozzle pressure plus friction loss plus appliance plus elevation — inside the time you set. Then check the back. Say the terms every time even when the answer is memorised, because the terms are what transfer to a layout you have not seen.

items.text: 200 ft of your standard attack line, ground level, standard nozzle.
items.teaching_focus: Baseline. The one the operator should be able to do without arithmetic.

items.text: The same line extended by one more 50 ft length at the door.
items.teaching_focus: Recalculating on an extension, which happens on real fires and surprises operators.

items.text: Your standard attack line, third floor, interior stairs.
items.teaching_focus: Elevation gain, correct sign.

items.text: Your standard attack line into a basement, one level below grade.
items.teaching_focus: Elevation loss — and whether your department's method even applies below grade.

items.text: Two attack lines off the same apparatus, different lengths, both flowing.
items.teaching_focus: Two discharge pressures at once, which is where operators start pumping the average.

items.text: A 2.5 in line, 250 ft, smoothbore, ground level.
items.teaching_focus: The big line, with a different nozzle pressure the operator uses less often.

items.text: Gated wye at 150 ft, two 100 ft attack lines beyond it, both flowing.
items.teaching_focus: Appliance loss plus a split flow, the layout that produces the most wrong answers.

items.text: Gated wye at 150 ft, two lines beyond it, only one flowing.
items.teaching_focus: The pair with the previous card. Flow through the supply section changed; the answer changed with it.

items.text: Standpipe operation, fourth floor, your department's standpipe kit and hose.
items.teaching_focus: Standpipe loss and the outlet pressure your department assumes — often a fixed policy figure.

items.text: Master stream from the apparatus, your standard supply arrangement.
items.teaching_focus: High flow, where a small coefficient error becomes a large pressure error.

items.text: Relay: you are the supply pumper, 600 ft of LDH to the attack engine.
items.teaching_focus: Residual pressure at the receiving engine as the target rather than a nozzle pressure.

items.text: Relay: you are the attack engine receiving that supply, working one attack line.
items.teaching_focus: The other half of the same problem, and the intake pressure it depends on.

items.text: Long stretch: 400 ft of your standard attack line, ground level.
items.teaching_focus: Where friction loss dominates and the operator has to decide whether the layout is even viable.

items.text: Your standard attack line, third floor, and the officer reports the nozzle feels soft.
items.teaching_focus: Diagnosing rather than calculating: kink, partially closed discharge, wrong pressure, or a supply problem.

items.text: Aerial or elevated stream at your device's working height, your department's arrangement.
items.teaching_focus: Elevation at scale, plus the device's own loss figure.

packs.title: Operating-Order Template — Blind Panel Walk
packs.summary: The operating-order sequence template the drill requires, structured by stage from arrival through shutdown with the reasoning prompt beside each stage, plus a control-location map the operator fills by feel and a playback review sheet for the filmed reps. Blank where the sequence is apparatus-specific, which is everywhere it matters.
packs.removes_prep: The drill's setup requires the operator to 'first write the correct operating-order sequence for THIS apparatus' before touching anything. Operators who have only ever learned the panel by watching someone else discover at this point that they cannot write the sequence down — which is the finding, but it stops the drill before the reps start.
packs.local_fill_note: Every step in this template is blank because the correct operating order is set by your apparatus's pump manufacturer and your department's procedure, and the consequences of a wrong order are mechanical. Fill it from the apparatus manual and your department's driver-operator procedure, and have a qualified operator or your training division check it before you rehearse it.

components.label: Operating-order sequence — by stage
components.instructions: Write the sequence for THIS apparatus, in order, one action per line. Then have it checked before you rehearse it: rehearsing a wrong order builds a wrong habit faster than not rehearsing at all. The pump stays disengaged and no water moves for the whole drill.

items.text: STAGE 1 — Arrival and securing the apparatus, before the pump
fields: Actions in order, one per line
Which action is the one that must never be skipped
What confirms each action is complete
items.teaching_focus: The stage where a missed step lets the apparatus move under power. Everything else is recoverable.

items.text: STAGE 2 — Engaging the pump
fields: Actions in order
The indicator that confirms engagement on this apparatus
What it looks and sounds like when engagement did NOT take
items.teaching_focus: The confirmation, not the action. Operators learn the lever and not the indicator.

items.text: STAGE 3 — Establishing water — tank
fields: Actions in order
Where tank level reads
The pressure state before any discharge is opened

items.text: STAGE 4 — Charging the first line
fields: Actions in order
Which discharge and how it is identified on this panel
The pressure target and where it is set
What tells you the line is actually charged

items.text: STAGE 5 — Transition to an external supply
fields: Actions in order
The step that prevents interrupting flow to a working line
How intake pressure is monitored during the change
items.teaching_focus: The stage with the highest cost of a wrong order: a crew on a line loses water.

items.text: STAGE 6 — Adding a second line while the first is flowing
fields: Actions in order
What happens to the first line's pressure and what you do about it

items.text: STAGE 7 — Shutdown
fields: Actions in order
What must be relieved before what
The step that protects the pump in freezing conditions, if applicable here

items.text: Control-location map — filled by feel, not by looking
fields: Control name
Where my hand finds it, described from a fixed reference on the panel
Direction that opens or increases
A control near it that I could confuse it with
items.teaching_focus: The last column is the useful one. Confusable neighbors are what the blindfold exposes.

components.label: Playback review sheet
components.instructions: One per filmed session. Watch the film with your written sequence beside it and mark against the sheet rather than from impression. The film is the scorer; the memory of the rep is not.

items.text: Sequence fidelity
fields: Steps performed out of order
Steps omitted
Steps performed but not confirmed
Hesitations longer than three seconds and at which control

items.text: Hands
fields: Controls found first time by feel
Controls groped for
Controls found by using a neighbor as a reference
Any control I could not find at all
items.teaching_focus: Using a neighbor as a reference is a legitimate technique and worth noticing when it works.

items.text: Next session
fields: The two controls I will drill in isolation
The stage I will rehearse before the whole sequence
Date

sources: Self-authored template and review sheet
Apparatus pump manufacturer's operating procedure and department driver-operator procedure (user-supplied and authoritative; no sequence supplied by this pack)

packs.title: Arrival-Sequence Checklist & Self-Timing Log
packs.summary: The arrival-sequence checklist frame the drill requires — brake, transmission, chocks, pump, and the department-specific steps in between — plus a self-timing log that separates the time spent on each phase, so the operator finds out which phase is actually slow rather than that the whole thing takes too long.
packs.removes_prep: The drill says 'The operator builds a written arrival-sequence checklist for THIS apparatus and department first — the exact steps and their order.' Nothing supplies the frame, so the operator either writes it from habit — which reproduces the errors the drill exists to find — or does not write it and times an unmeasured sequence.
packs.local_fill_note: The order of these steps is set by your apparatus and your department's procedure, and getting it wrong has mechanical consequences. Fill the checklist from the apparatus manual and your department's arrival procedure and have it checked before you rehearse it against a clock. Speed on a wrong sequence is not a training outcome.

components.label: Arrival-sequence checklist frame
components.instructions: Write one action per line in the exact order your apparatus and department require, then keep the sheet at the panel for the first few reps and put it away once the sequence is committed. Pump stays disengaged for the panel portion and no water moves.

items.text: PHASE 1 — Stopping and securing (from wheels-stopped to apparatus safe)
fields: Actions in order, one per line
The action that must be complete before anyone dismounts
How I confirm it rather than assume it
items.teaching_focus: The phase where haste causes the only irreversible failure available in this drill.

items.text: PHASE 2 — Dismount and chocks
fields: Actions in order
Where the chocks live and which hand takes them
Which wheel, per department practice

items.text: PHASE 3 — Pump engagement and panel ready
fields: Actions in order
Engagement confirmation indicator
Panel state I want before the first pull is called for

items.text: PHASE 4 — Ready to supply
fields: Actions in order
What I have set before a line is asked for
What I deliberately have NOT done yet, and why
items.teaching_focus: The last column stops the operator from pre-charging things that should not be pre-charged.

items.text: Position marking — before the timed reps
fields: Where the chalk or tape stopping spot is
What the spot represents — hydrant side, address side, aerial clearance
One position error this apparatus is prone to
items.teaching_focus: Stopping in the right place is part of arrival and is not measured by a clock.

components.label: Phase-split timing log
components.instructions: Time the phases separately, not just the whole run. Ten reps minimum. The useful output is the phase that varies most between reps, because a phase with high variance is one the operator has not automated yet — and that is the phase that will fail on a bad night.

items.text: Rep log — one row per rep
fields: Phase 1 time
Phase 2 time
Phase 3 time
Phase 4 time
Total
Any step missed or done out of order

items.text: Analysis after ten reps
fields: Slowest phase on average
Phase with the widest spread between best and worst
The step inside that phase that caused the spread
Fastest total, and was anything skipped to get it
items.teaching_focus: The variance column, not the average. And the honest last question.

items.text: Findings
fields: One change to where a tool or chock is carried
One step I was performing but not confirming
One step my written sequence had in the wrong place
Date of next session
items.teaching_focus: The third one is the highest-value finding the drill can produce.

sources: Self-authored checklist frame and timing log
Apparatus manual and department arrival procedure (user-supplied and authoritative; no sequence supplied by this pack)

packs.title: Gauge & Control Prompt Deck — 20 Targets, Randomised
packs.summary: Twenty gauge-and-control prompt targets covering the master gauges, individual discharges, engine instruments, tank and foam indicators, and the controls operators reach for least — with the panel inventory frame the drill uses as its answer key, and four pre-shuffled running orders so the sequence is not memorised.
packs.removes_prep: The drill's setup has the operator build 'a written inventory of every gauge and control on the panel' and then 'a shuffled prompt list or a recorded voice reading the 20 targets in random order'. Building the inventory is the valuable part and stays with the operator; picking and shuffling twenty targets is clerical work, and a self-shuffled list gets memorised by the third session.
packs.local_fill_note: Panels differ. Work through the twenty targets against your own apparatus first and strike any that do not exist on it, then add the ones yours has that are not listed — the inventory frame is where those go. Your inventory is the answer key, not this list.

components.label: Twenty prompt targets
components.instructions: Record yourself reading the targets in one of the running orders below, with a five-second gap between each, or have someone read them. Hand on the target before the next prompt, and call out what it reads or what it does. Film the panel and your hands so playback settles any disagreement about whether the hand was actually on it.

items.text: Master intake pressure
items.teaching_focus: The gauge that tells you about the supply rather than the fire.

items.text: Master discharge pressure
items.teaching_focus: Distinguishing it from an individual discharge gauge, which operators confuse under pressure.

items.text: The discharge gauge for the primary attack preconnect
items.teaching_focus: Identifying by function, not by position in a row.

items.text: The discharge gauge for the second attack line
items.teaching_focus: Whether the operator can tell two similar gauges apart by touch and label.

items.text: The discharge gauge for the largest handline or master device
items.teaching_focus: The one used least often and therefore found slowest.

items.text: Engine RPM
items.teaching_focus: Reading the engine, not the pump.

items.text: Engine oil pressure
items.teaching_focus: One of the instruments an operator can watch degrade during a long pumping operation.

items.text: Engine coolant temperature
items.teaching_focus: The instrument that decides whether a long operation is sustainable.

items.text: Water tank level indicator
items.teaching_focus: How the indicator reads on this apparatus, and how coarse it is.

items.text: Foam tank level, if the apparatus carries foam
items.teaching_focus: Strike this target if the apparatus has none — and note the strike.

items.text: Pump engagement indicator
items.teaching_focus: The indicator, distinct from the control that causes it.

items.text: Throttle or pressure governor control
items.teaching_focus: Which mode it is in, and what changes when it is switched.

items.text: Primer control
items.teaching_focus: A control most operators can describe and few can find blind.

items.text: Tank-to-pump valve
items.teaching_focus: The valve whose position decides whether there is water at all.

items.text: Tank fill / recirculation valve
items.teaching_focus: The valve next to the previous one, and the confusion between them.

items.text: Main pump intake valve or the largest intake
items.teaching_focus: Where external supply enters, and its cap or valve.

items.text: Pressure relief or governor set control
items.teaching_focus: The control that protects the crew on the line from a pressure spike.

items.text: Master drain or individual drains
items.teaching_focus: Shutdown-critical and rarely drilled.

items.text: Panel lighting control
items.teaching_focus: Trivial until it is 0300 and the operator is looking for it.

items.text: The one control on this panel I use least often — name it and find it
items.teaching_focus: A deliberately reflexive target. Whatever the operator names is the target they most needed.

components.label: Panel inventory frame — the answer key
components.instructions: One row per gauge and control on YOUR panel. This is the artifact that outlasts the drill: it is the answer key, the study sheet, and the thing to hand a new operator. Build it once with vision, then use it to score every blind session after.

items.text: Inventory row
fields: Gauge or control name as labelled on the panel
What it reads or does, in one line
Position described from a fixed reference — panel edge, a bank of gauges, the throttle
Normal or expected reading during a working pumping operation
The nearest control it could be confused with
items.teaching_focus: The last two columns are what makes this a training document rather than a parts list.

items.text: Targets I struck, and targets I added
fields: Struck — target and why it does not exist on this apparatus
Added — control on my panel that the deck did not name
Date the inventory was built and by whom it was checked
items.teaching_focus: Recording the strikes stops the same target being re-argued every session.

components.label: Four running orders
components.instructions: Use a different order each session, and rebuild the orders once you have been through all four. The point is that the operator never learns the sequence, only the panel.

sources: Self-authored prompt targets, inventory frame, and running orders
Apparatus panel configuration (user-supplied; the operator's own inventory is the answer key)

packs.title: Stretch Estimation Log — 12 Target Types and a Calibration Sheet
packs.summary: Twelve building-target types to hunt on walkarounds — the rear bedroom of a ranch, the third-floor rear apartment, the strip-mall unit reached from the wrong side — each with what to estimate and the specific error it exposes, plus a calibration sheet that turns verified measurements into a personal correction factor.
packs.removes_prep: The drill's equipment is 'Buildings in the district' and 'Notepad or app', and the setup says to 'pick target points'. Picking the targets is the skill and the burden at once: a crew left to pick their own targets picks the easy geometry, and nobody keeps a log, so the estimates are never calibrated against the measuring wheel that is in the equipment list.

components.label: Twelve target types
components.instructions: Work these on scheduled walkarounds, one or two per building. Estimate first, out loud, committed. Then wheel it. Never wheel first. The gap between the estimate and the wheel is the only product of this drill.

items.text: Single-story ranch — rear bedroom, from the most likely apparatus position
items.teaching_focus: The baseline estimate everyone thinks they are good at, and the one where the wrap-around distance gets forgotten.

items.text: Two-story dwelling — second-floor rear bedroom, interior stairs
items.teaching_focus: Adding the vertical and the turn at the top of the stairs, which is where a stretch comes up short.

items.text: Two-story dwelling — same room, but the apparatus stopped short of the driveway
items.teaching_focus: Position as a variable. The same building has several answers.

items.text: Garden apartment — third-floor unit, exterior stair or breezeway
items.teaching_focus: The multiplied vertical plus the walk from the stair head to the door.

items.text: Center-hall apartment building — top-floor unit at the far end of the hall
items.teaching_focus: The horizontal run inside the building, which is invisible from the street.

items.text: Strip mall — unit reached from the front, and the same unit from the rear service door
items.teaching_focus: Two answers for one occupancy, and which one your first-due would actually use.

items.text: Strip mall — the deepest unit in the row, front entry
items.teaching_focus: Commercial depth versus residential depth, which is the single biggest miscalibration in most crews.

items.text: Building with a setback or a courtyard — nearest door, then the far side
items.teaching_focus: Geometry the street view hides.

items.text: Below-grade — basement of a dwelling with an exterior walk-out and an interior stair
items.teaching_focus: Whichever route is chosen, the estimate has to say which.

items.text: A building where the closest hydrant is on the wrong side of the street
items.teaching_focus: The supply half of the estimate, which is the half crews leave out.

items.text: A gated or fenced property where the apparatus cannot reach the address side
items.teaching_focus: The estimate that reveals a pre-incident problem worth writing down and reporting.

items.text: Your own station — the far corner of the apparatus bay from the pump panel
items.teaching_focus: A free, repeatable calibration target you can wheel any time.

components.label: Estimate-and-verify log
components.instructions: One row per target. Estimate in the same units your preconnects come in, so the estimate converts directly into a decision about which line to pull. Log it even when you were close.

items.text: Target row
fields: Address or target description
Assumed apparatus position
Route chosen — front, rear, interior stair, exterior stair
My estimate, in feet AND in preconnect lengths
Wheel measurement
Error, signed — over or under
The line I would pull, before and after
items.teaching_focus: The last column is the point. An error that does not change the line pulled is an academic error; one that does is the one to fix.

items.text: Calibration after twelve targets
fields: Average signed error — do I run long or short
Building type where I am worst
Element I most often forget — the wrap, the vertical, the interior run, the setback
My correction factor, and how I will apply it on the next size-up
items.teaching_focus: Almost everyone estimates short, and knowing your own direction and size of bias is worth more than any single measurement.

sources: Self-authored target set and calibration log

packs.title: Hose Load Reference Diagrams & Pattern Fidelity Sheet
packs.summary: Eight labelled diagram specs of the common preconnect load patterns — flat, accordion, triple-layer, minuteman, and the two variants that only differ at the nozzle end — showing bed cross-section and the pull that each load is built for, plus a fidelity sheet that scores a reload against your own department's diagram rather than against the pictures.
packs.removes_prep: The drill's equipment list ends with 'The department's hose load diagram or a photo of a correctly loaded bed' — and most departments do not have one, or have one nobody can find. Without a reference the reload is scored against whoever loaded it last, which is how a pattern drifts across a shift until the pull fails.
packs.local_fill_note: These diagrams are generic illustrations of common patterns and are NOT your department's load. Your department's diagram, or a photograph of a bed loaded correctly by someone qualified, is the reference the fidelity sheet scores against. Use the diagrams to recognize which pattern yours is and to talk about it precisely.

components.label: Load pattern diagram specs
components.instructions: Diagrams, not photographs — schematic cross-sections and top views, deliberately generic. Use them to identify which family your preconnect belongs to and to learn the vocabulary. Images marked AI-GENERATED render with a visible synthetic label; they illustrate geometry only and are not a loading authority.

items.text: Flat load — bed cross-section
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical line diagram, cross-section view of a fire apparatus hose bed, showing hose laid flat in horizontal stacked layers filling the bed width, each layer drawn as a flattened oval in cross-section, with a simple arrow indicating the direction of the fold at each end. Plain white background, thin black lines, minimal labelling, engineering-drawing style. No text.
items.alt: Technical cross-section diagram of a hose bed with hose laid flat in stacked horizontal layers, arrows showing the fold direction at each end.
items.teaching_focus: The simplest pattern and the baseline for the vocabulary — layer, fold, bed width.

items.text: Accordion load — bed cross-section
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical line diagram, cross-section view of a fire apparatus hose bed with hose laid on edge in vertical folds side by side across the bed width, each length drawn as a tall narrow oval standing upright, arrows showing the vertical fold pattern. Plain white background, thin black lines, engineering-drawing style. No text.
items.alt: Technical cross-section diagram of a hose bed with hose laid on edge in vertical folds standing side by side across the bed.
items.teaching_focus: On-edge versus flat, and why the pull comes off differently.

items.text: Triple-layer load — top view showing the three folds
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical line diagram, top-down view of a hose length folded into three equal stacked layers before being loaded into a hose bed, showing the two fold points and the nozzle end position, with dimension lines indicating the three equal segments. Plain white background, thin black lines, engineering-drawing style. No text.
items.alt: Technical top-down diagram of a hose length folded into three equal layers with the two fold points and the nozzle end marked.
items.teaching_focus: The fold arithmetic that decides how far the shoulder carry reaches.

items.text: Minuteman load — top view showing the shoulder-carry stack
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical line diagram, side view of a minuteman hose load stacked so the load can be lifted onto the shoulder as a unit and paid off from the top, showing the stack orientation, the nozzle at the top of the stack, and an arrow indicating the direction hose pays out. Plain white background, thin black lines, engineering-drawing style. No text.
items.alt: Technical side-view diagram of a minuteman hose load stack with the nozzle at the top and an arrow showing hose paying out from the top of the stack.
items.teaching_focus: Why this load pays off the top and what happens if it is built upside down.

items.text: Nozzle-end placement — the difference that is not the pattern
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical line diagram showing two side-by-side hose bed cross-sections that are identical except for the position of the nozzle: in the left the nozzle sits on top of the load at the rear, in the right it is tucked into the side of the load. Simple circle marking the nozzle in each. Plain white background, thin black lines, engineering-drawing style. No text.
items.alt: Two side-by-side technical cross-sections of identical hose loads differing only in nozzle position: on top at the rear versus tucked into the side.
items.teaching_focus: The variation that causes most cross-shift disagreement, and it is not a different load.

items.text: Bed division for two preconnects of different lengths
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical line diagram, top-down view of a fire apparatus hose bed divided by a vertical partition into two unequal compartments, each containing a stacked hose load drawn as horizontal lines, with the compartments visibly different in depth. Plain white background, thin black lines, engineering-drawing style. No text.
items.alt: Technical top-down diagram of a hose bed split by a partition into two unequal compartments, each holding a stacked hose load.
items.teaching_focus: Reading a bed as several loads rather than one, and knowing which compartment is which by feel.

items.text: Correct versus incorrect fold at the bed edge
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical line diagram with two panels side by side: the left shows hose folds finishing flush and square at the edge of a hose bed, the right shows the same folds finishing unevenly with one fold protruding past the bed edge and another short of it. Simple tick and cross marks above the panels. Plain white background, thin black lines, engineering-drawing style. No text other than the tick and cross.
items.alt: Two-panel technical diagram contrasting hose folds finishing flush and square at the bed edge with folds finishing unevenly, one protruding and one short.
items.teaching_focus: The specific defect that causes a load to hang up on the pull, drawn rather than described.

items.text: Load height relative to the bed rail
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical line diagram, rear elevation of a fire apparatus hose bed showing a loaded hose stack with a dimension line indicating the clearance between the top of the load and the top of the bed rail, with a dashed line marking the rail height. Plain white background, thin black lines, engineering-drawing style. No text.
items.alt: Technical rear-elevation diagram of a loaded hose bed with a dimension line showing clearance between the top of the load and the bed rail.
items.teaching_focus: Overloaded height as a defect that only shows up when the load will not clear on the pull.

components.label: Pattern fidelity sheet
components.instructions: Score the finished reload against your department's diagram or reference photograph — not against the diagrams in this pack. Film the bed as it fills and check the film against the sheet, because the defects are easiest to see from above and hardest to see while your hands are in the bed.

items.text: Reference used
fields: Department diagram, reference photo, or qualified member's build
Pattern family it belongs to, using the deck's vocabulary
Preconnect length and hose diameter
Nozzle end position per the reference
items.teaching_focus: Naming the pattern precisely is what makes the disagreement resolvable.

items.text: Fidelity check
fields: Folds flush and square at the bed edge (Y/N)
Layer count matches the reference (Y/N)
Nozzle end positioned per the reference (Y/N)
Load height clears the rail (Y/N)
Couplings positioned where the reference puts them (Y/N)
Built in gloves (Y/N)
items.teaching_focus: The gloves row is not a formality: a pattern built bare-handed is not the pattern that will be built at 0300.

items.text: Proof of the build — the pull
fields: Did the load deploy clean on a test pull (Y/N)
Where it hung up, if it did
Which fidelity row predicted the hang-up
Rebuild required (Y/N)
items.teaching_focus: Closing the loop: a load is only correct if it pulls, and the pull tells you which check you scored wrong.

sources: Self-authored diagram specifications and fidelity sheet
Department hose load diagram or reference photograph (user-supplied and authoritative)
packs.synthetic_caveat: The load diagrams are AI-generated schematic illustrations of common pattern families. They exist to give crews shared vocabulary and to show geometry. They are not your department's load, they are not a loading procedure, and a reload is scored against your department's own diagram or a photograph of a correctly loaded bed — never against these.

packs.title: Appliance ID Deck — 14 Blind Prompts and Assembly Tasks
packs.summary: Fourteen prompt cards mixing single-appliance identification with two-piece assembly tasks and three deliberate impossible-combination cards, each with what a correct blind answer contains. The impossible cards are the point: a firefighter who assembles a double male to a double female in the dark has not been caught out by the deck, they have been caught out by the dark.
packs.removes_prep: The drill's setup has the crew lay every appliance out, learn the layout with vision, mix the order and cover their eyes — but supplies no prompts, so the person calling the drill names appliances in the order they are lying on the bench, and the reps become a memory test of the layout rather than an identification test of the hardware.
packs.local_fill_note: The drill states its own appliance inventory is an example. Strike any card naming hardware your apparatus does not carry and add cards for what it does — thread type, storz or other connection style, and any department-specific adapter belong on cards of your own.

components.label: Identification and assembly prompts
components.instructions: Blindfold or blacked-out facepiece, structural gloves, in quarters only — never in a confined or elevated space. Lay the appliances out, let the firefighter learn the layout with vision, then mix the order and cover their eyes. Read one prompt, time it, and require the answer spoken aloud: what it is, what it is for, and which end is which.

items.text: Find the gated wye. Name it, state what it does, and tell me which side is the inlet.
items.answer: Identifies by the two gated outlets and the single larger inlet. States it splits one supply into two controllable lines. Finds the inlet by size and thread direction, not by guessing.
items.teaching_focus: Inlet-versus-outlet by feel, which is the whole family of errors this deck targets.

items.text: Find the siamese. Name it, state what it does, and tell me how you know it is not the wye.
items.answer: Two inlets to one outlet — the reverse of the wye. Distinguished by the absence of gate handles on the paired side, or by the direction the clappers move if it has them.
items.teaching_focus: The pair that gets confused most often, and the tactile difference that resolves it.

items.text: Find a reducer. Name it, state which direction it reduces, and what you would use it for.
items.answer: Identifies the two different thread sizes by hand span, states large-to-small in the direction of flow, names a use — stepping a larger supply down to a smaller line.
items.teaching_focus: Direction of a fitting is a property the firefighter must feel, not read.

items.text: Find an increaser. Same three answers.
items.answer: Small-to-large in the direction of flow. States the flow consequence: an increaser does not create water, and a line increased beyond its supply is a slower line, not a bigger one.
items.teaching_focus: The hydraulic honesty behind the fitting.

items.text: Find the double female. Name it and tell me what problem it solves.
items.answer: Two female couplings, so it joins two male ends — the fix for two lengths laid out in the same direction.
items.teaching_focus: Naming the problem, not just the part.

items.text: Find the double male. Same two answers.
items.answer: Two male couplings, joins two female ends. States the situation that produces it: a length reversed in the lay.
items.teaching_focus: The other half of the pair, and the reason both live in the bag.

items.text: Find the hydrant wrench. Name it and demonstrate the grip you would use on a stiff operating nut.
items.answer: Identifies it by the head shape, demonstrates a two-hand grip with the body positioned so a slip does not put a knuckle into the hydrant.
items.teaching_focus: Tool use, blind, with the injury mechanism in mind.

items.text: Find a spanner. Name it and demonstrate breaking a tight coupling with it.
items.answer: Locates the spanner lug seat by feel on the coupling first, then seats the spanner. Demonstrates pulling rather than pushing where possible.
items.teaching_focus: Finding the lug before the tool, which is the sequence that works in the dark.

items.text: ASSEMBLY — Connect the gated wye to the 2.5 in length. Tell me when it is hand-tight and how you know.
items.answer: Threads engaged without cross-threading, seated by feel, confirmed by the resistance change rather than by counting turns.
items.teaching_focus: Hand-tight as a felt endpoint.

items.text: ASSEMBLY — Put the combination nozzle on one of the 1.75 in lengths, then take it off again.
items.answer: Correct end identified, threads engaged cleanly both directions, and the nozzle's bale position stated at the end.
items.teaching_focus: The bale check, which people forget the moment the task is a hardware task.

items.text: ASSEMBLY — Join the two 1.75 in lengths to each other.
items.answer: Male to female. If the two ends presented are the same gender, the firefighter must say so and ask for the fitting rather than force it.
items.teaching_focus: Setting up the impossible cards that follow.

items.text: IMPOSSIBLE — Connect the double male directly to the double female. Do it, or tell me why not.
items.answer: The correct answer is that it CAN be done and accomplishes nothing useful — it is two adapters in series with no hose. A firefighter who reports what they are holding rather than completing the task blindly has passed.
items.teaching_focus: Reporting rather than complying. The deck rewards the firefighter who says what is in their hands.

items.text: IMPOSSIBLE — Connect the reducer to the increaser and tell me what you have made.
items.answer: A fitting that returns to the original size with two extra failure points. Correct answer names it as pointless and says so.
items.teaching_focus: Understanding fittings well enough to recognize a nonsense combination by feel.

items.text: IMPOSSIBLE — Connect the 2.5 in length directly to the 1.75 in length, no fittings.
items.answer: Cannot be done; the correct answer is a request for the reducer, by name, and a statement of which direction it must face.
items.teaching_focus: The card that proves the whole deck: naming the missing part is the skill.

sources: Self-authored prompt and assembly card set
Apparatus appliance and adapter complement (user-supplied; the drill states its own inventory is an example)

packs.title: Ten-Fault Build List & Route Card
packs.summary: The ten specific faults the drill asks the firefighter to build into the lay, ordered easiest to hardest to find, each with how to build it and what it would do under water — plus the route card with the two corners and the doorway marked, and a find-rate log that tracks which fault type keeps getting missed.
packs.removes_prep: The drill says 'the firefighter deliberately builds ten faults into the lay' and leaves them to invent ten. Someone building their own faults builds the ones they know how to find, which inverts the drill: the faults that matter are the ones the builder would not have thought of, and a solo firefighter cannot hide a fault from themselves without a list.

components.label: Route card
components.instructions: Chalk the route before laying any hose. Two ninety-degree corners and one doorway, as the drill specifies. Mark the corner apexes and the door jambs so the same route is repeatable session to session and the times compare.

items.text: Route layout
fields: Total route length chalked
Distance to first corner
Distance between the corners
Doorway position along the route
Supply anchor — hydrant to be inspected but NOT charged, or fixed object
items.teaching_focus: Dry drill. The hydrant is inspected, never charged — the whole value is finding the fault before water is in the line.

items.text: Padding available
fields: Hose roller, salvage cover, or spare section at the corners (Y/N)
Which corner is padded and which deliberately is not
items.teaching_focus: Leaving one corner unpadded on purpose so the drill shows what padding is actually for.

components.label: Ten-fault build list
components.instructions: Build all ten into the 200 ft lay before the timed rep, in whatever positions the route allows. Cover the sheet, then hunt. Faults are listed easiest to hardest to find on purpose — if the last three are found as fast as the first three, the lay was too short or the faults were built too obviously.

items.text: FAULT 1 — A full hard kink at the midpoint of a straight run, hose doubled sharply back on itself.
items.answer: Under water: severe flow restriction at the nozzle, and the kink may not self-clear when charged. Easiest fault in the list; it is there to confirm the hunt method works.
items.teaching_focus: The obvious one, and the calibration for the rest.

items.text: FAULT 2 — A twist of a full turn in a length, so the coupling faces the wrong way.
items.answer: Under water: the line rolls and walks when charged, and the coupling ends up under the hose where it cannot be reached.
items.teaching_focus: Reading coupling orientation as information.

items.text: FAULT 3 — A length crossed over itself at the doorway so hose lies on hose in the jamb.
items.answer: Under water: the crossing pinches, and closing the door on it makes the pinch permanent.
items.teaching_focus: The doorway as a fault location rather than just a passage.

items.text: FAULT 4 — A hard bend taken at the unpadded corner with the hose against the corner edge.
items.answer: Under water: friction loss at the corner plus abrasion on the jacket. Shows exactly what the roller is for.
items.teaching_focus: Comparing the padded and unpadded corner directly.

items.text: FAULT 5 — A coupling left hand-loose rather than seated.
items.answer: Under water: a leak or a separation. The tell is tactile, not visual, so this fault teaches the hand-check habit.
items.teaching_focus: The first fault that cannot be found by eye.

items.text: FAULT 6 — A soft, wide S-bend across ten feet of the run — no sharp angle anywhere.
items.answer: Under water: mostly harmless, and that is the lesson. Not every deviation is a fault, and a firefighter who reports this one as a kink is over-calling.
items.teaching_focus: Deliberate false positive. Judgment, not pattern-matching.

items.text: FAULT 7 — Hose trapped under the edge of a salvage cover or a mat.
items.answer: Under water: a pinch that appears only when the line is charged and moved, so it is invisible on a dry walk unless the firefighter lifts what the hose runs under.
items.teaching_focus: Looking under things, which nobody does on a fast walk.

items.text: FAULT 8 — A length reversed in the lay, so two male ends or two female ends meet.
items.answer: Under water: nothing, because it never got charged — the lay cannot be completed. The fault is found by the connection failing, and it points straight back at ENG-012.
items.teaching_focus: A fault that is a build error rather than a route error.

items.text: FAULT 9 — A kink held open by the hose's own stiffness, so it looks like a bend and behaves like a kink.
items.answer: Under water: partial restriction that a visual check passes. Found only by running a hand along and feeling the wall of the hose fold.
items.teaching_focus: The hardest visual fault. This is the one that justifies hands on hose.

items.text: FAULT 10 — Nothing. One section of the route is deliberately clean.
items.answer: The firefighter must be willing to declare a section clear. A hunt that finds a fault in every section is not a hunt, it is an expectation.
items.teaching_focus: Clearing a section is a positive finding, and saying so takes more confidence than finding a kink.

components.label: Find-rate log
components.instructions: One row per session. Log which faults were found, in what order, and how long each took. Over a few sessions the pattern in the misses is the useful output — almost always the tactile faults, five, seven, and nine.

items.text: Session row
fields: Total time for the hunt
Faults found, by number
Faults missed, by number
Any section wrongly declared faulty
Fault I found last, and why

items.text: Pattern after three sessions
fields: Fault type I consistently miss — visual, tactile, coupling, or under-something
One change to how I run the hunt
Am I running a hand along the hose or only walking beside it
items.teaching_focus: The last question answers itself for most people, and the answer is the drill's whole point.

sources: Self-authored fault list, route card, and find-rate log

packs.title: Air Monitoring Card Set — 10 Readings and a Bump-Test Log
packs.summary: Ten reading-interpretation cards that give a meter display and ask what it means and what you do, plus the bump-test and calibration log the drill assumes exists and the sweep-pattern sheet. Every action threshold is blank — those belong to your meter and your policy.
packs.removes_prep: The drill needs scenario cards and supplies none, and interpreting a four-gas display is a lookup skill nobody can practice without a set of readings to interpret. Making up readings at the bench produces the obvious ones and never the combinations that matter.
packs.local_fill_note: NO ACTION THRESHOLDS ARE SUPPLIED. Your meter's alarm setpoints and your department's action levels are the only correct answers, and they differ by instrument and by jurisdiction. Fill them on the sheet first from your meter manual and your policy; the cards are unscoreable without them.

components.label: Our meter, our thresholds — fill first
components.instructions: Copy from the meter manual and your department's air-monitoring policy. If your department has no written action levels, that is the finding of this drill and it goes to your training officer rather than into a guess.

items.text: Instrument
fields: Make and model
Sensors fitted and their order on the display
Sensor response times
Date of last calibration and who did it

items.text: Our action levels
fields: Oxygen: our low and high action levels
Combustible gas: our action levels as a percentage of LEL
Carbon monoxide: our action levels
Hydrogen sulphide: our action levels
Policy document and date
items.teaching_focus: Five rows. A crew that cannot fill them is carrying an instrument they cannot act on.

items.text: Sensor limits we must remember
fields: What our combustible sensor does in a low-oxygen atmosphere
What it does NOT detect at all
What over-exposure or sensor poisoning does to our sensors, and how we would know
Which readings we cannot trust after a high-range exposure, and what we do about it
Do we have a PID, and what it does and does not detect
items.teaching_focus: Over-exposure and poisoning need explicit training: a damaged sensor reads plausibly and wrongly.

components.label: Reading interpretation cards
components.instructions: One card at a time. The member reads the display aloud, states what it means, states what they do, and states what they would check next. Score against your own threshold sheet, not against the card notes.

items.text: Oxygen reading NORMAL. Combustible gas reading zero. CO zero. H2S zero. You are at the doorway of a below-grade space with a reported odour.
items.answer: Clean at the doorway means clean at the doorway. It says nothing about the bottom of the space, where a heavier-than-air product would be. Correct answer monitors as you descend, in stages, and never treats an entry reading as a space reading.
items.teaching_focus: One reading is one point in space. This is the most consequential idea in the deck.

items.text: Oxygen reads 0.2 points below the meter's clean-air baseline (for example 20.7 after a 20.9 parking-lot bump). Everything else zero. Nothing is alarming.
items.answer: A significant finding, and the monitor will not tell you so. Confirm this meter's clean-air baseline first — parking lot, after a pass bump. A bay meter often reads 20.7 to 20.9 on clean air; treating any change from a printed 20.9 trains false alarms. A real drop of roughly 0.2 points from THAT baseline implies something on the order of 10,000 ppm of another gas displacing it — and if that gas is one the sensors are not fitted for, this deflection is the ONLY evidence you will get. Correct answer treats a real drop from the confirmed baseline as information, states it out loud, and does not wait for an alarm.
items.teaching_focus: Reading the meter rather than waiting for it to shout. Some materials only become visible as an oxygen deficit.

items.text: Oxygen reading LOW. Everything else zero.
items.answer: Something has displaced or consumed the oxygen, and the meter cannot tell you what. A displacing gas may be undetectable by the sensors fitted. Correct answer does not enter, and treats low oxygen as evidence of an unknown rather than as the whole problem.
items.teaching_focus: Low oxygen is a symptom. The cause may be invisible to the instrument.

items.text: Combustible gas reading rising steadily as you approach. Oxygen normal.
items.answer: A source, and you are getting closer to it. EXIT IMMEDIATELY once your action level is reached — nobody should ever be reporting back that there is 47% of the LEL in the basement. Retreat to a falling reading, isolate from there, and report the TREND rather than a single number. Two cautions: without the right correction factor a gas other than methane can read inaccurately on the LEL sensor, and 10% where you are standing can be far higher a few feet away or in another part of the structure.
items.teaching_focus: Reporting a trend, and leaving at the action level rather than exploring past it.

items.text: Combustible gas reading high, and oxygen reading LOW.
items.answer: MOST LEL sensors need oxygen to read correctly — catalytic bead and MPS both do — so in a low-oxygen atmosphere the combustible reading may be far below the true concentration. Treat the number as a MINIMUM, not a measurement, and withdraw. Verify which sensor technology YOUR monitor uses; the threshold sheet has a row for it.
items.teaching_focus: The combination that makes the instrument lie in the dangerous direction.

items.text: CO reading elevated. Everything else normal. Residential, no fire, occupants complaining of headache.
items.answer: A CO investigation. Correct answer evacuates on the basis of the reading and the symptoms, ventilates, and hunts the source — an appliance, a vehicle, a blocked flue — rather than ventilating and leaving.
items.teaching_focus: Fixing the reading is not fixing the problem.

items.text: H2S reading present, low. Below-grade utility space.
items.answer: Any H2S is significant given how quickly it disables the sense of smell and how heavy it is. Correct answer treats the space as prohibited to entry at operations level and monitors from outside.
items.teaching_focus: A material where 'low' and 'safe' are unrelated.

items.text: All readings normal, and a member reports they can smell something strongly.
items.answer: The nose has detected something the sensors are not fitted for. Correct answer believes the nose over the instrument for the existence of a product, does not enter, and escalates for identification.
items.teaching_focus: A four-gas meter measures four things. The world contains more.

items.text: Readings fluctuating rapidly between clean and alarm as you move a few feet.
items.answer: Stratification or an intermittent source. Correct answer maps it rather than averaging it: monitor high, mid and low, and at several points, and report the worst reading and where it was.
items.teaching_focus: Report the worst, with its location. An average is a fiction.

items.text: Meter alarms immediately on power-up, outdoors, in clean air.
items.answer: A fault, a sensor at end of life, or a failed self-test — not a hazard. Correct answer takes the instrument out of service and gets another, rather than acknowledging the alarm and carrying on.
items.teaching_focus: The instrument as something that can itself be wrong.

items.text: You have no bump-test record for this meter for the last week.
items.answer: The readings are unverified and the correct answer says so out loud before anyone acts on them. Bump testing is what makes a number evidence.
items.teaching_focus: The card that connects the deck to the log below.

items.text: PID reading present, four-gas clean. (Disregard this card if your monitor has no PID.)
items.answer: A PID detects volatile organics the four-gas sensors are blind to, so a PID reading with an otherwise clean meter means a product is present that the rest of the instrument cannot see. It does not identify the product and it responds differently to different compounds — the reading is a flag to escalate identification, not a measurement to act on numerically.
items.teaching_focus: The instrument that finds what the four-gas misses, and the limits of what its number means.

components.label: Bump-test log and sweep pattern
components.instructions: The log is a habit, not paperwork: an untested meter produces numbers nobody should act on. The sweep pattern is the physical half of the drill.

items.text: Bump-test log row
fields: Date and member
Gas used and concentration
Each sensor's response — pass or fail
Response time observed
Action taken on a fail

items.text: Sweep pattern
fields: Approach direction — upwind and upgrade confirmed
Monitor held high, mid, low at each stop (Y/N)
Stop interval
Where the worst reading was, in the space
Reading reported as a trend and a location (Y/N)
items.teaching_focus: High, mid, low at every stop. Gases stratify and a single height misses them.

sources: Self-authored reading cards, log and sweep sheet
Instrument manufacturer manual and department air-monitoring policy (user-supplied and authoritative; no thresholds supplied here)

packs.title: First-Due Hazmat Stations — 6 Scenarios and a Scoring Sheet
packs.summary: Six read-aloud station scenarios built out from the four the drill names — overturned cargo tank, marked railcar, mixed-placard box truck, unknown odour at a business, plus an IBC in a warehouse and a cylinder in a basement — each with what a correct isolate-deny-identify sequence contains, and a scoring sheet that marks the sequence rather than the guesses.
packs.removes_prep: The drill's setup names four scenario stations and its equipment list asks for a 'Placard/container photo deck or props', and supplies neither. A facilitator improvising stations produces the recognisable ones and never the awkward cases — the unknown odour with no placard at all, or the single cylinder that outranks the building it is in.
packs.local_fill_note: Isolation distances, your operations-level scope of practice, and who you call for technician response are all local. Write your department's hazmat response policy and your mutual-aid technician contact on the scoring sheet before the first station, and score against those rather than against these notes.

components.label: Station scenarios
components.instructions: Facilitator reads the scenario aloud, then stops talking. The crew works the sequence out loud: recognize, isolate at a distance they can justify, deny entry, identify from a safe reference, hand off to technician response. Nothing is approached — every identification is made from the vantage the crew chooses and states. Score against YOUR scope: mission-specific competencies mean some operations-level providers are trained and authorised for tasks others are not, so the right answer is the right answer for the crew standing there.

items.text: STATION 1 — A highway cargo tank is on its side on the shoulder of a divided road. It has an oval cross-section and bottom valve piping. A four-digit orange panel is visible; a diamond placard is on the other side, facing away from you. There is a wet patch spreading downhill toward a storm drain. No fire. The driver is walking around.
items.answer: Recognize: non-pressure cargo tank, flammable or combustible liquid family, active release. Isolate upwind and upgrade at a distance justified from the ERG, and state the number. Deny entry including the driver, who is now a patient and a contamination question. Identify from the panel by binocular from the isolation line — never walk the tank for the far-side placard. The storm drain is a second incident and crews CAN dam or divert the product away from it, from a defensive position. Request technician response and state what you are NOT going to do.
items.teaching_focus: The drain. Crews fixate on the tank and let the release leave the scene — damming and diverting is defensive work they are allowed to do.

items.text: STATION 2 — A single railcar is stopped on the siding behind the industrial park. It has a circular tank with rounded ends and one raised housing centerd on top. Placards are visible on the end. Nothing appears to be leaking. Somebody called it in because it 'looked wrong'.
items.answer: Recognize: pressure tank car, liquefied gas, very large quantity, no confirmed release. Isolate at a rail-scale distance from the ERG and say why a pressure car's distance is not a highway tank's distance. Deny entry to the siding and the parallel track. Identify by binocular from distance. State explicitly that no release is confirmed and that this does not reduce the isolation until it is verified by someone qualified. Request rail-carrier contact and technician response.
items.teaching_focus: Holding a large isolation on a container that appears to be doing nothing — the discipline crews find hardest to justify to themselves.

items.text: STATION 3 — A box truck has been rear-ended at an intersection. Its rear doors are sprung and you can see stacked drums and pallets inside, several leaning. A DANGEROUS placard is on the rear. Two occupants are out of the vehicles; one is complaining of throat irritation.
items.answer: Recognize: mixed load, no single class identified, and a symptomatic patient means an actual exposure. The DANGEROUS placard gives you nothing specific, so the shipping papers in the cab become the reference — and retrieving them is a decision to be justified, not an automatic step. Isolate, deny, move the patients upwind, and treat the symptom as evidence of an airborne product. Request technician response and hazmat medical.
items.teaching_focus: A symptomatic patient is a monitor reading. It changes the isolation before any paperwork is found.

items.text: STATION 4 — An unknown odour at a small business. Employees are outside, several with headaches. There are no placards, no visible container, no obvious source. The building is a single-story commercial unit in a row. The caller says it started about twenty minutes ago.
items.answer: Recognize: an unidentified atmosphere with multiple symptomatic people and no clues. Correct sequence: account for everyone who was inside and get them treated, isolate the unit and its neighbors including either side and above, deny entry to the public, and begin identification from outside — what business is it, what do they store, who is the owner, what changed twenty minutes ago. An unknown is NOT an excuse to do nothing. Monitoring starts at the threshold or doorway, on air, with a PID if fitted where the department's scope and equipment allow it. A sweep of the occupancy is only if the crew's mission-specific competency authorises it. pH and fluorine paper are for identification from a safe position, not permission to operate in a product that turnout gear and SCBA do not protect against. Anything beyond that is technician work.
items.teaching_focus: The station with no placard, which is what most first-due crews actually get. Identification starts with questions — and an unknown is not a reason to stand still.

items.text: STATION 5 — A warehouse with a forklift puncture in one intermediate bulk container on a rack. Product is running onto the floor. There are perhaps forty similar IBCs on the same rack run. The label on the punctured one is obscured by product. Warehouse staff are still working at the far end.
items.answer: Recognize: a few hundred gallons released, a very large quantity adjacent, and an unreadable label on the one container you care about. Isolate and evacuate the warehouse — the staff at the far end are inside the problem, not observers. Deny entry. Identify from the neighboring containers' labels, the rack signage, or the facility's inventory, not from the wet one. Name the floor drains and the sprinkler system, and ask what happens if this product reaches either.
items.teaching_focus: Identifying a container from its neighbors, and treating people still working as an evacuation rather than a bystander problem.

items.text: STATION 6 — A basement mechanical room in a small apartment building. A maintenance worker reports a hissing cylinder. It is squat, wide, with a collar and several valve fittings, and the label is on the far side. One occupant of the building has been coughing. It is below grade with one interior stair.
items.answer: Recognize: liquefied gas cylinder, active release, BELOW GRADE with a single egress and an occupied structure above. In a building like this the most likely container is a CO2 dewar. The word 'basement' should reorder everything — a heavier-than-air product collects and the stair is the only way out. Isolate by evacuating the building, not just the room. Deny entry, including to the maintenance worker who wants to show you. Identify from the facility, the supplier, or the worker's description — not by going down to read the far side of the label.
items.teaching_focus: The smallest container on the deck creating the most dangerous geometry. Below grade plus one egress plus occupied above.

components.label: Station props — placard and container specs
components.instructions: Print or display one per station as the crew's identification target, and place it at a genuine distance so the binocular read is real. Images marked AI-GENERATED show placard geometry and container silhouettes only. For a wider deck, HZM-006's twenty specs cover placards, labels, rail cars, cargo tanks, cylinders and marine marks — this is the subset the six stations need.

items.text: Station 1 target — an orange four-digit panel, read at distance from the isolation line.
items.synthetic_prompt: Flat straight-on illustration of a rectangular orange panel with a thin black border bearing four large dark numerals, mounted on a plain metal surface. Neutral even lighting, plain background, no vehicle context, no people, no damage.
items.alt: Rectangular orange panel with a black border bearing four large numerals, mounted on a plain metal surface.
items.teaching_focus: The specific-material clue, read from where the crew chose to stand.

items.text: Station 1 context — non-pressure cargo tank silhouette, for the container call.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical side-elevation line illustration of a highway cargo tank trailer with an oval cross-section tank, flat top with several small dome covers along the centerline, bottom-mounted valve piping midway along the underside, and a top rollover rail. Plain white background, thin dark lines, engineering-drawing style, no lettering, no placards, no damage, no context.
items.alt: Technical side-elevation drawing of an oval-cross-section highway cargo tank trailer with top dome covers, bottom valve piping and a rollover rail.
items.teaching_focus: Naming the container family from silhouette alone, which is all a crew at distance has.

items.text: Station 2 target — pressure rail tank car silhouette.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical side-elevation line illustration of a railroad tank car with a long circular tank, rounded ends, a single raised protective housing centerd on top, no other visible external fittings, resting on two rail trucks with wheels. Plain white background, thin dark lines, engineering-drawing style, no lettering, no placards, no damage, no context.
items.alt: Technical side-elevation drawing of a railroad tank car with one raised top housing and no other visible fittings, on two rail trucks.
items.teaching_focus: One housing means pressure means a rail-scale isolation.

items.text: Station 3 target — the DANGEROUS placard.
items.synthetic_prompt: Flat straight-on illustration of a standard diamond-shaped DOT hazard placard, upper half red and lower half white with a red lower band, bearing the word DANGEROUS in dark capital letters across the middle, no symbol and no class numeral. Neutral even lighting, plain background, no vehicle context, no people, no damage.
items.alt: Diamond hazard placard with red and white bands bearing the word DANGEROUS in capital letters, with no symbol or class number.
items.teaching_focus: The placard that sends the crew to the paperwork and makes retrieving it a decision.

items.text: Station 5 target — intermediate bulk container in a steel cage.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical illustration of a cubic intermediate bulk container: a translucent plastic inner vessel enclosed in a welded tubular steel cage on an integral pallet base, with a large screw cap on top and a discharge valve at the bottom front. Plain white background, thin dark lines, engineering-drawing style, no lettering, no placards, no damage, no context.
items.alt: Technical drawing of a cubic intermediate bulk container with a plastic vessel in a welded steel cage on a pallet, with a top screw cap and bottom discharge valve.
items.teaching_focus: Forty of these on one rack run is the quantity that matters, not the one that is leaking.

items.text: Station 6 target — liquefied gas cylinder, squat with a collar.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical illustration of a squat wide industrial liquefied gas cylinder standing upright, roughly as wide as it is tall, with a raised protective collar around the top and two or three valve fittings visible inside the collar, plain unmarked body. Plain white background, thin dark lines, engineering-drawing style, no lettering, no placards, no damage, no context.
items.alt: Technical drawing of a squat wide upright liquefied gas cylinder with a raised protective collar and two or three valve fittings inside it.
items.teaching_focus: Collar and multiple valves means liquid and vapour, in a basement.

components.label: Isolate–deny–identify scoring sheet
components.instructions: One sheet per station. Score the SEQUENCE, not whether the crew guessed the material. A crew that named the product but walked to the tank to do it has failed the station; a crew that never identified it but held a defensible line and called for technicians has passed.

items.text: My department's frame — fill this before the first station
fields: Our operations-level scope: what we are and are not authorised to do
Our mission-specific competencies — tasks WE may do that other ops providers may not
Detection we carry: four-gas, PID, pH paper, fluorine paper
Who provides technician response and how long they take
Our hazmat response policy reference
ERG edition on the apparatus
items.teaching_focus: Mission-specific competencies are the row that decides what 'correct' means for your crew at every station.

items.text: Station score
fields: Station number
RECOGNIZE — hazmat problem named before anyone moved (Y/N)
ISOLATE — distance stated as a number with a source (Y/N)
ISOLATE — position upwind AND upgrade (Y/N)
DENY — who was kept out, including drivers, staff and the person who wants to show you (Y/N)
IDENTIFY — done from a safe reference, no approach (Y/N)
HANDOFF — technician response requested with what they need (Y/N)
items.teaching_focus: The identify row is the one that fails most often, and it fails by the crew getting the answer the wrong way.

items.text: The honest question
fields: Did anyone move toward the container to get information
If yes: what would have told them the same thing from where they were
Was there a line-of-sight rescue available, and did we correctly identify it as such
Did the crew state anything they were NOT going to do
One correction for the next station
items.teaching_focus: Naming the limit out loud is an operations-level skill. A crew that never says what it will not do has not set a boundary.

sources: Self-authored station scenarios, image specifications, and scoring sheet
DOT/PHMSA Emergency Response Guidebook (public domain; the user's current edition supplies every distance — none are reproduced here)
Department hazmat response policy and operations-level scope (user-supplied and authoritative)
packs.synthetic_caveat: The station props are AI-generated illustrations of standardized placard designs and container silhouettes, for recognition of shape, color, symbol and class numeral only. They are not photographs of real shipments and depict no damage or release; nothing about a real incident should be inferred from them, and they assert no ERG guide number or isolation distance.

packs.title: Leak Control Kit Card & Patch Decision Sheet
packs.summary: A kit inventory card the technician fills from the actual kit on the apparatus, a patch-selection decision sheet keyed to breach type and container, and six dry practice scenarios. Technician-level: it structures the decision, it does not authorise the work.
packs.removes_prep: The drill names scenarios and supplies none, and a technician-level leak-control evolution needs an inventoried kit and a written selection logic before anyone touches a patch — otherwise the practice is whatever the most confident member reaches for.
packs.local_fill_note: This is technician-level work governed entirely by your team's SOPs, your kit, and your training authority. This pack supplies structure only: no procedure, no authorisation, and no product-specific guidance. If your team does not train and authorise this work, the pack is a reading exercise and nothing more.

components.label: Kit inventory card
components.instructions: Fill from the actual kit, physically, item by item. Do it as a two-person check. Most teams discover something missing, expired, or wrong-sized on the first pass — that is the point of doing it before a scenario rather than during one.

items.text: Kit contents
fields: Item
Quantity present
Size or rating
Condition and expiry
Where it sits in the kit
Which kit is this — chlorine-specific, Midland-type, or other
Compatible with the products we actually plan for (Y/N)
items.teaching_focus: The last column is the one that catches a kit assembled for somebody else's district.

items.text: Gaps found
fields: Missing or expired items
Sizes we do not carry but would need
Who orders the replacement and by when
Date of this inventory and the two members who did it

components.label: Patch selection decision sheet
components.instructions: Work top to bottom before touching anything. The sheet exists to make the reasoning explicit and reviewable; it is not a procedure and it does not replace your team's SOP or your training.

items.text: STEP 1 — Should this be patched at all?
fields: Product identified and its properties known (Y/N)
Is offensive leak control within our authorisation for this product (Y/N)
Can the leak be controlled by remote means instead — valve, rotation, containment
The reason we are choosing hands-on over remote
items.teaching_focus: The first question is whether to approach at all, and the honest answer is often no.

items.text: STEP 2 — The breach
fields: Container type and its pressure state
Breach location: liquid space, vapour space, valve, fitting, seam
Breach type: puncture, split, gouge, gasket, thread
Approximate size
Is the metal sound around it (Y/N)

items.text: STEP 3 — Selection
fields: Device chosen from the kit
Why this rather than the alternatives
Rated for the pressure present (Y/N)
Chemically compatible with the product (Y/N)
What we do if it does not hold
items.teaching_focus: The fallback is chosen before the attempt, not after.

items.text: STEP 4 — Before entry
fields: Backup team in place and briefed
Decon corridor established
Air time available versus estimated task time
Abort trigger, stated
items.teaching_focus: Task time versus air time. Technicians routinely underestimate a patch under a suit.

components.label: Six dry practice scenarios
components.instructions: Dry practice on props only, with no product, at whatever level your team is authorised and trained for. Each scenario is a decision exercise first: the crew completes the selection sheet before anyone picks up a device.

items.text: Small puncture in the liquid space of a non-pressure drum, product identified, sound metal around the breach.
items.answer: The straightforward case, present to establish the sheet's rhythm. Expect a plug or patch selection with a clear rationale and a stated fallback.
items.teaching_focus: Baseline. If the sheet is not filled here it will not be filled under pressure.

items.text: Split along a seam of a non-pressure container, product identified.
items.answer: A seam is a different problem from a puncture: it may extend under load, and the metal either side may not be sound. Listening for a recognition that patching may worsen it and that containment or transfer might be the better answer.
items.teaching_focus: Knowing when a patch is the wrong tool.

items.text: Weeping gasket at a fitting on a pressurised container.
items.answer: Pressure changes everything about approach and about what a patch can do. Listening for remote options first — closing a valve, rotating the container — and for a stated pressure rating on anything selected.
items.teaching_focus: Pressure as a reason to prefer the remote option.

items.text: Damaged valve on a cylinder of a product with a large green-bordered isolation distance.
items.answer: Very likely a no-approach decision, or a decision to move to isolation and specialist resources. Listening for the crew declining the task with a defensible reason.
items.teaching_focus: The scenario where the correct technical answer is to not do the technique.

items.text: Puncture in the vapour space above the liquid level, product identified, small release.
items.answer: Vapour-space breach behaves differently: rate depends on pressure and temperature, and the release may worsen as the day warms. Listening for a time dimension in the plan.
items.teaching_focus: A release that changes with the weather.

items.text: Any of the above, and your air time is shorter than your estimated task time.
items.answer: The task does not start. Listening for the abort trigger being honoured rather than negotiated, and for a plan that gets the same outcome in two shorter entries or by remote means.
items.teaching_focus: The card that exists because this is how technicians get hurt.

items.text: Chlorine cylinder or one-ton container with a leaking valve, and your team carries a chlorine kit. Work the selection sheet before anyone opens the case.
items.answer: The kit exists for exactly this, and the sheet still comes first: product identified, authorisation confirmed, remote options considered, device selected for THIS container type, fallback named, and task time checked against air time. Note which kit you actually have — a chlorine kit fits chlorine containers, while a Midland-type kit covers a wider range of products and fewer teams carry one. Applying a kit you have not inventoried is how a team discovers a missing component with the leak running.
items.teaching_focus: The scenario the drill is named for, run through the same discipline as every other — and an honest look at which kit is on the rig.

sources: Self-authored inventory card, decision sheet and practice scenarios
Team hazmat technician SOPs, kit documentation and training authority (user-supplied and authoritative; no procedure or authorisation supplied here)

packs.title: Product Behavior Tabletop — 12 Behavior Cards
packs.summary: Twelve cards each naming a physical or chemical property, what it looks like on a real incident, and the tactical consequence — vapour density, water reactivity, boiling point, polymerisation, corrosivity, oxidising potential. Plus the property-lookup frame the crew fills from their own references.
packs.removes_prep: The drill is a tabletop about chemistry that kills, and it names scenario cards it does not supply. Writing them requires knowing which properties actually change tactics — which is the knowledge the drill is meant to build, so a crew cannot bootstrap it.
packs.local_fill_note: Specific values for specific materials come from your ERG, your SDS, or CHEMTREC — not from this pack. The cards teach what a property MEANS; the numbers for the material in front of you are always a lookup.

components.label: Behavior cards
components.instructions: Tabletop. Draw a card, and the crew answers three questions out loud: what would we see, what does it do to our position, and what tactic does it rule out. Then apply it to a material that actually travels through your district.

items.text: VAPOUR DENSITY HEAVIER THAN AIR
items.answer: Looks like: nothing, usually — it collects low, in basements, trenches, storm drains and ditches, and travels downhill and downwind. Consequence: your position must be upgrade as well as upwind, and low points inside the isolation are occupied space you cannot see into. If the product is also flammable it can collect until it reaches its LEL down there. Rules out staging in a hollow because it is out of the wind.
items.teaching_focus: The property that makes 'upwind' insufficient on its own.

items.text: VAPOUR DENSITY LIGHTER THAN AIR
items.answer: Looks like: rapid rise and dispersion outdoors; accumulation at ceiling level and in attics indoors. Consequence: outdoors is more forgiving, indoors is worse, and the hazard is above you. Rules out: assuming a cleared floor means a cleared room.
items.teaching_focus: The mirror-image error to the previous card.

items.text: WATER REACTIVE
items.answer: Looks like: violent reaction, heat, gas generation, sometimes fire, when the instinctive tactic is applied. Consequence: the hoseline is a weapon against you, and rain or a wet floor is part of the problem. Rules out applying water to the SPILL, including for cooling, without identification. Patient decon follows your medical protocol.
