items.teaching_focus: The card where the fire service's default tool is the hazard.

items.text: BOILING POINT BELOW AMBIENT TEMPERATURE
items.answer: Looks like: a liquid that is boiling in the container at ordinary temperature, held liquid only by pressure. Consequence: any breach produces enormous rapid vapour expansion, and fire impingement is a container-failure question. Rules out: treating a pressurised liquid release as a spill.
items.teaching_focus: Why a round tank is a different problem from an oval one.

items.text: POLYMERISATION / UNSTABLE
items.answer: Looks like: a container getting warm with no external fire, possibly swelling. Consequence: the reaction is self-accelerating. RECOGNIZE IT HAVING STARTED — a thermal imager or a heat gun on the container is how you tell — and the action once it has is EVACUATE. Cooling may or may not arrest it and is not a reason to stay.
items.teaching_focus: Recognising that polymerisation has begun, and that the response is evacuation rather than intervention.

items.text: CORROSIVE
items.answer: Looks like: fuming, etched surfaces, damaged vegetation, injured skin. Consequence: structural PPE is not chemical protection, and runoff is a downstream problem. Rules out: any hands-on work in turnout gear.

items.text: OXIDISER
items.answer: Looks like: fire that will not smother and reignites, burning faster than the visible fuel should allow. Consequence: it supplies its own oxygen. TYPICALLY rules out smothering, foam blanketing and any tactic based on excluding air — large volumes of water are sometimes the correct answer, so identify the product before committing to a tactic.

items.text: FLASH POINT BELOW AMBIENT
items.answer: Looks like: an ordinary-seeming liquid spill that is producing an ignitable vapour cloud right now. Consequence: ignition-source control across the whole vapour travel path, not just at the spill. Rules out: apparatus positioning downwind or downgrade of the spill.

items.text: TOXIC BY INHALATION (TIH)
items.answer: Looks like: often nothing visible at all, with casualties appearing at distance. Consequence: the isolation distance is a green-bordered table distance, which is far larger than firefighters expect. Rules out: any approach to identify by sight.
items.teaching_focus: Ties directly to HZM-007's Table 1 work.

items.text: RADIOACTIVE
items.answer: Looks like: nothing at all — no smell, no cloud, no symptoms at the scene. Consequence: time, distance and shielding are the whole of your protection, and none of them is visible feedback. Rules out closing distance to identify, and rules out any assumption that an absence of signs means an absence of exposure. This is an isolate, monitor with the right instrument, and request specialist resources problem.
items.teaching_focus: The hazard with no sensory signature. Nothing else in the deck is invisible in this way.

items.text: DELAYED HEALTH EFFECT
items.answer: Looks like: patients who feel fine and deteriorate hours later. Consequence: everyone exposed goes to medical evaluation whether or not they are symptomatic, including your own members. Rules out: releasing an asymptomatic patient or member.
items.teaching_focus: The property whose consequence is administrative and gets skipped.

items.text: CRYOGENIC
items.answer: Looks like: heavy visible vapour cloud, frost on the container, embrittled surroundings. Consequence: cold injury, oxygen displacement, and an enormous expansion ratio on release. STRUCTURAL TURNOUT GEAR DOES NOT PROVIDE ADEQUATE THERMAL PROTECTION against cryogenic contact. Rules out contact with any part of the release, and standing in the visible cloud.

items.text: THE LOCAL CARD — a material that actually travels through your district
fields: Material name and where it comes from or goes
Its vapour density, boiling point and flash point, from a reference you name
Which two cards in this deck apply to it
What that rules out for us, at that location
items.teaching_focus: Twelve properties are academic until one of them is on a truck on your road.

components.label: Property lookup frame
components.instructions: One row per material the crew studies. The point is the habit of looking properties up and converting each one into a tactical consequence, rather than memorising materials.

items.text: Material row
fields: Material and UN/ID number
Reference used and its date
Vapour density — and so
Boiling point — and so
Flash point — and so
Special hazard: water reactive, oxidiser, TIH, other — and so
items.teaching_focus: The 'and so' in each row is the drill. A property with no consequence written next to it has not been learned.

sources: Self-authored behavior cards and lookup frame
NIOSH Pocket Guide to Chemical Hazards (public domain; user-supplied)
DOT/PHMSA Emergency Response Guidebook, safety data sheets, and CHEMTREC (user-supplied; no material-specific values reproduced here)

packs.title: Placard & Container Deck — 20 ID Specs and an ERG Key Frame
packs.summary: Twenty placard, label and container image specs spanning cargo tank silhouettes, rail cars, cylinders, marine placards and four-digit panels, each with the visual identification a correct answer contains — plus the self-scoring answer-key frame, with every ERG figure left blank because those belong to the edition in your hand.
packs.removes_prep: The drill's equipment list asks for a 'Self-built shuffled deck of 20-40 placard, label, and container photos' AND a 'printed or app placard/container reference (answer key you build while assembling the deck)'. Assembling forty photos and writing forty answers is a whole shift's work before the first 60-second rep.
packs.local_fill_note: This pack asserts what each image DEPICTS — placard class, panel, container silhouette. It supplies no UN/ID numbers, no ERG guide numbers and no distances. Those come from the current ERG in your hand: editions differ, and a guide number carried over from an old edition is the kind of error this drill exists to prevent. Write them on the key frame yourself.

components.label: Placard, label and container specs
components.instructions: Twenty cards. Prop one at the far end of a hallway or driveway so several reps force a binocular read at distance. Shuffle face down. Per card: name the clue out loud, then open the ERG to the correct orange-bordered guide inside 60 seconds. Eight of ten is the standard. Container answers give the common MC/DOT designation as well as the silhouette — on scene the shape is what matters, but the designations appear on hazmat examinations. Images marked AI-GENERATED show placard geometry and container silhouettes only.

items.text: Class 3 flammable liquid placard with a four-digit panel below it — name the class, the panel type, and what the four digits are for.
items.synthetic_prompt: Flat straight-on illustration of a standard diamond-shaped DOT hazard placard, red background, white flame symbol in the upper area, numeral 3 at the bottom point, mounted on a plain metal panel with a separate rectangular orange panel below it bearing four dark numerals. Neutral even lighting, plain background, no vehicle context, no people, no damage.
items.alt: Red diamond hazard placard with a white flame symbol and the numeral 3, above a rectangular orange panel bearing four numerals.
items.answer: Class 3, flammable liquid, identified by the red field and flame. The orange rectangular panel carries the four-digit UN/ID number, which is the specific-material lookup — the placard alone gives only the hazard class.
items.teaching_focus: Class versus specific material. The panel is what narrows an ERG lookup from a whole class to one guide.

items.text: Class 2 non-flammable gas placard — name the class and state what the color alone does and does not tell you.
items.synthetic_prompt: Flat straight-on illustration of a standard diamond-shaped DOT hazard placard with a green background, a white gas cylinder symbol in the upper area, and the numeral 2 at the bottom point. Neutral even lighting, plain background, no vehicle context, no people.
items.alt: Green diamond hazard placard with a white gas cylinder symbol and the numeral 2.
items.answer: Class 2.2 non-flammable gas. The green field and cylinder identify the division, not the material — a non-flammable gas can still be an asphyxiant, a cryogen, or acutely toxic. This is the placard ANHYDROUS AMMONIA actually travels under, which is the clearest possible proof that 'non-flammable' does not mean 'not dangerous'.
items.teaching_focus: Ammonia is placarded 2.2. That single fact does more to kill the 'green means fine' reflex than any explanation.

items.text: Class 2 flammable gas placard — name it, and state what changes about your approach versus the previous card.
items.synthetic_prompt: Flat straight-on illustration of a standard diamond-shaped DOT hazard placard with a red background, a white flame symbol in the upper area, and the numeral 2 at the bottom point. Neutral even lighting, plain background, no vehicle context, no people.
items.alt: Red diamond hazard placard with a white flame symbol and the numeral 2.
items.answer: Class 2 flammable gas. Red plus a 2 rather than a 3 means a compressed or liquefied flammable gas, so vapour behavior, BLEVE potential and ignition-source control all enter the size-up.
items.teaching_focus: Reading the numeral, not just the color. Red appears on two very different classes.

items.text: Class 2 poison / toxic gas placard — name it and state why it outranks almost everything else on a mixed load.
items.synthetic_prompt: Flat straight-on illustration of a standard diamond-shaped DOT hazard placard with a white background, a black skull-and-crossbones symbol in the upper area, and the numeral 2 at the bottom point. Neutral even lighting, plain background, no vehicle context, no people.
items.alt: White diamond hazard placard with a black skull-and-crossbones symbol and the numeral 2.
items.answer: Class 2.3 toxic gas. Skull and crossbones with a 2 is a toxic-inhalation-hazard gas, and it belongs in the ERG's green-bordered table. It does NOT automatically carry the largest isolation distance on a scene — some explosives distances are larger — so read the guide rather than ranking placards by memory.
items.teaching_focus: A placard that should change where the apparatus stops. Look the distance up; do not rank hazards by instinct.

items.text: Class 8 corrosive placard — name it and state what it means for PPE and for runoff.
items.synthetic_prompt: Flat straight-on illustration of a standard diamond-shaped DOT hazard placard, upper half white and lower half black, with a black symbol of liquid dripping from two test tubes onto a hand and a surface in the upper half, and the numeral 8 at the bottom point. Neutral even lighting, plain background, no vehicle context, no people.
items.alt: Diamond hazard placard with a white upper half and black lower half, showing liquid dripping from two test tubes onto a hand and a surface, with the numeral 8.
items.answer: Class 8 corrosive. Structural PPE is not chemical protection, and the runoff is a downstream and drainage problem as much as a scene problem.
items.teaching_focus: Recognising a class where turnout gear gives a false sense of protection.

items.text: Class 5.1 oxidizer placard — name it and state what it does to a fire you might otherwise treat as ordinary.
items.synthetic_prompt: Flat straight-on illustration of a standard diamond-shaped DOT hazard placard with a yellow background, a black circle with flames above it in the upper area, and the numerals 5.1 at the bottom point. Neutral even lighting, plain background, no vehicle context, no people.
items.alt: Yellow diamond hazard placard with a black flaming circle symbol and the numerals 5.1.
items.answer: Class 5.1 oxidizer. It supplies its own oxygen, so it accelerates combustion, can reignite, and defeats smothering tactics.
items.teaching_focus: The class that invalidates a tactic rather than adding a hazard.

items.text: Class 1 explosives placard with a division and compatibility group — name what the two characters after the 1 are.
items.synthetic_prompt: Flat straight-on illustration of a standard diamond-shaped DOT hazard placard with an orange background, a black exploding-bomb symbol in the upper area, a division numeral and a single capital letter in the middle area, and the numeral 1 at the bottom point. Neutral even lighting, plain background, no vehicle context, no people.
items.alt: Orange diamond hazard placard with a black exploding-bomb symbol, a division number and a capital letter, and the numeral 1.
items.answer: Class 1 explosives. The numeral after the class is the division and the capital letter is the compatibility group — both change the ERG guide and the isolation, so 'explosives' alone is not an identification.
items.teaching_focus: A class where reading only the word loses the information that matters.

items.text: Class 7 radioactive placard — name it and state the one action that precedes all others.
items.synthetic_prompt: Flat straight-on illustration of a standard diamond-shaped DOT hazard placard with a yellow upper half and white lower half, a black three-bladed trefoil symbol in the upper area, the word area below it, and the numeral 7 at the bottom point. Neutral even lighting, plain background, no vehicle context, no people.
items.alt: Diamond hazard placard with a yellow upper half and white lower half, a black three-bladed trefoil symbol, and the numeral 7.
items.answer: Class 7 radioactive. Time, distance and shielding, and a request for the resources your department does not carry — this is an isolate-and-wait placard at operations level.
items.teaching_focus: Knowing which placards mean your job is perimeter and nothing else.

items.text: DANGEROUS placard on a mixed load — name what it means and why it makes your job harder, not easier.
items.synthetic_prompt: Flat straight-on illustration of a standard diamond-shaped DOT hazard placard, upper half red and lower half white with a red lower band, bearing the word DANGEROUS in dark capital letters across the middle, no symbol and no class numeral. Neutral even lighting, plain background, no vehicle context, no people.
items.alt: Diamond hazard placard with red and white bands bearing the word DANGEROUS in capital letters, with no symbol or class number.
items.answer: A mixed load of two or more hazard classes in placardable quantities, with no single class identified. It tells you there is a hazmat problem and nothing about which one — the shipping papers become the primary reference, not the placard.
items.teaching_focus: The placard that forces you off the placard and onto the paperwork.

items.text: Non-pressure cargo tank silhouette (oval cross-section, bottom valves) — name the container family and the product family it usually carries.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical side-elevation line illustration of a highway cargo tank trailer with an oval cross-section tank, a flat top with several small dome covers along the centerline, visible bottom-mounted valve piping midway along the underside, and a rollover protection rail along the top edge. Plain white background, thin dark lines, engineering-drawing style, no lettering, no placards, no damage, no context.
items.alt: Technical side-elevation drawing of an oval-cross-section highway cargo tank trailer with dome covers on top, bottom valve piping, and a top rollover rail.
items.answer: A non-pressure cargo tank — the oval cross-section, multiple top domes and bottom-unloading valves are the tells. Commonly flammable and combustible liquids, typically in compartments, so a leak may involve only part of the load. Commonly designated MC-306 / DOT-406. The designation matters less on scene than reading the shape, but it appears on written hazmat examinations, so learn both.
items.teaching_focus: Compartmentation. The silhouette tells you the leak may not be the whole load.

items.text: High-pressure cargo tank silhouette (circular cross-section, rounded heads, no external frame) — name the family and what pressure changes.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical side-elevation line illustration of a highway cargo tank trailer with a uniform circular cross-section, smoothly rounded hemispherical ends, a single small protective housing on top, and no external ribs or frame. Plain white background, thin dark lines, engineering-drawing style, no lettering, no placards, no damage, no context.
items.alt: Technical side-elevation drawing of a circular-cross-section highway cargo tank trailer with rounded hemispherical ends and a single small top housing.
items.answer: A high-pressure cargo tank — round cross-section and rounded heads are the pressure tells. Liquefied compressed gases, so a release expands enormously, relief devices may operate, and fire impingement raises a container-failure question. Commonly designated MC-331. The designation matters less on scene than reading the shape, but it appears on written hazmat examinations, so learn both.
items.teaching_focus: Round means pressure means a failure mode that is not a spill.

items.text: Corrosive liquid cargo tank silhouette (small-diameter round tank with external reinforcing rings) — name the family.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical side-elevation line illustration of a highway cargo tank trailer with a relatively small-diameter circular tank, several evenly spaced external reinforcing rings around the tank body, flat ends, and top-mounted fittings in a small housing. Plain white background, thin dark lines, engineering-drawing style, no lettering, no placards, no damage, no context.
items.alt: Technical side-elevation drawing of a small-diameter round highway cargo tank with external reinforcing rings and top-mounted fittings.
items.answer: A corrosive liquid cargo tank — small diameter for a dense product, external rings, and top unloading. Dense product means a small tank can hold a heavy load. Commonly designated MC-312 / DOT-412. The designation matters less on scene than reading the shape, but it appears on written hazmat examinations, so learn both.
items.teaching_focus: Small container is not small quantity when the product is dense.

items.text: Dry bulk cargo tank silhouette (sloped hoppers underneath) — name the family and the hazard that is easy to underestimate.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical side-elevation line illustration of a highway dry bulk cargo trailer with a rounded tank body and two or three conical hoppers sloping down beneath it to discharge outlets, plus external piping running along the lower side. Plain white background, thin dark lines, engineering-drawing style, no lettering, no placards, no damage, no context.
items.alt: Technical side-elevation drawing of a dry bulk cargo trailer with a rounded body and conical hoppers sloping to discharge outlets underneath.
items.answer: A dry bulk carrier. Solids, often pressurised for unloading. Dust, reactivity with water, and the fact that a solid can still be a serious inhalation hazard. Commonly a pneumatic hopper / dry bulk carrier.
items.teaching_focus: Solid does not mean inert, and pneumatic unloading means pressure on a non-pressure-looking container.

items.text: Pressure rail tank car silhouette (single top housing, no visible fittings elsewhere) — name it and state the approach implication.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical side-elevation line illustration of a railroad tank car with a long circular tank, rounded ends, a single raised protective housing centerd on top, no visible external fittings elsewhere, resting on two rail trucks with wheels. Plain white background, thin dark lines, engineering-drawing style, no lettering, no placards, no damage, no context.
items.alt: Technical side-elevation drawing of a railroad tank car with a single raised protective housing on top and no other visible external fittings, on two rail trucks.
items.answer: A pressure tank car — all fittings gathered under one protective housing is the tell. Very large quantity of a liquefied gas, so the isolation distance is a rail-scale distance and approach is from upwind and upgrade only.
items.teaching_focus: One container that can exceed a whole district's water supply in consequence.

items.text: Non-pressure rail tank car silhouette (visible bottom outlet and multiple top fittings) — name it and state what the exposed fittings mean.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical side-elevation line illustration of a railroad tank car with a circular tank, a flat-topped expansion dome and several separate exposed fittings along the top, a visible bottom outlet valve beneath the center, and an external walkway along the side, resting on two rail trucks. Plain white background, thin dark lines, engineering-drawing style, no lettering, no placards, no damage, no context.
items.alt: Technical side-elevation drawing of a railroad tank car with exposed top fittings, an expansion dome, a bottom outlet valve, and a side walkway, on two rail trucks.
items.answer: A non-pressure (general service) tank car. Exposed fittings and a bottom outlet mean more points that can be damaged in a derailment and more places a release can originate.
items.teaching_focus: Counting the ways a container can leak from its silhouette.

items.text: Compressed gas cylinder, tall and slender with a valve cap — name the container and the failure mode to respect.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical illustration of a single tall slender industrial compressed gas cylinder standing upright, rounded shoulder, a threaded protective valve cap screwed on top, plain unmarked body. Plain white background, thin dark lines, engineering-drawing style, no lettering, no placards, no damage, no context.
items.alt: Technical drawing of a tall slender upright industrial compressed gas cylinder with a rounded shoulder and a threaded protective valve cap.
items.answer: A high-pressure compressed gas cylinder. Under fire impingement it can fail violently and the valve end is a projectile hazard; the cap protects the valve and its absence is itself a finding.
items.teaching_focus: The smallest container on the deck and one of the most dangerous under heat.

items.text: Liquefied gas cylinder, squat with a collar and multiple valves — name it and distinguish it from the previous card.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical illustration of a squat wide industrial liquefied gas cylinder standing upright, roughly as wide as it is tall, with a raised protective collar around the top and two or three valve fittings visible inside the collar, plain unmarked body. Plain white background, thin dark lines, engineering-drawing style, no lettering, no placards, no damage, no context.
items.alt: Technical drawing of a squat wide upright liquefied gas cylinder with a raised protective collar and two or three valve fittings inside it.
items.answer: A liquefied gas cylinder. Squat proportions and a collar with several valves rather than a single capped valve; it holds liquid and vapour, so both a liquid and a vapour release are possible from the same container.
items.teaching_focus: Two phases in one container means two different releases.

items.text: Intermediate bulk container in a steel cage on a pallet — name it and state what the cage does and does not do.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical illustration of a cubic intermediate bulk container: a translucent plastic inner vessel enclosed in a welded tubular steel cage, mounted on an integral pallet base, with a large screw cap on top and a discharge valve at the bottom front. Plain white background, thin dark lines, engineering-drawing style, no lettering, no placards, no damage, no context.
items.alt: Technical drawing of a cubic intermediate bulk container with a plastic inner vessel in a welded steel cage on a pallet, with a top screw cap and a bottom discharge valve.
items.answer: An IBC, typically several hundred gallons. The cage is handling protection, not fire or impact protection — the plastic vessel fails readily in fire, and a warehouse holds many of them together.
items.teaching_focus: The container firefighters meet most often and size up least carefully.

items.text: Marine pollutant mark — name it and state what it adds that a hazard class does not.
items.synthetic_prompt: Flat straight-on illustration of a standard marine pollutant mark: a black symbol of a dead fish and a leafless tree, with a thin black border, on a plain white background. Do not emphasise the outline shape. Neutral even lighting, plain background, no vehicle context, no people.
items.alt: Marine pollutant mark showing a black dead-fish and leafless-tree symbol with a thin black border on a white background.
items.answer: The marine pollutant mark. Identify it by the dead fish and tree symbol rather than by its outline — the official mark is a diamond but some labelling in the field shows a triangle, and arguing about the shape wastes the identification. It says nothing about acute human hazard and everything about the environmental consequence of runoff, which makes drainage and waterways part of the first-due problem.
items.teaching_focus: Identify by symbol, not outline. A mark that changes tactics without changing the health hazard.

items.text: An orange four-digit panel with no hazard diamond beside it — state what you can and cannot do with it.
items.synthetic_prompt: Flat straight-on illustration of a rectangular orange panel with a thin black border bearing four large dark numerals, mounted alone on a plain metal surface with no diamond placard nearby. Neutral even lighting, plain background, no vehicle context, no people.
items.alt: Rectangular orange panel with a thin black border bearing four large numerals, mounted alone with no hazard diamond nearby.
items.answer: A UN/ID number panel. It is the most specific clue on the deck: it identifies the material rather than the class, so it goes straight into the ERG's numerical index. Read it with binoculars from upwind and upgrade, and never move closer to read it.
items.teaching_focus: The best clue on the vehicle, and the discipline of reading it from distance.

They are not photographs of real shipments, nothing about an actual load or its condition should be inferred from them, and they assert no ERG guide number or isolation distance. packs.title: Keokuk Study Set — Decision Points, Handout, Flow-Path Rig
packs.summary: The incident handout and a six-point blind timeline cut from the Keokuk residential fire, plus a bay-scale flow-path demonstration plan and the debrief sheet that ties the findings to the crew's own door-control practice. Report linked at NIOSH, never reproduced.
packs.removes_prep: The drill's equipment list names a 'scenario handout' and the setup assumes someone has already cut the report into decision points and worked out how to demonstrate flow path indoors. That is two hours for a facilitator who has done it before and an evening for one who has not.

components.label: Incident handout and decision points
components.instructions: Give the crew the framing paragraph only, then work the decision points one at a time using the three-column sheet from LODD-006. The facilitator is the only person who reads the findings section beforehand. Read the actual NIOSH report before facilitating — this handout frames the study, it does not replace the report.

items.text: FRAMING — A residential fire with fire on a lower level and crews operating above it. Multiple firefighters are working interior; ventilation openings exist or are created during the incident. Read only this much before decision point 1.
items.source: NIOSH FFFIPP — Keokuk, Iowa residential fire; read the report for the actual sequence

items.text: DECISION POINT 1 — You are first-due. Fire is showing on the lower level of a residential structure and there is a report of children inside on an upper floor. State your initial report, your mode, and your first two assignments in order.
items.teaching_focus: Committing crews above a fire, and whether the rescue profile changes the tactical order.

items.text: DECISION POINT 2 — Your first line is being stretched. State exactly where it goes and what it is for: the fire, or the stairs the search crew is using. You cannot have both with one line.
items.teaching_focus: The line's purpose stated out loud. Protecting egress and attacking the fire are different jobs.

items.text: DECISION POINT 3 — A crew is above the fire searching. Somebody is about to open something — a window, a door, a roof. State who controls ventilation on this fireground and what they must confirm before opening anything.
items.teaching_focus: Ventilation authority. The pivot of the whole study.

items.text: DECISION POINT 4 — Conditions on the upper floor change rapidly and the crew above reports heat. State what you do in the next thirty seconds, and state what you would have needed in place already for that to work.
items.teaching_focus: The second half of the question is the useful one — most answers require something that was not done at decision point 2.

items.text: DECISION POINT 5 — You have a crew above the fire that you can no longer account for. State your sequence.
items.teaching_focus: Mayday for someone else, from a command position, on incomplete information.

items.text: DECISION POINT 6 — Same incident, same building, your department, tonight, with the staffing you will actually have. What is different about your answers to points 1 through 3?
items.teaching_focus: Where the study stops being about somebody else.

items.text: RECONCILE — Read the NIOSH report in full, including contributing factors, and complete column three on every sheet.

components.label: Bay-scale flow-path demonstration plan
components.instructions: A no-fire, no-smoke demonstration you can run on the apparatus floor in fifteen minutes. It shows air movement, not fire behavior — say so out loud to the crew, because a demonstration that overstates itself teaches worse than none.

items.text: Build it
fields: Two doorways or taped openings at opposite ends of a bay or corridor
A PPV fan, or a box fan, at one opening as the inlet
Ribbon, surveyor tape, or theatrical smoke at the midpoint as the tell-tale
A door or salvage cover that can close the outlet on command

items.text: Run it
fields: Outlet closed, fan on — observe the tell-tale
Outlet opened on command — observe the change
Time from opening to full flow at the midpoint
Repeat with the outlet at a different height

items.text: Say it
fields: What this shows: a path opens and air moves along it, fast
What this does NOT show: heat, fuel, smoke as fuel, or how quickly a room reaches untenability
The one sentence connecting it back to decision point 3
items.teaching_focus: The honesty step. A ribbon in a fan is not a flow-path fire and the crew must not leave thinking it was.

components.label: Debrief and one-change sheet
components.instructions: Finish here, in the same sitting. The LODD-008 one-change discipline applies: the study is not over until somebody rehearses something.

items.text: Findings to our practice
fields: Who controls ventilation on our fireground, by position
What our practice actually is when the truck opens up before the line is in place
Which buildings in our first-due put crews above a fire routinely
The one change we make on the next working fire

items.text: Hands on, before you leave
fields: The skill trained — door control on the advance is the usual answer
Drill used, from the library
Reps completed
What was awkward
items.teaching_focus: Ending in reps is what separates this from a safety meeting.

packs.title: Big-Fire Discipline Set — Charleston Decision Points & Scale Cards
packs.summary: A seven-point blind timeline for the Charleston furniture-showroom fire, plus scale cards that make a crew convert their own district's largest buildings into stretch lengths, flow requirements and search times before they argue about tactics. Report linked at NIOSH, never reproduced.
packs.removes_prep: The drill turns on discipline in a building far larger than the crew's normal work, and the setup assumes a facilitator has already cut the report and prepared the scale comparison. Without the scale work the discussion stays abstract, because nobody can feel the difference between a bedroom and a showroom from a narrative alone.
packs.local_fill_note: The scale cards are blank on purpose: the point is your own district's biggest buildings, your own preconnect lengths, and your own flow capability. Fill them from a walkaround and your apparatus inventory before the session, or the comparison is somebody else's.

components.label: Decision points
components.instructions: Framing paragraph first, then one decision point at a time on the LODD-006 three-column sheet. Facilitator reads the findings in advance; nobody else does. Read the NIOSH report before facilitating.

items.text: FRAMING — A very large single-story commercial furniture showroom with an attached warehouse, after business hours, with fire in the rear. The interior is an open span filled floor to ceiling with upholstered furniture. Read only this much.
items.source: NIOSH FFFIPP — Charleston, South Carolina furniture showroom fire

items.text: DECISION POINT 1 — Initial report and mode, before you know anything you do not already know from the framing.
items.teaching_focus: Whether building size and fuel load change the mode before fire is even seen.

items.text: DECISION POINT 2 — Water supply and hose length. State the numbers: how far to the seat, what you carry, and what that means.
items.teaching_focus: The arithmetic that decides whether an interior attack is even available.

items.text: DECISION POINT 3 — Crews are inside a compartment whose boundaries they cannot see. State what you require of them for orientation and egress, and how you verify it rather than assume it.
items.teaching_focus: Orientation in a space too large to feel like a compartment.

items.text: DECISION POINT 4 — State the observation that would make you reverse to defensive, now, before you have it. Write it down.
items.teaching_focus: Pre-committing a reversal trigger, which is the discipline the fireground will not give you later.

items.text: DECISION POINT 5 — Accountability of an interior crew becomes uncertain in a building this size. State your sequence and your realistic time to a PAR.
items.teaching_focus: How long accountability takes when the building is bigger than the radio's reliability.

items.text: DECISION POINT 6 — You are now committed deeper than your air supports. State what you do and what should have prevented it.
items.teaching_focus: Air as a function of distance, which is the RIT-008 skill at commercial scale.

items.text: DECISION POINT 7 — Your district. Name the building where this study applies and state the one thing you would do differently on arrival there.
items.teaching_focus: Local transfer, with a proper noun.

items.text: RECONCILE — Read the report in full including contributing factors and complete column three.

packs.title: Bailout & Egress Study Set — Black Sunday Decision Points
packs.summary: A six-point blind timeline for the Bronx Black Sunday fires, plus a self-rescue egress audit the crew runs on their own apparatus and buildings — what egress options exist, which are rehearsed, and which are theoretical. Reports linked at NIOSH, never reproduced.
packs.removes_prep: The drill needs the report cut into decision points and, to be worth anything, a crew that has actually checked what egress they carry and can use. Neither exists off the shelf, and the egress audit is the part everyone assumes somebody has already done.
packs.local_fill_note: The egress audit is entirely local: your apparatus, your bailout policy, your buildings, your training records. If your department has no bailout policy or no rehearsed system, that is the finding of the session and it belongs with your training officer rather than in a blank on this sheet.

components.label: Decision points
components.instructions: Framing first, then one point at a time on the LODD-006 sheet. Facilitator reads findings in advance. This is a respectful-framing study above all others: firefighters jumped because staying was worse, and the session must not read as second-guessing them.

items.text: FRAMING — Fire in a multiple-dwelling apartment building. Crews are operating on a floor above the fire. Interior conditions deteriorate rapidly and the path back to the interior stairs becomes untenable. Read only this much.
items.source: NIOSH FFFIPP — Bronx, New York apartment fires

items.text: DECISION POINT 1 — You are assigned to search a floor above the fire in a multiple dwelling. Before you enter, state your egress plan: primary, secondary, and what you carry that creates a third.
items.teaching_focus: Naming egress before entry, which almost nobody does.

items.text: DECISION POINT 2 — You are inside, searching, and the apartment layout is not what you expected. State how you are maintaining orientation and what tells you the interior stair is still available.
items.teaching_focus: Egress as a thing that is monitored, not assumed.

items.text: DECISION POINT 3 — Conditions worsen behind you. Your way back to the stair is now questionable. State your next three actions in order.
items.teaching_focus: The order. Transmit, move to a defensible position, prepare egress — arguments about the order are the value here.

items.text: DECISION POINT 4 — You are at a window above grade. There is no ladder. State everything you would do before going out the window, and state what would have to be true for going out to be the better option.
items.teaching_focus: The hardest question in the library, asked calmly, in a bay, in advance.

items.text: DECISION POINT 5 — You are command. You have crews above a fire in a multiple dwelling and conditions are deteriorating. State what you do about laddering, and when you should have done it.
items.teaching_focus: Ladders to upper-floor windows as a command decision made early or not at all.

items.text: DECISION POINT 6 — Your district. Name the buildings where crews routinely operate above a fire, and state what egress exists there tonight.
items.teaching_focus: Local transfer with proper nouns.

items.text: RECONCILE — Read the reports in full including contributing factors, and complete column three.

packs.title: Monthly Study Bank — 12 Themes, Facilitator Card, Skill Map
packs.summary: A twelve-month rotation of report themes with the search terms that find them in the public NIOSH library, the facilitator prep card that turns any report into a blind timeline in twenty minutes, and a theme-to-skill map that names the trainable skill and the DrillGround drill that trains it — so the HANDS ON block is decided before the study starts rather than improvised at minute forty-five.
packs.removes_prep: The drill's setup is one sentence — 'Facilitator (rotate this role monthly) prepares the blind timeline and identifies the one trainable skill the report points to' — and it is two hours of work for someone who has never done it. A rotating facilitator is a new novice every month, which is the drill's own stated benefit and its practical failure point.

components.label: Twelve-month theme rotation
components.instructions: One theme per month, in this order — it moves from the failures that kill the most firefighters to the more specialised ones, and it alternates interior and exterior so the hands-on block varies. Search the public NIOSH library with the terms given and pick a report the crew has not read. Reports are linked at their source, never reproduced.

items.text: MONTH 1 — Flow path and coordinated ventilation. Search terms: flow path, ventilation, wind-driven, door control.
items.teaching_focus: The mechanism behind the largest share of modern interior fatalities. Start here every rotation.

items.text: MONTH 2 — Size-up and missed basement fire. Search terms: basement, below grade, floor collapse, size-up.
items.teaching_focus: The 360 and what the first report failed to say.

items.text: MONTH 3 — Air management and running out of air. Search terms: air management, SCBA, out of air, low air alarm.
items.teaching_focus: Consumption versus plan, and the exit that was decided too late.

items.text: MONTH 4 — Mayday delay and RIT deployment. Search terms: mayday, rapid intervention, RIT, delayed.
items.teaching_focus: The interval between the trouble and the transmission.

items.text: MONTH 5 — Accountability and crew integrity. Search terms: accountability, PAR, separated, freelancing.

components.label: Facilitator prep card — twenty minutes, in order
components.instructions: Hand this to whoever has the month. Follow it in order and stop when the boxes are filled; the temptation is to over-prepare and deliver a lecture. The facilitator is the only person who reads the ending, and that is the whole responsibility of the role.

One-sentence incident summary
Occupancy and construction
Resources on scene at the point of injury

items.text: STEP 2 (5 min) — Cut the decision points using the six triggers from LODD-006. Six to nine is a session.

What the crew knows at each — one line each
Which point is the pivot

items.text: STEP 3 (5 min) — Now read the findings. Pick ONE for the SO WHAT, HERE block.
fields: The chosen contributing factor
Two other findings deliberately set aside
Why this one for this crew, this month

items.text: STEP 4 (5 min) — Pick the hands-on skill and confirm you can actually run it today.
fields: The skill
DrillGround drill it corresponds to, from the skill map
Equipment needed and confirmed on hand
Twenty-minute plan for the block
items.teaching_focus: Confirmed on hand. A hands-on block that fails on equipment turns the drill back into a safety meeting, which is the one failure the drill names.

items.text: Respectful framing check — before you present anything
fields: Am I presenting the crew's decisions as choices made with what they had (Y/N)
Have I removed anything that reads as blame (Y/N)
Would I run this session in front of that department (Y/N)

components.label: Theme-to-skill map
components.instructions: Use this to pick the HANDS ON block once the theme is chosen. Each row names the skill the theme points to and the DrillGround drill that already trains it, so the twenty-minute block is a drill you can open rather than something to invent.

items.text: Flow path and ventilation → door control on the advance, with the nozzle. Drill: ENG-002 Nozzle Mechanics & Door Control.
items.teaching_focus: The single highest-value hands-on block in the rotation.

items.text: Size-up and missed basement → the initial radio report from a cold look, with a strategy declared. Drill: OFF-001 Photo-Based Size-Up & Initial Radio Report.
Air management → turnaround arithmetic on the member's own gauge. Drill: RIT-008 Air Decision Points.
Mayday delay → LUNAR under a five-second decision. Drills: RIT-001 Mayday Declaration & LUNAR, and RIT-006 Mayday Trigger Recognition.
Accountability and crew integrity → PAR management from a command position. Drill: OFF-003 Accountability & PAR Management.
Lightweight construction collapse → reading engineered construction on a real building. Drill: LODD-005 Reading Engineered Construction.
Large commercial → stretch estimation on a deep commercial occupancy. Drill: ENG-006 Stretch Estimation Walkaround.
Water supply failure → hydrant hookup and forward lay against a clock, or pump panel under two lines. Drills: ENG-003 Hydrant Hookup & Forward Lay, DRV-001 Pump Panel Evolution.
Communications failure → the emergency button and PASS, gloved and blind. Drill: RIT-007 Emergency Button & PASS.
Roof operations → ground ladder throws to a marked target, and the decision not to go. Drill: TRK-004 Ground Ladder Throws.
Wildland-urban interface → no library drill yet. Use the report's own recommendation and log the gap; a theme with no drill behind it is a content request worth sending in.
items.teaching_focus: Naming the gap honestly instead of substituting a loosely related structural drill.

items.text: Near-miss month → whatever the reporter says they would do differently, done with hands for twenty minutes. Pick the drill from the report, not from this map.

packs.title: Engineered Construction Set — 10 Specs, Floor Plan, Survey Sheet
packs.summary: Ten labelled image specs of engineered structural members and their connections, a schematic floor plan showing where lightweight assemblies hide behind conventional finishes, and the district survey sheet that turns the study into a list of addresses. Geometry and identification only — no fire, no damage.
packs.removes_prep: The drill's equipment list names floor plans, photos and a worksheet, and supplies none. Crews cannot photograph what is behind a finished ceiling, so the members they most need to recognize are precisely the ones they have never seen.
packs.local_fill_note: The survey sheet is your district. Construction era, local building practice and renovation history all vary; the specs show what the members look like, and only a walkaround and your building department tell you which of your buildings have them.

components.label: Structural member specs
components.instructions: Show one at a time. The member names it, states what carries the load, and states the failure mode and roughly how fast. Images marked AI-GENERATED are schematic illustrations for identification and geometry only; they depict no fire, no heat and no damage, and nothing about time-to-failure should be inferred from a picture.

items.text: Lightweight parallel-chord wood truss — identify the members and state what fails first.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical side-elevation line illustration of a parallel-chord lightweight wooden floor truss: two horizontal chords of dimensional lumber connected by a repeating pattern of short diagonal webs, joined at each intersection by a flat toothed metal connector plate. Plain white background, thin dark lines, engineering-drawing style, no lettering, no damage, no fire.
items.alt: Technical side-elevation drawing of a parallel-chord lightweight wooden floor truss with two horizontal chords, diagonal webs, and flat toothed metal connector plates at the joints.
items.answer: Parallel-chord truss. The connector plates are the weak point: they have shallow penetration and lose grip as the wood chars or the plate heats and distorts. Failure is of the connection, not of a big member burning through.
items.teaching_focus: The plate, not the timber. This is the single most important identification in the deck.

items.text: Toothed connector plate, close up — identify it and state how deep it goes.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical close-up line illustration of a flat galvanised toothed connector plate pressed into the joint between a wooden chord and two diagonal web members, showing the short teeth punched from the plate penetrating only a short distance into the wood, drawn in cutaway. Plain white background, thin dark lines, engineering-drawing style, no lettering, no damage, no fire.
items.alt: Technical cutaway close-up of a galvanised toothed connector plate at a truss joint, showing short teeth penetrating a shallow depth into the wood.
items.answer: A gang-nail or truss plate. The teeth are short — a fraction of an inch. There is no through-bolt and no significant embedment, so heat or char at the surface is enough to release the joint.
items.teaching_focus: Seeing the shallowness makes the failure mode obvious in a way a description does not.

items.text: Wooden I-joist — identify the members and state what the web is made of.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical side-elevation and end-section line illustration of an engineered wooden I-joist: a thin vertical web panel of oriented strand board set into grooves in a top and bottom flange of solid lumber, forming an I shape in cross-section. Plain white background, thin dark lines, engineering-drawing style, no lettering, no damage, no fire.
items.alt: Technical drawing of an engineered wooden I-joist in side and end view, showing a thin oriented-strand-board web between solid lumber top and bottom flanges.
items.answer: An I-joist. The web is thin OSB — very little mass. It burns through quickly and the joist loses its shear capacity long before the flanges are consumed.
items.teaching_focus: Thin web, low mass, fast failure. The opposite of a sawn joist's behavior.

items.text: Web penetration through an I-joist — identify it and state what it changes.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical side-elevation line illustration of an engineered wooden I-joist with a large circular hole cut through the thin web panel near mid-span, with a duct and an electrical cable passing through the hole. Plain white background, thin dark lines, engineering-drawing style, no lettering, no damage, no fire.
items.alt: Technical side-elevation drawing of a wooden I-joist with a large circular hole cut through its web, with a duct and cable passing through it.
items.answer: A service penetration. It reduces the web further and, more importantly, it connects the joist bays into one continuous void, so fire and smoke travel the whole floor system rather than one bay.
items.teaching_focus: The penetration turns separate voids into one void. That is what makes the whole floor go at once.

items.text: Open-web steel bar joist — identify it and state its failure mode.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical side-elevation line illustration of an open-web steel bar joist: two horizontal steel angle chords connected by a continuous zigzag round steel bar web, with bearing seats at each end. Plain white background, thin dark lines, engineering-drawing style, no lettering, no damage, no fire.
items.alt: Technical side-elevation drawing of an open-web steel bar joist with steel angle chords, a continuous zigzag round-bar web, and bearing seats at each end.
items.answer: A bar joist. Unprotected steel elongates then loses strength as it heats, and the thin web bars have very little mass to absorb heat. Failure can be sudden and can push out the bearing wall as the joist elongates.
items.teaching_focus: Steel does not burn, and that is not reassuring — it sags, elongates, and pushes.

items.text: Lightweight concrete over steel deck on bar joists — identify the assembly.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical cutaway section line illustration of a floor assembly: corrugated steel decking spanning across open-web steel bar joists, with a thin layer of lightweight concrete poured over the decking. Plain white background, thin dark lines, engineering-drawing style, no lettering, no damage, no fire.
items.alt: Technical cutaway section of a floor assembly with lightweight concrete over corrugated steel decking supported on open-web steel bar joists.
items.answer: A composite deck. The top surface feels utterly solid to someone standing on it while the unprotected joists beneath are being heated. Sounding tells you nothing about the joists.
items.teaching_focus: A floor that feels reassuring from above while failing from below.

items.text: Glue-laminated beam — identify it and distinguish it from a solid timber.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical end-section and side-elevation line illustration of a glue-laminated structural beam, showing many thin horizontal laminations bonded together through the full depth of the beam, with visible glue lines between each lamination. Plain white background, thin dark lines, engineering-drawing style, no lettering, no damage, no fire.
items.alt: Technical end-section and side view of a glue-laminated beam showing many thin horizontal laminations with visible glue lines.
items.answer: Glulam. Distinguished from heavy timber by the visible glue lines. It has real mass and chars more predictably than a truss, but the adhesive lines are a delamination path under sustained heat.
items.teaching_focus: The one engineered member with mass on its side, and its specific weakness.

items.text: Truss roof behind a conventional-looking soffit — trace what is hidden.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical cutaway section line illustration of a residential roof edge: from outside, a conventional-looking eave with fascia and soffit; cut away to reveal lightweight parallel-chord roof trusses with connector plates inside, and a continuous open attic void above the ceiling line. Plain white background, thin dark lines, engineering-drawing style, no lettering, no damage, no fire.
items.alt: Technical cutaway of a residential eave showing a conventional-looking fascia and soffit outside, with lightweight plated roof trusses and a continuous attic void revealed inside.
items.answer: A conventional exterior over a lightweight structure. Nothing visible from the street distinguishes it. The soffit vents feed the void directly, and the void is continuous over the whole floor plan.
items.teaching_focus: Why exterior size-up cannot answer the construction question by itself.

items.text: Renovated ceiling — original joists plus a newer lightweight assembly above.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical cutaway section line illustration showing two stacked floor structures: below, older solid sawn dimensional joists with a finished ceiling; above them, a newer lightweight engineered joist assembly with a subfloor, leaving a concealed void between the two systems. Plain white background, thin dark lines, engineering-drawing style, no lettering, no damage, no fire.
items.alt: Technical cutaway showing older solid sawn joists with a finished ceiling below, a newer lightweight engineered joist assembly above, and a concealed void between them.
items.answer: A renovation stack. There is a void nobody knows about between two structural systems of different eras and different failure times, and opening the ceiling from below tells you about the old system only.
items.teaching_focus: The building that is two buildings. Renovation history is a structural question.

items.text: The card you fill — how to find out what you actually have.
fields: Our building department's records: who to ask, what they will tell us
What the year built does and does not imply locally
Buildings under construction right now, where the frame is visible
Which of our target buildings have had a roof or floor replaced
items.teaching_focus: A building under construction is a free look at a structure you will otherwise never see. Photograph it while you can.

components.label: Void-path schematic
components.instructions: Print at a size a crew can gather round. Use it to trace, with a finger, how a fire in one bay reaches the whole floor system — then ask which of your own buildings this is.

items.text: Continuous floor void with service penetrations — trace the path from one bay to the far side of the structure, and mark where you would open up to find it.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical schematic plan-view line drawing of a rectangular residential floor framing layout: parallel engineered I-joists running across the plan, with a line of circular service penetrations through the webs forming a continuous route across all joist bays, plus a mechanical chase shown at one end connecting to the floor above. Plain white background, thin dark lines, engineering-drawing style, minimal labelling, no fire, no smoke, no damage.
items.alt: Technical plan-view schematic of a floor framing layout with parallel engineered I-joists, a line of circular web penetrations forming a continuous route across all bays, and a mechanical chase at one end.
items.teaching_focus: Seeing the route in plan is what makes the whole-floor failure mode believable.

items.text: Where to open up
fields: Two places on this schematic where a hook would find fire early
Two places that would tell you nothing
The place a crew would instinctively open, and whether it is one of the first two
items.teaching_focus: Instinct and the schematic often disagree, and the schematic is right.

components.label: District survey sheet
components.instructions: One row per target building. This is the artifact that outlives the drill and belongs in the pre-incident file, not in somebody's notebook.

items.text: Building row
fields: Address and occupancy
Year built, and how we know
Roof structure: sawn, truss, I-joist, bar joist, unknown
Floor structure, same options
How we determined it — looked, asked, or assumed
Renovation history known (Y/N)
items.teaching_focus: The 'how we determined it' column. Most entries start as 'assumed', and that is the honest starting point.

items.text: Survey findings
fields: Buildings where the structure is confirmed lightweight
Buildings where it is genuinely unknown
The one address we will confirm this month, and how
Who this list goes to

NIOSH Fire Fighter Fatality Investigation and Prevention Program (public domain; collapse findings referenced at pattern level)

packs.synthetic_caveat: These are AI-generated schematic illustrations of structural members and assemblies, for identification and geometry only. They depict no fire, no heat and no damage, and no time-to-failure or safe-operating conclusion should be drawn from a drawing. Verify construction in your own buildings by looking, by asking your building department, or by photographing structures under construction.

packs.title: Contributing-Factor Map — Template and Eight Recurring Factors
packs.summary: The four-column mapping template the drill requires, plus the eight contributing factors that recur across the NIOSH literature, each written as a question about your own district rather than a finding about someone else's. The factors give the firefighter somewhere to start when a report's findings are worded too generally to map.
packs.removes_prep: The drill needs a four-column mapping template and a district in mind. The template is quick to draw; the hard part is that NIOSH findings are often worded at a level — 'inadequate risk assessment' — that a firefighter cannot map to a street without a translation step, so the mapping stalls in generalities. That translation is what this pack supplies.

components.label: Four-column mapping template
components.instructions: One sheet per factor you map, three to five factors per session. This framework is not blind — read the report all the way through first. The third column is the only one that matters and it must contain a proper noun: a street, an address, an occupancy you can name, a rig, a shift.

items.text: Mapping row
fields: Factor, as the report words it
Mechanism — how it actually caused harm in that incident, in one sentence
Where it lives in MY district — name the building, street, apparatus, or habit
Our current status — solved, partly, not at all, or don't know
items.teaching_focus: 'Don't know' is a legitimate and useful answer in column four. It converts into a question for the training officer.

items.text: Session close
fields: Factors mapped this session
The one with the worst status
Who needs to hear about it
What I will do about it myself this week, regardless of whether anyone else acts
items.teaching_focus: The last field keeps the exercise from becoming a list of other people's problems.

components.label: Eight recurring factors, translated into district questions
components.instructions: When a report's finding is too general to map, find it in this list and use the questions instead. These are the factor families that appear again and again across the public NIOSH literature; the questions are written to force a proper noun out of you.

items.text: FACTOR — Inadequate size-up or incomplete 360. QUESTIONS: Which buildings in my first-due cannot be walked around, and what do I do instead at those addresses? Which of them have a grade change that hides a below-grade floor from the street? Name three.
items.teaching_focus: Turning 'inadequate size-up' into a list of addresses.
items.source: Recurring factor family across NIOSH FFFIPP reports

items.text: FACTOR — Uncoordinated ventilation or uncontrolled flow path. QUESTIONS: On my rig, whose job is the door? What is our actual practice when the truck opens up before the line is in place — not our policy, our practice? Which occupancy type in my district makes this most likely?
items.teaching_focus: Separating what the department says from what the shift does.
items.source: Recurring factor family across NIOSH FFFIPP reports

items.text: FACTOR — Ineffective or absent incident command. QUESTIONS: At what point on a working fire in my district does command actually get established, in minutes? Who fills it before the chief arrives, and have they practiced transferring it? Which address has the worst approach for establishing a command position?
items.teaching_focus: Command as a timeline rather than a role.
items.source: Recurring factor family across NIOSH FFFIPP reports

items.text: FACTOR — Lack of accountability or crew integrity. QUESTIONS: When was the last PAR taken on a real incident on my shift? What happens on my rig when one member goes to the rear alone — is it noticed, and by whom? Name the building where our accountability would fail first.
items.teaching_focus: Accountability measured by the last real incident, not the last drill.
items.source: Recurring factor family across NIOSH FFFIPP reports

items.text: FACTOR — Inadequate water supply or insufficient flow. QUESTIONS: Which addresses in my first-due are beyond the reach of my longest preconnect? Where is the nearest hydrant that will not deliver what a 2.5 in line needs? Which street has the supply problem nobody has written down?
items.teaching_focus: The engine-company factor family, which crews under-map because it feels like the driver's problem.
items.source: Recurring factor family across NIOSH FFFIPP reports

items.text: FACTOR — Failure to recognize structural collapse hazards. QUESTIONS: Which buildings in my district are lightweight or engineered construction, and how do I know — did someone look, or is it an assumption from the year built? Which renovation has hidden a truss roof behind a conventional facade?
items.teaching_focus: Construction knowledge as verified fact rather than inference.
items.source: Recurring factor family across NIOSH FFFIPP reports

items.text: FACTOR — Poor or failed communications. QUESTIONS: Where in my district does the radio not work — which basement, which stairwell, which strip of the highway? Has anyone tested it, or do we all just know? What is our actual practice when a transmission goes unanswered?
items.teaching_focus: Radio dead spots as mapped facts, which almost no department has written down.
items.source: Recurring factor family across NIOSH FFFIPP reports

items.text: FACTOR — Inadequate air management or SCBA discipline. QUESTIONS: What does my department's policy actually say, and can I quote the number? What is the real practice on my shift about working past the low-air alarm? Which of our regular occupancies has a long enough entry that air becomes the limiting factor?
items.teaching_focus: The factor that maps to a habit rather than a building, and is therefore the hardest to be honest about.
items.source: Recurring factor family across NIOSH FFFIPP reports

items.text: Where to read the reports themselves. Do not map from this list alone — it is a translation aid, not a substitute for reading a specific report about specific people.

sources: NIOSH Fire Fighter Fatality Investigation and Prevention Program (public domain; factor families summarised at pattern level, no report text reproduced)
Self-authored template and district questions

packs.title: Two-In/Two-Out Scenario Cards — 10 Arrivals
packs.summary: Ten arrival scenarios varying occupancy, conditions and staffing, each stating exactly what is on scene and what dispatch has said, with the two-in/two-out and initial-RIT questions the crew must answer out loud — including three where the correct answer is that an interior attack cannot begin yet, and one where the known-life-hazard exception is live.
packs.removes_prep: The drill's equipment list says 'Scenario cards' and its setup says the crew 'arrives at scenarios varying occupancy, conditions, and staffing'. Nothing supplies them, so the officer running the drill improvises arrivals — and improvised arrivals almost never include the ones where the honest answer is 'we wait', which is the entire discipline the drill is named after.
packs.local_fill_note: Two-in/two-out and initial-RIT obligations are set by your department's policy and the regulations that apply to you. Write your department's rule at the top of the scoring sheet and score against it. Where a card's stated answer differs from your policy, your policy is correct and the card is wrong.

components.label: Arrival scenario cards
components.instructions: Read the arrival aloud to the crew. They answer out loud, in order: is this interior or exterior right now, who is the outside team, who is the incident commander, and what has to arrive before the picture changes. Then reveal the discussion note. Run several cards in one session — the value is in the contrast between them.

items.text: Single-family dwelling, working fire visible in a rear bedroom, light smoke to the street. On scene: your engine with an officer, a driver, and two firefighters. Nothing else for six minutes. Dispatch has no report of anyone home.
items.answer: Two interior, two out — but the driver is the pump operator and cannot be counted as the outside team while operating. That leaves one. The honest answer is that a two-in interior attack begins when the second company arrives, or the crew works from outside meanwhile. State who the IC is.
items.teaching_focus: The pump operator problem, which is the single most common way departments talk themselves into a compliant-sounding non-compliance.

items.text: Same dwelling, same fire. On scene: your engine, four members, and a second engine two minutes out. A neighbor is on the lawn saying the occupant's car is in the driveway.
items.answer: A known life hazard may permit initiating rescue under your policy's exception. The crew must name the exception, say who authorised it, and state what makes it a KNOWN hazard rather than a possible one. A car in a driveway is not a person in a building — that is the argument to have.
items.teaching_focus: Using the exception deliberately and out loud, rather than sliding into it.

items.text: Two-story garden apartment, smoke from a second-floor unit, occupants self-evacuating in the parking lot. On scene: two engines, eight members total, no truck. Dispatch reports one occupant unaccounted for.
items.answer: Sufficient staffing for two in and two out with an IC. The harder questions are which two go in, who the outside team actually is by name, and whether the outside team has a way to reach the second floor if the interior team needs them.
items.teaching_focus: An outside team that cannot get to where the trouble is, is not an outside team.

items.text: Commercial strip unit, moderate smoke, security bars on the front, no rear access confirmed. On scene: one engine, four members. Second-alarm response requested and eight minutes out.
items.answer: Not an interior attack. Access is unconfirmed, egress is compromised by the bars, and the outside team could not effect a rescue through a barred front. Exterior operations, forcible-entry preparation, and a stated trigger for reassessment.
items.teaching_focus: Egress as part of the two-out calculation, not just personnel count.

items.text: Single-family dwelling, heavy smoke from the eaves, nothing showing. On scene: engine with three members — officer, driver, one firefighter. Next unit unknown ETA.
items.answer: No interior attack. Three members with one on the panel is not two in and two out under any reading. State the exterior plan and the specific arrival that changes it.
items.teaching_focus: The short-staffed reality many departments actually arrive with, stated honestly instead of worked around.

items.text: House fire, fully involved, no exposures threatened, nobody reported inside. On scene: two engines, a truck, ten members.
items.answer: Defensive. Two-in/two-out does not apply because nobody is going in. The card is in the deck so the crew practices saying 'this is not an interior fire' when staffing is not the constraint — the discipline is about the fire, not only the roster.
items.teaching_focus: Separating a staffing decision from a strategy decision.

items.text: Basement fire in a two-story dwelling, smoke pushing from a basement window well, interior stair the only known access. On scene: two engines, eight members.
items.answer: Staffing is sufficient. The RIT question is different below grade: the outside team needs a plan to reach a member in a basement, which the interior stair may not provide. Name the second means of access before anyone goes down.
items.teaching_focus: Initial RIT as a plan for a specific building, not a pair of people standing by the rig.

items.text: Vacant, boarded structure, fire showing on two floors, known to be occupied by squatters in the past. On scene: one engine, four members, second engine four minutes out.
items.answer: The argument is whether 'previously occupied by squatters' constitutes a known life hazard. Most policies say it does not. The crew must state the decision and the reason, and say what would change it — a report from a witness, a visible victim.
items.teaching_focus: Risk-benefit stated out loud on the building the fire service loses people in most often.

items.text: Working fire in a single-family dwelling. Two engines on scene, eight members, and the first crew is already inside when you arrive as the second engine officer. You cannot identify an outside team.
items.answer: State it on the radio. The correct answer is a transmission to command that the outside team is not established, and then establishing it — not an interior entry to help, and not silence.
items.teaching_focus: The card where the crew arrives into a non-compliant scene, which is the most realistic card in the deck.

items.text: Small kitchen fire, contained, light smoke, homeowner outside and accounted for. On scene: one engine, four members.
items.answer: Two in, two out with the driver on the panel leaves one outside — and for a contained incident many policies permit entry. The crew must say which reading of their policy they are relying on, and mean it. A drill that only practices the big fires never practices the decision people actually make ten times a year.
items.teaching_focus: The routine call, deliberately last. This is where habits are actually formed.

components.label: Answer scoring sheet
components.instructions: One row per card. Fill in your department's rule at the top before the first card. Score the crew's answer against your rule, not against the card's note.

items.text: My department's rule — write this first
fields: Policy or regulation that governs two-in/two-out for us
Whether the pump operator may count as the outside team
The known-life-hazard exception as our policy words it
Who may authorise the exception
items.teaching_focus: Four questions. A crew that cannot fill this in has found the drill's real finding.

items.text: Card score
fields: Card number
Interior or exterior called correctly per our policy (Y/N)
Outside team named by name (Y/N)
IC identified (Y/N)
The arrival or change that would alter the decision, stated (Y/N)
Time to a committed answer
