packs.title: Standpipe Handoff Kit — Lobby Card, 8 Building Cards, Handoff Sheet
packs.summary: A lobby-control reference card, eight building cards varying standpipe arrangement and access, and the company-to-company handoff sheet that makes the lobby-to-attack transfer explicit. All pressure figures blank — standpipe outlet pressure is a policy number.
packs.removes_prep: The drill names an image and a report and supplies neither, and a standpipe handoff needs a stated building arrangement to hand off in. Improvising it means the lobby company and the attack company each imagine a different building, which is exactly the failure the drill is trying to surface.
packs.local_fill_note: Standpipe outlet pressure, your high-rise pack contents, and your department's lobby-control assignment are all local. Write them on the lobby card first. No pressures are supplied here — a wrong standpipe pressure is pumped at a real fire.

components.label: Lobby control card
components.instructions: Fill from your SOP and your apparatus inventory before the first rep. The lobby company's job is a checklist, and a checklist nobody wrote gets improvised at the worst moment.

items.text: OUR NUMBERS
fields: Standpipe outlet pressure our SOP specifies
Our high-rise pack: hose diameter, length, nozzle
Inline gauge carried (Y/N)
Pressure-reducing device policy
items.teaching_focus: Four numbers the attack company is betting on.

items.text: ON ARRIVAL — the lobby company's list
fields: Fire floor confirmed, and how
Building systems checked: alarm panel, elevator recall, HVAC
Stair chosen for attack, and the stair chosen for evacuation
Standpipe system type and whether it is charged

items.text: THE CONNECTION
fields: FDC located and its condition
Supply established from which apparatus
Pressure set, and who confirmed it with whom
Who stays at the FDC
items.teaching_focus: The confirmation is a two-person, two-radio act. Set-and-assume is the failure.

items.text: WHAT THE ATTACK COMPANY MUST BE TOLD
fields: Which stair
Which floor to connect on and why
Outlet condition and any missing handwheels or caps
Anything wrong with the system
items.teaching_focus: The handoff content, on a card, so it does not depend on who is on duty.

components.label: Eight building cards
components.instructions: Deal one to the lobby company only. They must convey what the attack company needs without reading the card aloud. Then the attack company states their plan and the facilitator reveals the card — the gap between what was conveyed and what was on the card is the drill.

items.text: Six-story residential, two stairs, standpipe in both, outlets on every landing, system charged, all outlets in good order.
items.answer: The easy case. Everything the attack company needs is a floor number and a stair. Present to establish the pattern.
items.teaching_focus: Baseline handoff.

items.text: Eight-story residential, two stairs, standpipe in ONE only, and it is not the stair nearest the lobby entrance.
items.answer: The stair choice is the whole message. An attack company that goes up the convenient stair arrives with no water.
items.teaching_focus: The single most common standpipe error.

items.text: Ten-story commercial, standpipe outlets in the stair, but the outlet on the fire floor is missing its handwheel.
items.answer: Connect on the floor below and stretch up the stair. The lobby company must convey the defect, not just the floor.
items.teaching_focus: Conveying a defect. Most crews report the floor and stop.

items.text: Twelve-story, pressure-reducing devices fitted at each outlet, set by the building.
items.answer: The attack company needs to know they are there, because the pressure at the nozzle will not be what the pump is sending. Listening for the inline gauge being used rather than assumed.
items.teaching_focus: Why the inline gauge is on the equipment list.

items.text: Five-story, dry standpipe system, not charged on arrival.
items.answer: Nobody advances until it is charged and confirmed. The handoff must include the confirmation step and who gives it.
items.teaching_focus: A dry system is a sequencing problem, and the sequence must be stated.

items.text: Nine-story, standpipe present, but the FDC is on the opposite side of the building from the apparatus and partially obstructed.
items.answer: A supply-time problem that the attack company must know about, because their water is delayed. Listening for a stated time expectation rather than silence.
items.teaching_focus: Telling the attack company when their water will arrive, not just that it will.

items.text: Seven-story mixed-use, stairs that do not both reach the top floor.
items.answer: The stair that serves the fire floor may not be the stair that serves the floor above it. Listening for the lobby company checking, not assuming.
items.teaching_focus: Buildings whose stairs are not what a floor plan implies.

items.text: Any of the above, and the radio does not work in the stair.
items.answer: The handoff has to happen face to face before the attack company leaves the lobby, and a relay or a runner has to be planned. Listening for the plan being made in the lobby rather than discovered on floor six.
items.teaching_focus: The card that makes crews plan for the comms failure they all know about.

components.label: Handoff sheet
components.instructions: Filled by the facilitator during the rep, then shown to both companies together. Comparing what was conveyed against the building card settles every argument.

items.text: Conveyed by the lobby company
fields: Stair stated (Y/N)
Connection floor stated (Y/N)
Defects stated (Y/N)
Pressure-reducing devices mentioned if present (Y/N)
System charged status stated (Y/N)
Water timing stated (Y/N)

items.text: Gap
fields: What was on the card but not conveyed
What the attack company assumed instead
What that would have cost on a real fire
One change to how we hand off
items.teaching_focus: The third row is the one that makes the drill land.

sources: Self-authored lobby card, building cards and handoff sheet
Department standpipe SOP, high-rise pack inventory and lobby-control assignment (user-supplied and authoritative; no pressures supplied here)

packs.title: Transitional Attack Cards — 8 Handoffs and a Confirm Sheet
packs.summary: Eight scenarios pairing an exterior knock with an interior handoff, each stating what the exterior company saw and did, plus the three-part confirm sheet — water off, conditions checked, entry authorised — that the drill's reset-confirm-commit sequence depends on.
packs.removes_prep: The drill names an image and scenario material and supplies neither. A transitional attack drill needs a stated set of exterior conditions and a stated exterior action to hand over, and without them the two companies rehearse a handoff of nothing.
packs.local_fill_note: Your department's position on transitional attack — when it is used, who authorises entry after a knock, and what the radio sequence is — governs every card. Write it on the confirm sheet first.

components.label: Eight handoff scenarios
components.instructions: Brief the exterior company privately on what they see and what they did. The interior company hears only the radio. Then run the handoff live. Facilitator plays command and controls the water. The interior company may not enter until the confirm sheet is satisfied out loud.

items.text: Single-family dwelling, fire venting from one first-floor window, exterior company has flowed into the window for 20 seconds from outside and conditions have visibly improved.
items.answer: The straightforward reset. Listening for: water off announced, the interior company confirming improvement themselves rather than accepting it, and entry authorised by a named person.
items.teaching_focus: Baseline. Establishes the three-part sequence.

items.text: Same dwelling, but the exterior stream was flowed for 60 seconds and steam is now obscuring everything.
items.answer: Nobody can assess anything through the steam. Listening for a deliberate wait, or an assessment from a different position, rather than entering into an unreadable interior.
items.teaching_focus: Over-application creates its own blindness.

items.text: Fire venting from two windows on different sides. Exterior company hit one.
items.answer: Half the fire has been addressed. Listening for the interior company being told explicitly which side was NOT hit, and adjusting their entry accordingly.
items.teaching_focus: Conveying what was not done.

items.text: Exterior company flowed into a window and conditions worsened.
items.answer: A sign that the stream pushed, or that the fire is not where it appeared, or that a flow path was created. Listening for the handoff carrying bad news honestly and the interior entry being reconsidered rather than proceeding on schedule.
items.teaching_focus: The handoff nobody wants to make.

items.text: Exterior knock complete, and there is a reported victim on the floor above the fire.
items.answer: The reset still happens, but the clock is different. Listening for the sequence being kept rather than skipped for the rescue — and for someone stating explicitly that it is being kept.
items.teaching_focus: Where the discipline is most tempting to abandon.

items.text: Exterior company reports the stream did not reach the seat — it hit a ceiling and deflected.
items.answer: There has been little or no knock. Listening for the interior company being told that plainly, and treating this as an ordinary interior attack rather than a post-knock entry.
items.teaching_focus: A knock that did not happen must not be handed over as one.

items.text: Two companies both begin flowing water from different sides without coordination.
items.answer: The drill's real failure mode. Listening for someone stopping it on the radio, and for the reset then happening once, properly, from one position.
items.teaching_focus: Opposing streams. Command's problem, and any officer can name it.

items.text: Everything went right, and the interior company enters and immediately loses water.
items.answer: The supply problem that the transitional sequence can hide, because the exterior flow proved the pump worked at that moment and nothing since. Listening for the interior company backing out and for the supply being confirmed rather than debugged from inside.
items.teaching_focus: A successful knock is not a confirmed water supply.

components.label: Reset-confirm-commit sheet
components.instructions: The interior company may not enter until every box in the first three blocks is spoken aloud and answered. Facilitator holds the sheet and refuses entry until it is done — that refusal is where the habit is built.

items.text: OUR POLICY — fill first
fields: When our department uses transitional attack
Who authorises interior entry after an exterior flow
The radio words our SOP uses for water off and for entry
Maximum exterior flow duration, if we set one

items.text: RESET — water off
fields: Exterior flow stopped and announced by name (Y/N)
Acknowledged by the interior company (Y/N)
Time of water off
items.teaching_focus: Announced AND acknowledged. One-way traffic is not a handoff.

items.text: CONFIRM — conditions
fields: Interior company assessed conditions themselves (Y/N)
What the exterior company hit, and what they did NOT hit, stated (Y/N)
Any worsening or steam obscuration reported honestly (Y/N)
Water supply confirmed still established (Y/N)

items.text: COMMIT — entry
fields: Entry authorised by a named person (Y/N)
Time from water off to entry
Anything skipped, and why
items.teaching_focus: The interval is the measurement. Too short means the confirm was theatre.

sources: Self-authored scenarios and confirm sheet
Department transitional-attack position and radio procedure (user-supplied and authoritative)

packs.title: Size-Up Kit — Format Card, Scoring Sheet, Building Deck
packs.summary: The report format card the drill scores against, a stopwatch scoring sheet for the recorded playback, a deck-build specification for the fifteen-image session, and eight building-geometry image specs for construction and access reading. Smoke and fire conditions are deliberately NOT generated — those images stay real and user-supplied, and the pack says why.
packs.removes_prep: The drill needs a 'Report format card per SOP' and a deck of fifteen images seen cold. The format card does not exist in most departments as a card, and the solo variant asks the officer to build the deck 'the night before, so you see them cold' — which is real work, done at the wrong time, by someone who then knows what is in the deck.
packs.local_fill_note: The format card is a frame, not your SOP. Fill in your department's required radio report elements and their order — the order is what you will be scored on internally and it varies. Where your SOP names elements this frame omits, add them; where it omits elements this frame names, your SOP wins.

components.label: Report format card
components.instructions: Print at pocket size and fill in your department's elements before the first rep. Hold it in front of you during playback, not during the transmission — the whole drill is transmitting without it.

items.text: BUILDING — size, height, occupancy, construction
fields: How my SOP words this element
Its position in our required order
The construction descriptors our department expects to hear
items.teaching_focus: Construction is the element most often dropped under time pressure, and the one with the highest consequence.

items.text: CONDITIONS — smoke and fire location, volume, velocity, density, color
fields: How my SOP words this element
Position in our order
Do we report a stage, and in what words
items.teaching_focus: Reading smoke is a trained skill in its own right. This card only asks whether it was reported.

items.text: ACTIONS — mode declaration and first assignment
fields: Our mode words — offensive, defensive, investigating, transitional
Position in our order
What our SOP requires of a first assignment
items.teaching_focus: The declaration that commits the fireground. A report without it is the failure the drill names first.

items.text: NEEDS — additional alarms, utilities, water supply
fields: How my SOP words this element
Position in our order
What we are expected to request at this point versus later
items.teaching_focus: Asking early, which officers under-do because it feels like an admission.

items.text: CAN update — Conditions, Actions, Needs, at two minutes
fields: Our CAN format if we have one
Interval our SOP expects
What triggers an unscheduled update
items.teaching_focus: The follow-up round of the drill, and the habit that stops an officer going silent.

components.label: Playback scoring sheet
components.instructions: One row per image, fifteen rows per session. Score from the recording with the image open beside you — never from memory. The unforgiving rule: a report missing construction or a strategy declaration is a fail regardless of how good the rest was.

items.text: Image row
fields: Image number
Transmission length in seconds
Building — size, height, occupancy, construction: all four present (Y/N)
Conditions — smoke read given (Y/N)
Mode declared out loud (Y/N)
First assignment given (Y/N)
Needs stated (Y/N)
Wasted air time — filler, restarts, self-correction (seconds)
items.teaching_focus: Wasted air time is the number that improves fastest and that officers are least aware of.

items.text: Session totals
fields: Reports under 30 seconds, of 15
Reports declaring a strategy, of 15
Fails — missing construction or strategy
Fail count last session, for comparison
The one element I will fix before the next session
items.teaching_focus: Session-to-session fail count is the drill's own scoring instruction, and it only works if the sheet is kept.

components.label: Deck-build specification — 15 images, seen cold
components.instructions: Follow this to build a deck you have not studied. Collect by search and save without examining: the discipline is not to look. Rebuild a third of the deck every fourth session so you are never reciting from memory.

items.text: Composition of a 15-image deck
fields: 5 from your own first-due — street-level views of buildings you will actually go to
4 residential of construction types you rarely see
3 commercial or mixed-use with a difficult approach
2 with a visible complication — solar array, security bars, grade change, exposure
1 that is not a fire building at all, so 'nothing showing' stays in the answer set
items.teaching_focus: The last row matters: an officer who has only practiced on fire buildings will find a fire in every photo.

items.text: Sourcing rules — read before you collect
fields: Photographs you took yourself: always fine
Your department's own photographs: fine with your department's permission
Someone else's fireground photographs: not yours to redistribute, and not to be loaded into a shared deck
Mapping and street-view services: check the service's terms before saving or sharing images from them
Where you saved this deck, and whether it stays on your own device
items.teaching_focus: A personal deck on your own phone and a deck circulated around the department are different things with different rules.

items.text: Session mechanics
fields: Slideshow set to 10 seconds per image
Voice recorder running for the whole session, not per image
Format card face down until playback
No stopping and restarting — a fumbled report is a rep

components.label: Building-geometry specs — construction and access only
components.instructions: These eight generated images train construction reading, access reading, and the geometry of an approach. They contain no smoke and no fire, on purpose. Use them for the BUILDING element of the report and for the walk-around questions; use real photographs for the CONDITIONS element, because that is the one a generated image cannot teach.

items.text: Balloon-frame two-and-a-half story dwelling — identify the construction, the void spaces it implies, and where fire travels that you cannot see.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clear daytime architectural photograph-style image of a two-and-a-half story older American wood-frame house with clapboard siding, a steep gable roof with a dormer, a full-width front porch, and tall narrow windows. Neutral overcast light, no smoke, no fire, no people, no vehicles. Three-quarter view from the street showing the front and one side.
items.alt: Two-and-a-half story older wood-frame house with clapboard siding, steep gabled roof with a dormer, full-width front porch, and tall narrow windows, seen from the street at a three-quarter angle.
items.teaching_focus: Age and form as construction evidence, and the vertical void the form implies.

items.text: Lightweight-truss single-story ranch with a renovated facade — identify what the facade hides and state what you would want confirmed before committing to the roof.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clear daytime architectural photograph-style image of a single-story suburban ranch house with a low-pitched roof, recently updated stone veneer on the front elevation, vinyl siding on the visible side elevation, and an attached two-car garage. Neutral overcast light, no smoke, no fire, no people. Three-quarter view showing the mismatch between the front and side finishes.
items.alt: Single-story ranch house with a low-pitched roof, new stone veneer on the front and vinyl siding on the side, with an attached two-car garage.
items.teaching_focus: A renovation that changes the appearance and not the structure. The finish mismatch is the tell.

items.text: Three-story garden apartment building — identify the access, count the units in view, and state where your line goes.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clear daytime architectural photograph-style image of a three-story garden apartment building with brick lower level and siding above, exterior stairs and open breezeways serving the upper floors, multiple identical entry doors visible, and a parking lot in the foreground. Neutral overcast light, no smoke, no fire, no people, no vehicles.
items.alt: Three-story garden apartment building with brick lower level, siding above, exterior stairs and open breezeways, several identical entry doors, and a parking lot in front.
items.teaching_focus: Turning a repeating facade into a stretch estimate and an apartment number.

items.text: Commercial strip with security bars and a deep footprint — identify the occupancy type, the access problem, and what you require before entry.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clear daytime architectural photograph-style image of a single-story commercial strip building with four adjacent storefronts, flat roof with a parapet, large plate-glass display windows fitted with metal security bars, roll-down shutter on one unit, and a wide sidewalk with parking in front. Neutral overcast light, no smoke, no fire, no people, no vehicles.
items.alt: Single-story commercial strip with four storefronts, flat parapet roof, plate-glass windows fitted with metal security bars, and a roll-down shutter on one unit.
items.teaching_focus: Egress and access as size-up elements, and the depth you cannot see from the front.

items.text: Dwelling on a downslope with a walk-out below grade — identify the floor count from the front and from the rear, and state what the difference does to your size-up.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clear daytime architectural photograph-style image of a suburban house built on a downward-sloping lot, appearing as a single story from the street side and revealing an additional full walk-out lower level with a patio door at the rear because of the grade change. Wide three-quarter view capturing both the street elevation and the drop in grade along the side. Neutral overcast light, no smoke, no fire, no people.
items.alt: House on a downward-sloping lot appearing single-story from the street and revealing a full walk-out lower level with a patio door at the rear due to the grade change.
items.teaching_focus: The building that is a different building from the back, which is the mechanism behind a large share of basement-fire reports.

items.text: Ordinary-construction mixed-use main-street building — identify the construction, the occupancies stacked in it, and the collapse concern.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clear daytime architectural photograph-style image of a three-story brick mixed-use main-street building with a commercial storefront at ground level, residential windows on the two upper floors, a flat roof with a decorative cornice and parapet, and a fire escape on the visible side elevation. Neutral overcast light, no smoke, no fire, no people, no vehicles.
items.alt: Three-story brick mixed-use building with a commercial storefront at street level, residential windows above, flat roof with cornice and parapet, and a fire escape on the side.
items.teaching_focus: Occupancy stacking, and the parapet and cornice as collapse features.

items.text: Large single-story open-span commercial building — identify the construction and state what the span does to your interior operations.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clear daytime architectural photograph-style image of a large single-story big-box commercial building with concrete tilt-up walls, a very wide flat roof, roof-mounted HVAC units visible along the roofline, a single main customer entrance, and a loading dock at one end. Wide view from across a large empty parking lot. Neutral overcast light, no smoke, no fire, no people, no vehicles.
items.alt: Large single-story big-box commercial building with concrete tilt-up walls, wide flat roof with roof-mounted HVAC units, one main entrance, and a loading dock at one end.
items.teaching_focus: Span, distance to the seat, and the orientation problem — the LODD-002 lesson, in a building with nothing showing.

items.text: Nothing showing — a residential street view with no visible complication. Give the report anyway.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clear daytime architectural photograph-style image of an unremarkable two-story suburban wood-frame house with vinyl siding, an attached garage, a concrete driveway and a small front lawn. Completely ordinary, nothing unusual, no smoke, no fire, no people, no vehicles. Straight-on view from the street.
items.alt: Ordinary two-story suburban wood-frame house with vinyl siding, attached garage, concrete driveway and front lawn, seen straight on from the street.
items.teaching_focus: The report for the building with nothing showing, which is most of the calls and none of the practice.

sources: Self-authored format card frame, scoring sheet, and deck-build specification
Department radio report SOP (user-supplied and authoritative; not reproduced)
Reading Smoke curriculum (Dodson) — cited by the drill; not reproduced here
packs.synthetic_caveat: The building images are AI-generated and contain no smoke or fire by design. They train the BUILDING element — construction, height, occupancy, access, grade — and nothing else. Smoke reading depends on volume, velocity, density and color behaving the way real fire behaves, and a generated image can get that wrong in ways a trainee cannot detect, teaching a false read of a real fire. Use real photographs or video for conditions; this pack will not supply them.

packs.title: Tactical Decision Game Set — 12 Sand-Table Problems
packs.summary: Twelve tabletop problems with the sketch to draw, the information the crew is given, the information deliberately withheld, and the decision the facilitator is listening for — plus a facilitator card on how to run a TDG without turning it into a lecture and a debrief sheet.
packs.removes_prep: A tactical decision game is only as good as the problem, and writing a good one is genuinely hard: it needs enough information to decide, a real dilemma with no free answer, and something important left out on purpose. A facilitator inventing one at the table produces a problem with an obvious answer.
packs.local_fill_note: Every problem says 'your district' and 'your staffing'. Set the resources to what actually responds to you, not to a textbook first alarm, or the crew will solve a problem they will never have.

components.label: Twelve problems
components.instructions: Sketch the layout on the whiteboard or sand table before reading the brief. Read the brief, state the resources on scene and en route, then give a strict time limit — two minutes to a committed answer. Do not answer questions during the clock; what they ask you is diagnostic. Take answers from the most junior member first.

items.text: Single-family dwelling, fire in a rear bedroom, one car in the drive, no report of occupants. Your actual first-alarm staffing. Two minutes.
items.answer: Listening for: a mode declared, a line assigned with a stated purpose, a search decision justified by the car rather than assumed, and an explicit statement of what is NOT being done with the staffing available.
items.teaching_focus: The baseline problem. Everyone should solve this one; it calibrates the group.

items.text: Same dwelling, same fire, but the only hydrant is 600 ft away on the opposite side of a divided road.
items.answer: Listening for: a water-supply decision made before committing to interior operations, tank-water arithmetic stated out loud, and whether the officer holds the attack until supply is established or accepts a limited window and says so.
items.teaching_focus: Supply as a decision with a clock on it.

items.text: Two-story dwelling, fire on the first floor, a person at a second-floor window.
items.answer: Listening for: whether the ladder and the line are assigned in a defensible order with the staffing present, and whether the officer states the risk they are accepting. There is no free answer here and the facilitator must not supply one.
items.teaching_focus: A genuine dilemma. If the crew reaches consensus quickly, push them on what they gave up.

items.text: Commercial strip, smoke from one unit, security bars front, rear access unconfirmed, 8 minutes to the second alarm.
items.answer: Listening for: exterior posture stated without embarrassment, forcible-entry preparation started, a reassessment trigger named, and somebody sent to confirm the rear.
items.teaching_focus: Deciding to wait, out loud, with a reason.

items.text: Apartment building, fire in a second-floor unit, occupants self-evacuating, one unaccounted for.
items.answer: Listening for: search assignment that accounts for the reported missing occupant, a line between the fire and the egress route, and accountability for who is where in a building with repeating layouts.
items.teaching_focus: Search and protect-egress as competing uses of the same crew.

items.text: Basement fire, two-story dwelling, smoke from a window well, interior stair the only known access.
items.answer: Listening for: recognition that this is a below-grade fire before anyone descends, a second means of access sought, and an explicit decision about attacking from the stair versus from outside.
items.teaching_focus: The basement problem, which NIOSH findings return to repeatedly.

items.text: Vacant boarded structure, fire on two floors, known previous squatter occupancy.
items.answer: Listening for: risk-benefit stated explicitly and a defensive decision reached without apology, plus what specific new information would change it.
items.teaching_focus: The building the fire service loses people in most often.

items.text: Working fire, and en route you are told your second-due is committed elsewhere.
items.answer: Listening for: the plan changing on the information rather than after arrival, a request made early, and the officer's first assignment reflecting the reduced resources.
items.teaching_focus: Re-planning before arrival, which officers rarely rehearse.

items.text: Fire in a large single-story commercial with an unknown interior layout, nothing showing from the front.
items.answer: Listening for: a 360 demanded before commitment, stretch length estimated out loud, and orientation requirements set for anyone going in.
items.teaching_focus: The Charleston lesson at district scale.

items.text: Car fire against the exterior wall of an occupied dwelling.
items.answer: Listening for: the exposure treated as the actual problem, and a decision about whether anyone needs to go inside.
items.teaching_focus: The routine call where the risk is not where the fire is.

items.text: Working fire; five minutes in, an interior crew reports they cannot find their way out.
items.answer: Listening for: the mayday handled as a mayday, RIT deployed rather than a nearby crew grabbed, the attack maintained rather than abandoned, and a PAR started.
items.teaching_focus: Doing two things at once — the OFF-006 skill in a tabletop.

items.text: Your worst building. Somebody names it, the group sketches it, and the officer commands it.
items.answer: No answer key. The value is that the group argues about a real address, and the argument is the pre-incident planning nobody scheduled.
items.teaching_focus: Deliberately last, deliberately open. This is the problem crews remember.

components.label: Facilitator card — how not to ruin a TDG
components.instructions: Read this once before your first session. Every failure mode listed here is one that makes the game feel productive while teaching nothing.

items.text: Give a hard clock. Two minutes to a committed answer. A TDG without time pressure rehearses deliberation, which is not the skill.
items.teaching_focus: Time pressure is the whole mechanism.

items.text: Junior member answers first, every time. Otherwise the senior officer answers and everyone agrees, and you have learned one person's tactics.
items.teaching_focus: Answer order determines whether you get twelve opinions or one.

items.text: Do not answer questions on the clock. Note what was asked — a question about the building is size-up they should have assumed; a question about resources is something you should have stated.
items.teaching_focus: The questions are data about your brief and about their habits.

items.text: Never supply the right answer on a dilemma problem. If the group wants absolution, make them state what they gave up instead.
items.teaching_focus: Problems with free answers are not problems.

items.text: Insist on a mode. An answer without offensive or defensive in it is not an answer, and this is the most common gap.
items.teaching_focus: Same failure OFF-001 scores for.

items.text: Stop while it is still interesting. Three problems well argued beats twelve rushed.

components.label: Debrief sheet
components.instructions: One row per problem. Fill it during the session, not afterwards. The patterns across a few sessions matter more than any single answer.

items.text: Problem row
fields: Problem number
Mode declared without prompting (Y/N)
Line purpose stated (Y/N)
What was NOT being done, stated (Y/N)
Time to committed answer
Where the group disagreed

items.text: Patterns after a few sessions
fields: The element most often missing
Who we have never heard answer first
The problem type we are weakest on
One thing to drill with our hands as a result
items.teaching_focus: Ending a tabletop by naming a hands-on drill is what keeps it from being a talk.

sources: Self-authored problems, facilitator card and debrief sheet

packs.title: PAR Injects — 10 Accountability Events and a Board Sheet
packs.summary: Ten timed injects for the facilitator to feed a command element — a company that answers for a member who is not with them, a unit that never checked in, a PAR taken during a mayday — plus an accountability board sheet the IC keeps, so the debrief compares the board against what was actually true.
packs.removes_prep: The drill distributes companies through a building 'on simulated assignments' with a 'command element with the accountability board' and supplies no injects. Without them the drill becomes a PAR that everybody passes, because nothing is ever wrong. The failures have to be engineered or the board is never tested.
packs.local_fill_note: Accountability hardware and PAR procedure differ sharply — tags, passports, electronic, or a grease board — and so does what a PAR is expected to contain. Write your system and your PAR script on the board sheet before the first inject and score against those.

components.label: Facilitator injects
components.instructions: Facilitator only. Feed one inject at a time by radio to the company concerned, privately, so the command element learns of it only through the accountability system. Note the time you injected and the time command detected it — the gap is the drill's primary measurement. Do not tell command an inject has happened.

items.text: INJECT 1 — Tell Engine 2's officer that one of their members has been sent to the apparatus for a tool and will not return for four minutes. Instruct the officer to answer the next PAR for their full crew.
items.answer: Detected when command's PAR asks for a count and the officer's answer is checked against the board, or when the member is seen at the apparatus. Most command elements accept the officer's word. That is the lesson: a PAR is a report, and a report can be wrong.
items.teaching_focus: The most common real accountability failure, and the one no PAR script catches by itself.

items.text: INJECT 2 — Tell a company to change floors without announcing it.
items.answer: Detected when command's board no longer matches where the company is. Score how long the board was wrong and what finally surfaced it.
items.teaching_focus: The board as a live document rather than a record of assignments given.

items.text: INJECT 3 — Instruct one company to be slow answering the PAR — fifteen seconds late, then answer normally.
items.answer: Detected by whether command notices a delay at all, and what they do in those fifteen seconds. Correct handling is a repeat call and a clock started, not waiting quietly.
items.teaching_focus: The interval between a missed answer and an action, which is where mayday delays begin.

items.text: INJECT 4 — Instruct a company not to answer the PAR at all.
items.answer: Command must escalate: repeat, then a second means, then treat it as a mayday for that company. Score the time from the missed answer to a declared emergency.
items.teaching_focus: The full escalation, which most command elements have never actually run.

items.text: INJECT 5 — Send a company to a task command did not assign them, on their own initiative.
items.answer: Detected by the board, or not at all. The debrief covers both the freelancing and the accountability system that permitted it.
items.teaching_focus: Freelancing as an accountability event rather than a discipline issue.

items.text: INJECT 6 — Have a member report to a different company mid-incident because that crew needed hands.
items.answer: Both officers and the board must reflect the move. Almost never does. Score which of the three records was wrong.
items.teaching_focus: Crew composition changing during an incident, which real fires do constantly.

items.text: INJECT 7 — Have a company report they are exiting, then not exit for three minutes.
items.answer: Command's board says outside; the company is inside. Score whether anything reconciles the report against reality, and what would have.
items.teaching_focus: The dangerous direction of error — believing someone is out when they are in.

items.text: INJECT 8 — Feed a mayday from a member, then require command to take a full PAR while managing it.
items.answer: The PAR must continue and be completed, because the point of a PAR during a mayday is to establish who else is unaccounted for. Score whether command abandoned the PAR to work the mayday.
items.teaching_focus: Doing both at once, which is what the fireground actually requires and what drills usually separate.

items.text: INJECT 9 — Have a late-arriving unit begin work without checking in with command.
items.answer: A unit operating that is not on the board. Score how it was discovered and how long it took.
items.teaching_focus: The arriving-unit failure, which grows worse as the incident grows.

items.text: INJECT 10 — Nothing. Take a PAR where everything is exactly as the board says.
items.answer: Everything matches. The inject is here so command practices a clean PAR at the same tempo, and so the crew does not learn that a PAR is a game of find-the-error.
items.teaching_focus: The control card. Without it the drill trains suspicion instead of process.

components.label: Accountability board sheet
components.instructions: Kept by the command element for the whole evolution. Write your PAR script and your system at the top. After the last inject, put the sheet beside the facilitator's inject log and compare — that comparison is the debrief.

items.text: My system and script — before the first inject
fields: Accountability system in use — tags, passport, electronic, board
Our PAR script, word for word
What a complete PAR answer contains for us
Our interval for routine PARs

items.text: Live board
fields: Company
Members and count
Assignment as given
Location as last reported
Time of last contact
Air state if reported
items.teaching_focus: The time-of-last-contact column is the one that turns a board into an accountability tool rather than a roster.

items.text: Debrief comparison
fields: Injects detected, by number
Injects missed, by number
Longest interval between an inject and its detection
Which column of the board would have caught the missed ones
One change to the PAR script
items.teaching_focus: Fixing the script or the board, rather than telling people to pay more attention.

packs.title: Smoke Reading Session Kit — Source Guide, Worksheet, Scoring
packs.summary: A guide to the public video sources worth using and how to prepare a clip for a session, the four-attribute observation worksheet, a pause-point protocol, and a scoring sheet. Contains no imagery at all, by design — smoke reading has to be trained on real fire.
packs.removes_prep: The drill needs fireground videos and a worksheet and supplies neither. Finding clips that are usable — long enough, steady enough, showing the building and the smoke together, and not just the dramatic ten seconds — is an evening of searching, and the worksheet is the part that turns watching into training.
packs.local_fill_note: Your department's smoke-reading terminology and your SOP's condition-reporting language are what the worksheet scores against. Write them at the top. Where a source video's narration disagrees with your training, your training governs the session.

components.label: Source guide — where clips come from, and what makes one usable
components.instructions: Read once, then use it as a checklist while building a session. This pack contains no video and no images: smoke reading depends on how fire actually behaves, and a generated or reconstructed image can be wrong in ways a trainee cannot detect. Clips must be real.

items.text: USABLE CLIP TEST — Does it show the building AND the smoke in the same frame for at least thirty continuous seconds, from a fixed or slow-moving viewpoint, before anything dramatic happens?
items.answer: If not, it is unusable for this drill regardless of how impressive it is. The reading happens in the boring part.
items.teaching_focus: The single filter that removes most of what a search returns.

items.text: SOURCES WORTH USING — Your own department's incident footage, with permission. Neighboring departments' training footage, with permission. Publicly posted training and fire-behavior research footage from fire-service educational organisations and research institutes.
items.teaching_focus: Research footage is often the best: fixed camera, known fuel load, known ventilation.

items.text: SOURCES TO BE CAREFUL WITH — Bystander clips posted publicly. They are real, which is what matters, but they are somebody else's material: use them by playing the clip from its source in a training session rather than downloading, re-editing and redistributing it.
items.teaching_focus: The difference between showing a crew a video and building a product out of it.

items.text: WHAT TO CHECK BEFORE THE SESSION — Watch the whole clip yourself first. You need to know what happens so you can set the pause points, and you must not be surprised in front of the crew by an injury, a fatality, or a family member on camera.
items.teaching_focus: The respectful-framing check. Somebody's worst day is not session filler.

items.text: SESSION SHAPE — Four to six clips, thirty to ninety seconds of usable footage each. Pause at 0:10 for the initial read, at 0:30 and 1:00 for updates, then play to the end and reconcile.
items.teaching_focus: Reading change over time is the thing photos cannot teach, so the pauses are the drill.

items.text: YOUR TERMINOLOGY — before clip one
fields: Our department's words for smoke conditions
Do we report a stage, and in what terms
Our SOP's required condition-reporting elements
items.teaching_focus: Score against your own language, not the video narrator's.

components.label: Four-attribute observation worksheet
components.instructions: One sheet per clip. Fill in the first block at the 0:10 pause, before any discussion — writing first and talking second is what stops the group converging on whoever spoke loudest.

items.text: 0:10 — first read
fields: VOLUME — how much, relative to the size of the building
VELOCITY — how fast, and is it pressure or buoyancy
DENSITY — how thick; what does that say about the fuel in it
COLOR — and what it suggests about stage and location
Where is the fire — floor and area
What would you transmit
items.teaching_focus: Velocity misread as volume is the classic error. Force the two apart on paper.

items.text: 0:30 and 1:00 — updates
fields: What changed in each attribute
Is the change telling you the fire is growing, being ventilated, or being controlled
Would your mode change (Y/N) and why
What you would transmit now
items.teaching_focus: Change over time. The whole reason this drill needs video and not photographs.

items.text: After the reveal
fields: Where the fire actually was
Which attribute you read correctly
Which attribute misled you, and what you would look at next time
Anything visible in hindsight that you looked straight past

components.label: Session scoring sheet
components.instructions: Track across clips and across sessions. Individual clips are noisy; the pattern in a member's errors is the useful signal.

items.text: Per clip
fields: Clip number
All four attributes recorded before discussion (Y/N)
Fire location called correctly (Y/N)
Mode implied or stated (Y/N)
Update at each pause (Y/N)

items.text: Pattern
fields: The attribute this member consistently misreads
Do they over-call or under-call severity
One thing to look at first on the next clip
Next session date
items.teaching_focus: Over-calling and under-calling are different faults with different fixes.

packs.title: Transfer of Command Kit — 8 Handovers, Card, Floor Plans
packs.summary: Eight transfer scenarios with the incident state the first-in IC has to hand over, a pocket handover card structured so nothing important can be forgotten under pressure, and three simple floor plans to command from. Scored on what survived the handover, not on how it sounded.
packs.removes_prep: The drill's equipment list names a card, a worksheet and floor plans and supplies none. Worse, a transfer drill needs a plausible incident STATE to hand over — resources committed, assignments given, conditions changing — and inventing a consistent one on the spot is most of the work.
packs.local_fill_note: Your department's transfer-of-command procedure and its required elements govern. Write them on the card before the first rep; where the card's structure differs from your procedure, your procedure wins.

components.label: Eight handover scenarios
components.instructions: Give the first-in IC the incident state privately and two minutes to command it on the floor plan. Then the arriving chief walks up and the transfer happens face to face, on the radio, in real time. Nobody prepares notes. The receiving officer is then questioned by the facilitator about the incident — what they cannot answer is what did not survive the handover.

items.text: SIMPLE — Single-family dwelling, one line in operation on a room-and-contents fire, two companies on scene, primary search underway, everyone accounted for, conditions improving.
items.answer: Should transfer cleanly. Listening for: conditions, what has been done, who is where, what is left. If this one does not survive, nothing harder will.
items.teaching_focus: Baseline. Calibrates the group before the hard ones.

items.text: MID-INCIDENT CHANGE — Same dwelling, but you have just requested a second alarm and it has not arrived. One company is committed interior, one is on supply.
items.answer: The pending request is the item most often lost. Listening for: what has been ordered but not arrived, and what the receiving IC is now waiting on.
items.teaching_focus: Handing over the future, not just the present.

items.text: UNRESOLVED SEARCH — Two-story dwelling, primary search of the second floor incomplete, one occupant reported and not found, crew still working.
items.answer: The unresolved item must be stated first and unambiguously. Listening for whether the receiving IC repeats it back.
items.teaching_focus: The one thing that must not be lost, and the read-back that proves it was not.

items.text: ACCOUNTABILITY GAP — You believe everyone is accounted for but your last PAR was four minutes ago and one company has changed floors since.
items.answer: The honest handover states the uncertainty. Listening for whether the first-in IC says 'my accountability is four minutes old' or implies it is current.
items.teaching_focus: Handing over doubt. Officers smooth this over instinctively.

items.text: DEFENSIVE TRANSITION IN PROGRESS — You have just ordered crews out and the collapse zone is being established. Not everyone is out yet.
items.answer: Listening for: the order given, who has acknowledged, who has not, and where the zone is. A transfer during a withdrawal is the highest-risk handover on the list.
items.teaching_focus: Transferring mid-manoeuvre, when the incident is between two states.

items.text: MAYDAY ACTIVE — A mayday was declared ninety seconds ago, RIT is deploying, the attack is still in place.
items.answer: Most procedures counsel against transferring during an active mayday. Listening for whether the arriving chief takes command anyway, delays deliberately, or takes it and immediately states the mayday status back. Any of the three can be right; not deciding is not.
items.teaching_focus: Whether the arriving officer knows their own procedure well enough to decline.

items.text: COMMERCIAL, LARGE — Open-span commercial, long stretch, two lines, orientation concerns, air a limiting factor, second alarm arriving.
items.answer: Listening for: distances and air state as numbers rather than impressions, and a statement of the reversal trigger the first-in IC had set.
items.teaching_focus: Handing over numbers. Impressions do not transfer.

items.text: YOU ARE THE ARRIVING CHIEF AND THE HANDOVER IS BAD — The first-in IC gives you a vague, disordered picture. State what you do.
items.answer: Listening for: specific questions asked in priority order, a PAR called, and command assumed with a clear announcement rather than a drifting half-transfer. The failure mode is politeness.
items.teaching_focus: The receiving officer's responsibility. A bad handover is a shared problem.

components.label: Handover card
components.instructions: Pocket size. Fill in your department's required elements first. The order matters: unresolved and unsafe items go first, because a handover can be interrupted and the first thirty seconds are the only guaranteed part.

items.text: FIRST — anything unresolved or unsafe
fields: Anyone unaccounted for, or search incomplete
Any mayday, injury, or withdrawal in progress
Any collapse or structural concern
How old is my accountability information
items.teaching_focus: Front-loading the items that kill people if the handover is cut short.

items.text: CONDITIONS
fields: Building — size, height, occupancy, construction
Fire location and behavior, and the direction it is going
What has changed since arrival

items.text: ACTIONS
fields: Mode, and any change to it
Every company and its assignment and location
Water supply status
What I ordered that has NOT arrived

items.text: NEEDS AND INTENT
fields: What I was about to do next
The reversal trigger I had set
What I need from you
items.teaching_focus: Intent is the part that is almost never handed over, and it is what stops the incident restarting from zero.

items.text: CONFIRM
fields: Receiving officer repeats back the unresolved items (Y/N)
Command announced on the radio (Y/N)
Time
items.teaching_focus: The read-back. Without it a handover is a monologue.

components.label: Three command floor plans
components.instructions: Print at a size two officers can both point at. Mark companies with tokens or dry-erase. They are deliberately generic and simple — the incident state is what makes the scenario, not the drawing.

items.text: Plan A — single-family dwelling, two floors plus basement, one stair.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical plan-view line drawing of a simple two-story single-family house floor plan, showing the ground floor with living room, kitchen, hall and a single staircase, and the upper floor with three bedrooms and a bathroom off a landing, plus a basement outline shown inset. Plain white background, thin dark lines, minimal room labels, architectural-drawing style, no furniture, no fire, no smoke.
items.alt: Technical plan-view drawing of a two-story single-family house showing ground-floor living room, kitchen and hall with one staircase, an upper floor with three bedrooms and a bathroom, and an inset basement outline.
items.teaching_focus: One stair, three bedrooms, a basement. Most of the residential scenarios happen here.

items.text: Plan B — garden apartment building, three floors, exterior stairs, repeating units.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical plan-view line drawing of a three-story garden apartment building floor plan, showing six identical apartment units per floor arranged either side of an open breezeway, with exterior stairs at both ends and unit numbers. Plain white background, thin dark lines, minimal labels, architectural-drawing style, no furniture, no fire, no smoke.
items.alt: Technical plan-view drawing of a garden apartment floor with six identical units either side of an open breezeway and exterior stairs at both ends.
items.teaching_focus: Repeating layouts are an accountability problem before they are a tactical one.

items.text: Plan C — single-story open-span commercial with a rear warehouse.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical plan-view line drawing of a large single-story commercial building floor plan: a wide open sales floor with scattered structural columns, a front customer entrance, a rear stockroom separated by a partition wall, a loading dock at the rear, and two marked exit doors on the side elevations. Plain white background, thin dark lines, minimal labels, architectural-drawing style, no furniture, no fire, no smoke.
items.alt: Technical plan-view drawing of a large single-story commercial building with an open sales floor, structural columns, front entrance, rear stockroom, loading dock and two side exits.
items.teaching_focus: Distances on a plan make the stretch and the air problem visible to both officers at once.

packs.title: Mayday Command Kit — 8 Injects, 60-Second Card, Floor Plans
packs.summary: Eight mayday injects with the incident state around them, a first-60-seconds command card in strict order, and the floor plans to command from. The injects are built so the mayday is never the only thing happening — because the failure this drill hunts is abandoning the fire to work the mayday.
packs.removes_prep: The drill's equipment list names cards, a worksheet and floor plans, and supplies none. A mayday command drill also needs a running incident for the mayday to land inside; without it the officer manages a mayday in a vacuum, which is the one situation that never happens.
packs.local_fill_note: Your department's mayday procedure, your RIT assignment, and your emergency-traffic channel plan govern the order on the command card. Fill them in first — an officer rehearsing the wrong order is worse off than one rehearsing nothing.

components.label: Eight injects
components.instructions: Set the incident up first and let the officer command it for two or three minutes so there is something real to lose. Then deliver the mayday by radio, in the member's own voice, and start a visible clock. Facilitator plays every other company. Do not help. At sixty seconds, stop and freeze the board.

items.text: INJECT 1 — Through the floor. A nozzle firefighter on the first floor of a two-story dwelling has fallen into the basement. Two other companies are working. Attack line is flowing.
items.answer: Listening for, inside 60 seconds: mayday acknowledged by name, RIT deployed with a location and a route, the attack MAINTAINED, a PAR started, and a resource request. The commonest failure is stopping the attack — which removes the only thing protecting the member below.
items.teaching_focus: Keeping the fire under control is part of the rescue, not a distraction from it.

items.text: INJECT 2 — Disorientation, location unknown. A member is lost on the second floor and cannot say where they are.
items.answer: Listening for: everything that narrows the location extracted by question — which side they entered, which direction they searched, how long. Then RIT committed to a named side rather than 'the second floor'.
items.teaching_focus: Turning 'I do not know' into a search sector.

items.text: INJECT 3 — Entanglement, member calm and breathing, air adequate. Meanwhile a second company reports the fire is extending.
items.answer: Listening for: both problems held at once. A calm mayday still gets RIT; the extension still gets a line. Officers who serialise these lose one of them.
items.teaching_focus: Two problems, one officer. The core skill of the drill.

items.text: INJECT 4 — Low air, egress compromised, member oriented. Second alarm arriving simultaneously.
items.answer: Listening for: the arriving companies assigned rather than parked, air state used to set a clock, and the clock stated out loud to RIT.
items.teaching_focus: Air as the incident's timer, announced so everyone shares it.

items.text: INJECT 5 — Officer-declared mayday for a member who has stopped answering. Nobody knows if there is a problem.
items.answer: Listening for: treated as a full mayday without waiting for confirmation, and a PAR run in parallel rather than instead.
items.teaching_focus: Acting on absence of information.

items.text: INJECT 6 — Mayday, and forty seconds later a second, unrelated mayday from a different company.
items.answer: Listening for: two separate rescue efforts, not one merged one; a request for enough resources for both; and an explicit statement of which is more urgent and why. Also listening for a defensive decision — two maydays is often the moment to get everyone out.
items.teaching_focus: The scenario that breaks a single-RIT plan, and the withdrawal decision it should prompt.

items.text: INJECT 7 — Mayday from a member on the roof. Interior crews are unaffected and do not know.
items.answer: Listening for: the interior told, because a roof problem changes what is above them, and RIT tasked with an exterior approach rather than an interior one.
items.teaching_focus: Information flowing to the people the emergency affects indirectly.

items.text: INJECT 8 — Mayday resolved: the member self-rescues thirty seconds in. Everything is still deployed.
items.answer: Listening for: a clear all-clear transmitted, the member accounted for physically and medically, RIT reconstituted before anyone goes back to work, and the incident resumed deliberately. The failure mode is relief and drift.
items.teaching_focus: Closing a mayday properly, which no drill ever practices because they all end at the rescue.

components.label: First 60 seconds card
components.instructions: Pocket size, and rehearse it in order until the order is automatic. Fill in your department's specifics first. Under stress an officer will retrieve a rehearsed sequence and nothing else, so the sequence is the deliverable.

items.text: 0-10s — ACKNOWLEDGE
fields: Repeat the member's identity back so they know they were heard
Our procedure's words for acknowledging a mayday
Emergency traffic channel or tone we use
items.teaching_focus: The member's next action depends on knowing someone heard. Ten seconds of silence is a self-rescue attempt starting.

items.text: 10-25s — GET LUNAR AND FIX A LOCATION
fields: The two questions that narrow location fastest for us
Air state asked for explicitly (Y/N)
Where I write it down

items.text: 25-40s — DEPLOY RIT
fields: Who is our RIT, by position, on a first alarm
Route and entry point stated
What they take

items.text: 40-55s — HOLD THE FIREGROUND
fields: Attack maintained — who confirms it
PAR started for everyone else
What I do NOT change
items.teaching_focus: The step officers skip. Written down so it cannot be.

items.text: 55-60s — RESOURCES AND CLOCK
fields: Alarm level requested
Air clock stated out loud
Second RIT considered (Y/N)

items.text: AFTER — closing it out
fields: All-clear transmitted
Member accounted for and evaluated
RIT reconstituted before work resumes
Incident resumed deliberately
items.teaching_focus: Inject 8's lesson, on the card so it is not an afterthought.

components.label: 60-second scoring sheet
components.instructions: Facilitator marks this live against the clock. Freeze the board at sixty seconds and score what was actually done, not what the officer intended.

items.text: The clock
fields: Seconds to acknowledgement
Seconds to RIT deployed
Seconds to PAR initiated
Was the attack ever stopped (Y/N) — and for how long
items.teaching_focus: Four numbers. They improve fast and they are the whole drill.

items.text: Content
fields: Location narrowed to something RIT could act on (Y/N)
Air state obtained (Y/N)
Resources requested (Y/N)
Everything else on the fireground still managed (Y/N)

items.text: Debrief
fields: The one step that came last and should not have
What the officer said they would do versus what the sheet shows
Next inject to run with this officer

components.label: Command floor plans
components.instructions: Reuse the three plans from OFF-005 if you have that pack; these two add the geometry the mayday injects need — a basement and a roof.

items.text: Plan D — dwelling with basement shown in section, so a through-the-floor mayday has somewhere to be.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical section-view line drawing of a two-story house cut vertically, showing basement, ground floor, upper floor and attic as distinct levels, with a single interior staircase connecting them, a basement window well on one side, and an exterior grade line. Plain white background, thin dark lines, minimal labels, architectural-drawing style, no furniture, no fire, no smoke.
items.alt: Technical vertical section drawing of a two-story house showing basement, ground floor, upper floor and attic, one interior staircase, a basement window well and the exterior grade line.
items.teaching_focus: A section, not a plan. Below-grade problems are vertical problems and a plan view hides that.

items.text: Plan E — single-story commercial roof plan, for the roof mayday.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical plan-view line drawing of a flat commercial roof: rectangular outline with a parapet edge, several roof-mounted mechanical units, two skylights, one roof hatch, and a marked ladder access point at one corner. Plain white background, thin dark lines, minimal labels, architectural-drawing style, no fire, no smoke, no damage.
items.alt: Technical plan-view drawing of a flat commercial roof with parapet edge, roof-mounted mechanical units, two skylights, a roof hatch and a marked ladder access point.
items.teaching_focus: Where the ladder is, and how far the member is from it, is the whole roof-mayday problem.
