packs.title: Nance Drill Set — Prop Card, 6 Variations, Timing Sheet
packs.summary: The prop build card with the dimensions the drill turns on, six variations that change what the crew must solve, and the timing sheet that records where the minutes actually went. Built around the drill's own honesty: this is a rescue that has failed more often than it has worked.
packs.removes_prep: The drill names scenario material and supplies none, and a through-the-floor rescue needs a prop built to consistent dimensions or the times mean nothing between sessions. Working the dimensions out from the drill text costs an afternoon and a tape measure.
packs.local_fill_note: Prop dimensions here are a starting point, not a standard: measure yours and brief any difference before the first rep, exactly as the drill instructs. Your department's rope, harness and rescue-system policy governs anything load-bearing, and nothing here authorises a technique your team is not trained in. Nothing in this pack authorises an improvised mechanical advantage, a live victim, or a technique your team is not trained and authorised to rig. If Method 3 on the drill is above your certification, skip it. Manikin only.

components.label: Prop build card
components.instructions: Build once, photograph it, and record the actual dimensions. Times only compare across sessions if the prop is the same. Anything load-bearing is inspected before every session by a second person.

items.text: The opening
fields: Opening dimensions, measured
Height from the lower level floor to the underside of the opening
Edge protection fitted (Y/N)
How the manikin's position below is standardized each rep
items.teaching_focus: The drop height is the variable that changes everything. Record it or the drill is not repeatable.

items.text: The load
fields: Manikin weight, confirmed on a scale
Dressed in full PPE and SCBA (Y/N)
Facepiece obscured (Y/N)
Position at the start of each rep — supine, prone, on a side
items.teaching_focus: A light manikin lets crews cheat the mechanics. Weigh it.

items.text: Safety before every session
fields: Manikin only. Never a live firefighter in the hole. If there is no manikin, the session does not run. (Y/N)
Edge protection is on. If it is not, the session does not run. (Y/N)
Safety officer named. Abort signal briefed. Load-bearing inspected by a second person. (Y/N)
Load-bearing components inspected by a second person (Y/N)
Anchor points rated and confirmed (Y/N)
Safety officer designated by name
Abort signal briefed to everyone (Y/N)
items.teaching_focus: A rescue drill that hurts someone has cost more than it taught.

components.label: Six variations
components.instructions: Run variation 1 until the crew has a working method, then change one thing at a time. Changing two at once means you learn nothing about either.

items.text: V1 — BASELINE. Member has fallen through, is on their back, conscious, can assist a little, opening clear, RIT arrives with a pack and a ladder.
items.answer: Establishes the crew's method and their baseline time. Listening for: air managed before movement, a plan stated before hands go on, and the ladder used rather than improvised around.
items.teaching_focus: Air first. Crews consistently move the member before addressing the air.

items.text: V2 — UNCONSCIOUS. Same geometry, no assistance from the member.
items.answer: Time typically doubles. Listening for the crew recognising early that this is now a lifting problem and calling for the hands they need instead of trying harder.
items.teaching_focus: Knowing when to ask for more people rather than more effort.

items.text: V3 — RESTRICTED OPENING. Reduce the opening so the member and a rescuer cannot both occupy it.
items.answer: Forces a decision about whether anyone goes below and how. Listening for a plan that does not put two members in a hole with one exit. Nobody goes below without their own air, their own radio, and a retrieval or second egress your rescue policy allows. Two members in a hole with one exit is a stop, not a working method.
items.teaching_focus: The rescuer-becomes-a-victim geometry.

items.text: V4 — ENTANGLED. Member is caught on something below.
items.answer: The lift will not work until the entanglement is cleared, and pulling harder makes it worse. Listening for the crew stopping and diagnosing rather than escalating force.
items.teaching_focus: Diagnose before force. The most transferable lesson in the set.

items.text: V5 — AIR CRITICAL. Member's air is nearly gone at the start of the rep.
items.answer: Air transfer or a facepiece change becomes the first task, not the rescue. Listening for the crew doing the air first even though it delays the extraction, and for a stated clock.
items.teaching_focus: The trade the crew must make deliberately, against instinct.

items.text: V6 — SECOND MEMBER. Partway through, a second member reports they are in trouble elsewhere.
items.answer: One RIT cannot do two rescues. Listening for that being said on the radio, a second RIT requested, and a defensible priority stated. Often the right answer is a withdrawal of everyone else.
items.teaching_focus: The scenario that exposes a single-RIT plan, and the honest conclusion it leads to.

components.label: Timing sheet
components.instructions: One row per rep, timed in segments rather than as a single total. The segment breakdown is the whole value: crews are usually slow in one specific place and cannot tell you which.

items.text: Segment times
fields: Arrival to plan stated
Plan to air addressed
Air to member packaged or secured
Packaged to member out of the hole
Out to a safe area
TOTAL
items.teaching_focus: Six numbers. The largest one is next session's drill.

items.text: Observations
fields: Was a plan stated before hands went on (Y/N)
Was air addressed before movement (Y/N)
Did anyone below have their own egress (Y/N)
Number of people used, and whether more were asked for

items.text: The honest column
fields: Would this have worked with the staffing that actually shows up here
What we would have to change to make it work
What this drill does NOT cover about a real one
One change for the next session
items.teaching_focus: The drill's own honesty, kept in writing. This rescue has failed more often than it has worked, and a crew that leaves believing otherwise has been taught the wrong thing.

sources: Self-authored prop card, variations and timing sheet
Department rope, harness and rescue-system policy (user-supplied and authoritative; no technique authorised here)

packs.title: Mayday Trigger Deck — 30 Conditions, Three Piles
packs.summary: Thirty condition cards written from inside the building, each sorted to MAYDAY NOW, URGENT-NOT-MAYDAY, or NORMAL with the reasoning on the back. Deliberately loaded with the borderline cases: the deck is only useful if a fair number of cards are genuinely arguable, because the argument is where the five-second decision gets built.
packs.removes_prep: The drill's setup says 'Write one fireground condition per card — the conditions you can find yourself in, not the ones you would see from outside.' Thirty cards is forty minutes of writing, and a member writing their own deck writes the conditions they already recognize. The cards they need are the ones they would not have thought of.
packs.local_fill_note: Sort placement follows widely taught mayday criteria, but your department's policy is the authority. Work through the deck once against your own SOP and re-sort any card where your policy differs — then keep your sort, not this one.

components.label: Condition cards
components.instructions: Write one condition per index card with the sort on the back, or use the pack on a phone one card per screen. Lay out three piles: MAYDAY NOW, URGENT-NOT-MAYDAY, NORMAL. Five-second timer per card, audible. Sort without deliberating, then check the backs. Second half: don the full PPE and SCBA, air off, and run the deck again — the sort should not change and the times will.

items.text: You are through the floor into a basement.
items.answer: MAYDAY NOW. Location changed involuntarily, below grade, egress unknown.
items.teaching_focus: The uncontested case. It is in the deck to calibrate the timer, not to teach.

items.text: You are tangled in wire and one pull did not free you.
items.answer: MAYDAY NOW. Entanglement that resists the first attempt burns air at working rate with no progress.
items.teaching_focus: One attempt, not five.

items.text: You have lost contact with your partner and you can still see the doorway you came in.
items.answer: URGENT-NOT-MAYDAY. Separation is urgent traffic; you are oriented and have egress. It becomes a mayday the moment either of those changes.
items.teaching_focus: Separation is not automatically a mayday — orientation is the discriminator.

items.text: You have lost contact with your partner and you do not know which way the door is.
items.answer: MAYDAY NOW. Separation plus disorientation.
items.teaching_focus: The pair with the previous card. Same event, different member state, different call.

items.text: Your low-air alarm activated and your exit is clear and short.
items.answer: NORMAL. Planned exit on an expected activation. Announce you are exiting.
items.teaching_focus: Not every alarm is an emergency, or the word stops meaning anything.

items.text: Your low-air alarm activated earlier than you expected and you are further in than you planned.
items.answer: MAYDAY NOW or urgent per policy — a mismatch between air and position is the classic run-out-of-air sequence starting.
items.teaching_focus: The surprise is the signal. An unexpected activation means the member's model of their own air was wrong.

items.text: You cannot find the wall you were searching.
items.answer: MAYDAY NOW. Loss of the orientation reference is disorientation, whatever else is fine.
items.teaching_focus: The card members most often put in the wrong pile.

items.text: Your facepiece seal broke and you have reseated it.
items.answer: MAYDAY NOW. Airway compromise, and the member cannot assess what they inhaled.
items.teaching_focus: 'I am fine now' is not an assessment available to the person who took the breath.

items.text: Your regulator is free-flowing and you cannot stop it.
items.answer: MAYDAY NOW. Uncontrolled air loss on a fixed supply.
items.teaching_focus: The clock is now much shorter than the gauge suggests.

items.text: You hear a PASS device somewhere ahead of you.
items.answer: MAYDAY NOW — for them. Transmit it as another member's emergency and be explicit that you are not the one in trouble.
items.teaching_focus: Calling for someone else without confusing the rescuers about who to look for.

items.text: The floor feels spongy under your knees and you have not fallen.
items.answer: URGENT-NOT-MAYDAY. Immediate withdrawal and urgent traffic so it protects everyone else on that floor.
items.teaching_focus: The transmission whose purpose is other people.

items.text: You are on a roof and you have found a second soft spot.
items.answer: URGENT-NOT-MAYDAY. Off the roof by the ladder, and transmit the hazard.
items.teaching_focus: Retreat still available means urgent, not mayday.

items.text: Your radio will not transmit and you are oriented with a clear exit.
items.answer: URGENT-NOT-MAYDAY in effect — you cannot transmit, so exit and report. Do not treat the exit as optional.
items.teaching_focus: The card with no radio answer. The action is physical.

items.text: Your radio will not transmit and you are lost.
items.answer: MAYDAY NOW by every non-radio means: PASS, tool on structure, get to an exterior wall or window, retry from a different body position.
items.teaching_focus: A mayday is a state, not a transmission. It is declared by whatever works.

items.text: You are pinned under a ceiling assembly and you can breathe and reach your radio.
items.answer: MAYDAY NOW. Transmit, then PASS.
items.teaching_focus: Sequence, again.

items.text: You are caught by the coat and you have already freed yourself.
items.answer: NORMAL. Note it, keep working, mention it in the debrief. A snag you cleared is not an event.
items.teaching_focus: Guarding against over-calling, which is how a deck teaches judgment rather than reflex.

items.text: You are three rooms in on a search and your gauge reads less than you would need to retrace your path at working rate.
items.answer: MAYDAY NOW. Air insufficient for known egress is a mayday before the alarm sounds, not after.
items.teaching_focus: The arithmetic version, which is the RIT-008 skill landing in a sort decision.

items.text: Conditions above you are deteriorating and your officer is beside you.
items.answer: URGENT-NOT-MAYDAY. Recommend withdrawal to the officer and get it on the radio.
items.teaching_focus: Having a superior beside you does not remove your obligation to transmit.

items.text: You have entered a basement by an interior stair and the stair is now producing heat you would not want to climb through.
items.answer: MAYDAY NOW. Below grade, primary egress compromised.
items.teaching_focus: Below-grade plus compromised egress is the most lethal combination in the deck.

items.text: You are in a large commercial space and you cannot see any boundary of the compartment you are in.
items.answer: MAYDAY NOW if you have also lost your reference; URGENT if you still have a hoseline or wall. Sort it by which is true for you.
items.teaching_focus: A card that is deliberately conditional. The member must state which version they are in.

items.text: Your hoseline has gone slack and you do not know why.
items.answer: URGENT-NOT-MAYDAY. Transmit it — a slack line means a supply problem, a burst, or a crew problem behind you — and begin following it out.
items.teaching_focus: Treating the line as an information channel, not just a tool.

items.text: You have followed your hoseline the wrong way for what feels like too long.
items.answer: MAYDAY NOW. You are disoriented on your own reference, which is worse than having none.
items.teaching_focus: Following the line the wrong way is a real and specific failure mode.

items.text: You are searching alone because your partner was reassigned and command knows.
items.answer: URGENT-NOT-MAYDAY. You are a crew of one inside. That is not a mayday and it is not normal. Transmit your location, that you are alone, and that you are coming out or holding for a partner. Command already knowing does not make a lone interior search a normal state.
items.teaching_focus: The sort this card is in is the lesson. Do not put lone interior search in the NORMAL pile.

items.text: You have found a civilian victim and you cannot move them alone.
items.answer: URGENT-NOT-MAYDAY. Urgent traffic with a location and a specific resource request. You are not in trouble; you have work you cannot do.
items.teaching_focus: Keeping 'I need help' distinct from 'I am in trouble'.

items.text: You have found a civilian victim, you cannot move them alone, and your air is low.
items.answer: MAYDAY NOW. The moment your own air enters the problem, you are in the problem.
items.teaching_focus: The pair with the previous card, and the honest one — members will hold this one back.

items.text: You are on the nozzle and the water has stopped.
items.answer: URGENT-NOT-MAYDAY. Transmit immediately, then decide about position. Water failure with conditions holding is urgent; water failure with conditions deteriorating around you is a mayday.
items.teaching_focus: The condition-dependent escalation, stated out loud.

items.text: You are disoriented but you can see daylight through smoke in one direction.
items.answer: MAYDAY NOW, and move toward it while transmitting. Seeing a possible exit does not un-lose you.
items.teaching_focus: The false-reassurance card.

items.text: You have a leg injury that you can still walk on and your exit is clear.
items.answer: URGENT-NOT-MAYDAY. Report the injury, exit, get evaluated. Do not finish the assignment on it.
items.teaching_focus: Injuries the member will minimize to avoid leaving the fire.

items.text: You have a leg injury you cannot walk on.
items.answer: MAYDAY NOW. Immobility is a mayday whatever your air and orientation.
items.teaching_focus: Mobility as an independent trigger.

items.text: Everything is fine, the job is going well, and you notice you have no idea how long you have been inside.
items.answer: URGENT-NOT-MAYDAY at least: check your gauge and your position immediately and report your air. Losing time awareness is a documented precursor, not a personality trait.
items.teaching_focus: The last card on purpose. Nothing is wrong, and that is the condition most reports describe just before something was.

sources: Self-authored condition cards
Sort reasoning drawn at pattern level from published NIOSH FFFIPP contributing factors
Department mayday policy (user-supplied, authoritative over this deck)

packs.title: Air Decision Deck — 12 Cards and a Policy Answer Key
packs.summary: Twelve air-decision scenario cards that force a turnaround call from a stated gauge reading and a stated distance in, plus the answer-key template the drill requires the member to build from their own air-management policy — blank where the numbers are local, structured so a wrong answer is visible.
packs.removes_prep: The drill says to write twelve cards and, before that, 'write your department's air-management decision points at the top of the answer key before you write a single card'. Members who do not know their policy's decision points cannot build the key, and so they build twelve cards that score against a guess.
packs.local_fill_note: Every number in this deck is a placeholder. Your department's air-management policy supplies the exit pressure, what a low-air activation means locally, and when the reserve becomes untouchable. Fill the key first; the cards are unscoreable without it.

components.label: Policy answer key — fill this first
components.instructions: Copy your department's air-management policy onto this key before you look at a single card. If your department has no written policy, that is the finding of this drill and it belongs in a conversation with your training officer, not in a guess on a card.

items.text: My department's stated decision points
fields: Pressure or fraction at which policy says begin exiting
What a low-air alarm activation means locally — exit now, or already late
The reserve that is not to be worked into, if stated
Policy document name and date
items.teaching_focus: Without these four, no card in the deck has a correct answer.

items.text: My own consumption, measured not assumed
fields: Cylinder rated duration
My measured working duration on a hard evolution
Ratio of measured to rated
Date measured
items.teaching_focus: The rated duration is a bench number. The member's own ratio is the one that predicts anything.

items.text: My out-and-back arithmetic
fields: Pressure used on the measured out-and-back path in this drill
So: pressure needed to retrace a path of that length at working rate
Margin I will hold above that
items.teaching_focus: Converting a distance into a pressure, which is the actual skill the deck tests.

components.label: Air decision cards
components.instructions: One card per index card. Draw, read the situation, and state out loud within five seconds: continue, turn around now, or declare. Then justify it against your key in one sentence. Record the calls; a card you got right with a wrong reason is a miss.

items.text: Two rooms in on a residential search, gauge at two-thirds. Conditions stable, partner with you, exit path known and short.
items.answer: Continue. Compare against your key's exit pressure and state the margin remaining.
items.teaching_focus: The easy continue, present so the deck is not all turnarounds.

items.text: Same search, gauge at half. You have covered about a third of the floor.
items.answer: Judgment: the arithmetic says a third of the floor cost a third of your air on the way in, and the way out costs the same. State whether your key leaves room for the remaining two-thirds. Usually it does not.
items.teaching_focus: Air as a budget with a return leg, not a countdown.

items.text: Commercial occupancy, long entry, gauge at half, and you are past the point where you can see your entry point.
items.answer: Turn around now. Long path plus no visual reference means the return leg is longer and slower than the trip in.
items.teaching_focus: The return leg is never as fast as the way in.

items.text: Gauge at your policy's exit pressure exactly. Nothing is wrong. You are one room from finishing the primary.
items.answer: Turn around now. The policy number is the decision point, not a target to shave. State out loud what the one room is worth against your key.
items.teaching_focus: The most common real-world violation, and the one members most want to argue about.

items.text: Gauge below your exit pressure and you did not notice until now. Exit is clear and short.
items.answer: Exit immediately and announce it. Whether this is urgent traffic or a mayday depends on the margin — check your key.
items.teaching_focus: The overrun that is discovered rather than chosen.

items.text: Gauge below your exit pressure and you are not certain of the way out.
items.answer: Declare. Air insufficient for uncertain egress is a mayday, not a fast walk.
items.teaching_focus: The combination that kills, stated plainly.

items.text: Low-air alarm activates. You expected it in about four more minutes.
items.answer: Declare or urgent per your key — an early activation means either a leak, a partial valve, or a consumption rate you did not predict. All three change your remaining time.
items.teaching_focus: The surprise activation as a diagnostic, not just a deadline.

items.text: You are on the nozzle at a working fire, gauge at half, and your officer tells you to hold position for two more minutes.
items.answer: State your air out loud to the officer as a number, then comply or object with the arithmetic. The correct answer is the transmission, not the obedience or the refusal.
items.teaching_focus: Air state as information the officer needs, delivered before it becomes an argument.

items.text: You are with a partner whose gauge reads considerably lower than yours. They have not mentioned it.
items.answer: The crew's air is the lower gauge. Say the number out loud, and both of you turn on their gauge, not yours.
items.teaching_focus: Crew air is a minimum, not an average.

items.text: You have found a victim. Moving them will take longer than you have above your exit pressure.
items.answer: Declare and request resources with the victim's location. Do not spend your reserve on a drag you cannot finish — a second casualty helps nobody.
items.teaching_focus: The hardest card in the deck, and the one worth the most argument in the debrief.

items.text: You are exiting on schedule and you find a second, closer exit you did not know about.
items.answer: Use it and report it. Then note the pre-incident lesson: the exit you did not know about was there the whole time.
items.teaching_focus: Rewarding the good outcome, and tying it back to building familiarisation.

items.text: You have been inside on air twice today already. Gauge on a fresh bottle, two rooms in, and you are more tired than the gauge knows.
items.answer: Continue with a raised margin and say so. Fatigue raises consumption and no gauge accounts for it; the key's number assumes a rested member.
items.teaching_focus: The card that has no number on it, because the variable is the member.

sources: Self-authored decision cards and key template
Department air-management policy (user-supplied and authoritative; not reproduced)

packs.title: Air Consumption Log & Work Circuit Card
packs.summary: The log sheets the drill's equipment list asks for, structured so a member ends up with their own consumption rate rather than a number from a manual, plus the work-circuit card that makes the circuit repeatable so the numbers compare across sessions.
packs.removes_prep: The drill's equipment list ends with 'Log sheets or app tracking' and nothing supplies them. Without a structured log the session produces an impression — 'that was hard' — instead of the one number the drill exists to generate: this member's own working duration, on this pack.
packs.local_fill_note: Your department's air-management policy supplies the decision points the log compares against. Write them at the top. The cylinder's rated duration comes from the manufacturer; your measured duration comes from this log, and it is the one that predicts anything.

components.label: Work circuit card
components.instructions: Build the circuit once and write it down, then run the identical circuit every session. A circuit that changes between sessions produces numbers that cannot be compared, which wastes the whole exercise.

items.text: The circuit — fix it and record it
fields: Station 1: hose drag — weight, distance, surface
Station 2: stair climb — flights, with or without a load
Station 3: forcible entry simulation — tool, target, reps
Station 4: crawl — distance, surface
Rest between stations, if any
Total circuit length and expected duration
items.teaching_focus: Written down to the detail. 'A hose drag' is not repeatable; '150 ft of charged 1.75 in on concrete' is.

items.text: Conditions on the day
fields: Ambient temperature
PPE worn — full structural, and anything omitted
Member's rest state — start of shift, after a call, end of a busy tour
Cylinder size and rated duration
items.teaching_focus: Temperature and fatigue move consumption a long way. A number without conditions attached is not usable.

components.label: Consumption log
components.instructions: Read the gauge at every station boundary and write it down immediately — not from memory at the end. The between-station deltas are the useful data because they show which work costs the member the most air.

items.text: Gauge readings
fields: Start pressure
After station 1
After station 2
After station 3
After station 4
Low-air alarm activated at which station
Pressure at the end

items.text: Per-station consumption
fields: Station 1 delta
Station 2 delta
Station 3 delta
Station 4 delta
The most expensive station
Was it the one I expected
items.teaching_focus: The station that costs most is rarely the one that feels hardest, and that mismatch is the lesson.

items.text: MY NUMBERS — the output of the drill
fields: Total working time on air
Cylinder rated duration
My measured duration as a fraction of rated
Time from low-air alarm to empty, measured
Working time I can rely on, allowing a margin
items.teaching_focus: The fourth row is the one nobody knows and everybody assumes. Measure it.

items.text: Against policy
fields: Our policy's exit decision point
At which station of this circuit I would have reached it
How much of the circuit I could complete inside policy
What that means for a real search of a real building
items.teaching_focus: Converting the number into a distance in a building is where the drill becomes tactical.

items.text: Trend across sessions
fields: Date
Measured duration
Conditions note
Change from last time
Anything I did differently — breathing, pace, technique
items.teaching_focus: Consumption is trainable. The trend is the evidence.

sources: Self-authored circuit card and consumption log
SCBA manufacturer cylinder ratings and department air-management policy (user-supplied and authoritative)

packs.title: Air Emergency Cards — Six Events and an Answer-Key Frame
packs.summary: Six air-emergency event cards matching the drill's six-event structure, each paired with the answer-key frame the member fills from their own SCBA manual and SOP — the events are universal, the correct responses are pack-specific and stay blank on purpose.
packs.removes_prep: The drill's setup is explicit: 'Before any reps, build the answer key: open your SCBA manufacturer's emergency procedures and your department's SCBA and mayday SOPs, and write the correct response for each of six events on the back of its card.' The member has to know which six events before they can look anything up, and picking the six is the part they get wrong.
packs.local_fill_note: The back of every card is deliberately blank. Fill it from your SCBA manufacturer's emergency-procedures section and your department's SCBA and mayday SOPs. A response written from memory or from another pack's manual is worse than an empty card, because you will practice it under the belief that it is correct.

components.label: Six air-emergency event cards
components.instructions: One event per card. Write your own correct response on the back from the manual and the SOP before the first rep. Then: PPE and SCBA on, off air, recorder running. Draw a card, and inside ten seconds transmit the call-out your SOP requires for that event. Play it back against the key you wrote.

items.text: EVENT 1 — Regulator failure: your regulator stops delivering air on demand.
fields: My pack's manufacturer procedure for this event
My department's radio call-out for this event
Is this a mayday under my SOP (Y/N)
Manual section and SOP reference
items.teaching_focus: The event that has a manufacturer-specific answer members most often assume is universal.

items.text: EVENT 2 — Free-flow: air will not stop flowing and you cannot shut it off at the regulator.
fields: Manufacturer procedure
Radio call-out
Mayday under my SOP (Y/N)
Remaining working time this leaves me — my own estimate, and how I got it
items.teaching_focus: The one where the gauge stops predicting anything and the member needs a different number.

items.text: EVENT 3 — Facepiece seal loss: the seal breaks and you take a breath of products of combustion.
fields: Manufacturer procedure
Radio call-out
Mayday under my SOP (Y/N)
What my department requires afterwards — medical evaluation, reporting
items.teaching_focus: The after-action requirement, which is the part members skip because they feel fine.

items.text: EVENT 4 — Low-air alarm activating earlier than expected.
fields: Manufacturer's stated activation point for my cylinder
Radio call-out
Mayday or urgent under my SOP
The three things that could cause an early activation on my pack
items.teaching_focus: Diagnosing rather than just reacting: leak, partial valve, or consumption rate.

items.text: EVENT 5 — Cylinder or high-pressure line leak: you can hear air escaping and it is not the regulator.
fields: Manufacturer procedure
Radio call-out
Mayday under my SOP (Y/N)
Can I isolate it on this pack, and how
items.teaching_focus: Whether the member's specific pack even offers an isolation option.

items.text: EVENT 6 — Out of air, still inside, facepiece on.
fields: Manufacturer procedure — what my pack offers in this state
Radio call-out
My department's position on filtering through the coat, buddy breathing, and RIC transfill
SOP reference
items.teaching_focus: The last-resort card. Departments differ sharply here and the member must know which side their department is on before it happens.

sources: Self-authored event set and key frame
SCBA manufacturer emergency-procedures manual (user-supplied, not reproduced)
Department SCBA and mayday SOPs (user-supplied, not reproduced)

packs.title: Profile Reps — Layout Card and Descending-Height Log
packs.summary: The taped-opening layout card with the footprint dimensions and the height-bar build, plus a descending-height rep log in three-inch steps that records the technique used at each height and the height at which it failed — which is the number the drill exists to find.
packs.removes_prep: The drill needs a taped rectangular footprint, a height bar adjustable in three-inch steps, and a per-rep log on index cards. Building the geometry from the setup paragraph takes a tape measure and guesswork, and without a log the member finishes knowing only that it got harder.

components.label: Layout card — footprint and height bar
components.instructions: Build this once and photograph it; you will rebuild it in two minutes every session after. Bay floor only. No wall prop, no breaching, no entanglement material, no confined space — the drill is a profile-reduction rep, not a search prop.

items.text: Taped footprint
fields: Opening width taped (start wide enough to pass standing sideways)
Opening depth taped
Clear approach marked on both sides
items.teaching_focus: The footprint stays fixed all session. Only the height changes, so the variable is one thing.

items.text: Height bar
fields: What forms the uprights — cones, chairs, hose rollers, spanner rack
What forms the bar — pike pole, ground ladder beam laid flat
Starting clear height, measured
Three-inch step marks on both uprights
items.teaching_focus: A bar that falls when touched is the correct design: it gives honest feedback and it cannot trap anyone.

items.text: Safety confirmations before the first rep
fields: Bar falls freely if struck (confirmed Y/N)
Floor dry and clear (Y/N)
Facepiece donned, regulator attached, air OFF (Y/N)
Nothing overhead that can be pulled down
items.teaching_focus: Solo drill, so the check is written rather than shouted to a safety officer.

components.label: Descending-height rep log
components.instructions: Start at the height you can walk through sideways and drop three inches per round. Log every round. Stop when a technique fails twice at the same height — that height, and the technique that failed, are the session's result.

items.text: Round log — one row per height
fields: Clear height this round
Technique used — sideways, low crawl, pack shifted to one shoulder, pack off one arm
Time
Cleared without touching the bar (Y/N)
What contacted the bar if it did
items.teaching_focus: The technique column is the important one. The height at which the member changes technique is more useful than the minimum they achieved.

items.text: Failure height
fields: Lowest height cleared cleanly, twice
Height at which it failed twice
Which part of the pack or body hung up
Was the waist strap loose
items.teaching_focus: A loose waist strap is the most common single cause, which is why SCBA-006 pairs with this drill.

items.text: What this does not cover
fields: Note to self: this was a dry bay floor, off air, with a bar that falls away
A real reduced opening has debris, heat, and does not yield
One thing I will ask to train with a crew
items.teaching_focus: Carrying the drill's own honesty about the solo limitation into the member's own words.

sources: Self-authored layout card and rep log

packs.title: Trench Non-Entry Kit — Schematics, Refusal Card, Assessment Sheet
packs.summary: Two trench schematics showing the failure geometry, a non-entry discipline card, and the assessment sheet that turns a trench into stated numbers — depth, spoil position, soil, water, adjacent load. Built around the drill's premise: the disciplined answer is usually not to go in.
packs.removes_prep: The drill names floor plans and supplies none, and a trench drill needs the failure geometry made visible before anyone can be talked out of entering. Nobody can sketch a secondary collapse convincingly on a whiteboard at 0900.
packs.local_fill_note: Trench rescue is governed by regulation and by your team's training and authorisation. This pack supplies assessment structure and non-entry discipline only. components.label: Failure geometry schematics
components.instructions: Show these before any discussion of tactics. The point is that the crew sees where the next collapse comes from and that it comes from where they would have been standing.

items.text: Schematic A — secondary collapse from the spoil pile side.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical cross-section line drawing of an excavated trench in soil: vertical trench walls, a large spoil pile heaped close to the edge on one side, a dashed curved line indicating the wedge of soil that would shear away from the spoil side into the trench, and dimension arrows showing trench depth and spoil setback distance. Plain white background, thin dark lines, minimal labels, engineering-drawing style, no people, no equipment, no casualties.
items.alt: Technical cross-section of a trench with vertical walls and a spoil pile close to one edge, with a dashed curve showing the wedge of soil that would shear into the trench and dimension arrows for depth and spoil setback.
items.teaching_focus: The spoil pile is the load that causes the second collapse, and it is always on the side people stand.

items.text: Schematic B — surcharge load from adjacent plant and structures.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical cross-section line drawing of an excavated trench with vertical walls, a heavy tracked machine positioned on the ground surface near one edge and a building foundation on the other side, with dashed lines indicating the load paths spreading downward and outward from each toward the trench walls, and dimension arrows for depth and standoff. Plain white background, thin dark lines, minimal labels, engineering-drawing style, no people, no casualties.
items.alt: Technical cross-section of a trench with a tracked machine near one edge and a building foundation on the other, dashed lines showing load paths spreading toward the trench walls, with depth and standoff dimensions.
items.teaching_focus: Everything near the edge is a load. The machine that dug it is the biggest one.

components.label: Non-entry discipline card
components.instructions: Read aloud at the start of every trench session. The card exists because the pull to enter is strongest when a victim is visible and partially buried, and that is exactly when entry kills the rescuer.

items.text: NOBODY enters an unprotected trench. Not to assess, not to reach, not briefly. Protective systems go in first or nobody goes in.
items.teaching_focus: The whole drill in one line.

items.text: KNOW YOUR NUMBERS, BOTH OF THEM. The regulation sets a minimum spoil setback in feet and a depth at which a protective system becomes mandatory — commonly a trench 5 feet deep or more, and a spoil setback of at least 2 feet from the edge. Write your jurisdiction's actual figures on the assessment sheet. Alongside them, carry the working heuristic: the wedge of soil that shears in a secondary collapse scales with the DEPTH of the trench, so a setback that is fine at 4 feet is not fine at 12. The regulation is the floor; the ratio is how you think about a trench deeper than the one the number was written for.
items.teaching_focus: Both numbers. The regulatory minimum is what you are held to; the depth ratio is what predicts the collapse.

items.text: A visible victim does not change the rule. It changes how badly you want to break it.
items.teaching_focus: Naming the pull, out loud, in the bay, before it happens.

items.text: The first job is stopping everything: plant off, traffic stopped, vibration sources shut down, edges cleared of loads and people.
items.teaching_focus: Actions that reduce the chance of the collapse that kills your crew.

items.text: The second job is calling for what you do not have. Trench rescue resources, a competent person, and shoring take time and must be started immediately, not after an assessment.
items.teaching_focus: Order matters: the request goes before the assessment finishes.

items.text: Things you CAN do from outside: request the resources this will actually take (technical rescue team, vacuum truck, utilities, additional alarm) EARLY; lay ground pads to spread rescuer weight away from the edge; supply air to the victim if they are conscious enough to help with it; ladders positioned for later access; dewatering; communication; and preventing the second collapse. That list is the whole of your job at operations level, and it is not a short one.
items.teaching_focus: A real list, so the rule is not just a prohibition. Resources requested early is the item that most changes the outcome.

packs.title: Zero-Energy Kit — Schematics, Proof Card, LOTO Sheet
packs.summary: Three machinery and elevator schematics showing where stored energy hides after the power is off, a proof-of-zero-energy card built around verification rather than isolation, and the lockout-tagout sheet with the verification step that most crews skip.
packs.removes_prep: The drill names floor plans and scenario material and supplies neither. Stored energy is invisible and counter-intuitive — a crew cannot reason about a counterweight or an accumulator they have never seen drawn — so the schematics are the drill's precondition.
packs.local_fill_note: Machinery and elevator rescue depends on the specific installation, the building's own maintenance personnel, and your team's authorisation. This pack structures the verification discipline; it does not supply a procedure for any machine, and nothing here authorises work on equipment your team is not trained for.

components.label: Stored-energy schematics
components.instructions: Show each one and ask the crew to point at every place energy could still be stored after the main disconnect is opened. They will miss some; that is the drill.

items.text: Schematic A — traction elevator: car, counterweight, hoist machine, governor.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical section-view line drawing of a traction elevator installation in a hoistway: elevator car on guide rails, hoist ropes running up over a sheave on a hoist machine at the top, down to a counterweight on its own rails on the other side of the hoistway, plus a governor with a rope loop and a pit with a buffer at the bottom. Plain white background, thin dark lines, minimal labels, engineering-drawing style, no people, no fire.
items.alt: Technical section drawing of a traction elevator hoistway with car on guide rails, hoist ropes over a top sheave and hoist machine, a counterweight on separate rails, a governor, and a pit buffer.
items.answer: Stored energy after power off: the counterweight is a suspended mass that will move the car if the brake releases; the ropes hold tension; the governor and buffer are spring energy; and the car itself is a load at height.
items.teaching_focus: Cutting power does not remove a suspended counterweight. It only removes the ability to control it.

items.text: Schematic B — hydraulic press or lift: cylinder, accumulator, valves, reservoir.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical schematic line drawing of a hydraulic machine circuit: a vertical ram cylinder with its piston partway extended, connected by pipework to a control valve block, a pressure accumulator vessel, a pump and a reservoir tank, with a pressure gauge on the accumulator line. Plain white background, thin dark lines, minimal labels, engineering-drawing style, no people, no fire.
items.alt: Technical schematic of a hydraulic circuit with a partially extended ram cylinder, control valve block, pressure accumulator, pump, reservoir and a pressure gauge on the accumulator line.
items.answer: Stored energy after power off: the accumulator holds pressure indefinitely and will drive the ram when a valve opens; the ram's own weight and the load on it are gravitational energy; and trapped fluid between closed valves is pressurised.
items.teaching_focus: An accumulator is a charged spring that does not look like one, and it does not discharge because the pump stopped.

items.text: Schematic C — belt and gear driven machine with a flywheel.
items.synthetic_prompt: Clean technical side-elevation line drawing of an industrial machine drive train: an electric motor with a pulley, a belt running to a larger pulley on a shaft, a heavy flywheel on the same shaft, a gear reduction box, and an output shaft with a roller, plus a guard outline shown dashed. Plain white background, thin dark lines, minimal labels, engineering-drawing style, no people, no fire.
items.alt: Technical side-elevation drawing of a machine drive train with motor and pulley, belt to a larger pulley, a heavy flywheel on the shaft, a gear box and an output roller, with a dashed guard outline.
items.answer: Stored energy after power off: the flywheel keeps turning, sometimes for a long time; belt and spring tension remains; and a raised or partly-driven component can move under gravity when the drive is released.
items.teaching_focus: Rotational inertia. The machine can still be moving when everything is switched off, and it is quiet.

components.label: Proof-of-zero-energy card
components.instructions: The card's whole point is the difference between ISOLATED and VERIFIED. Isolation is something you did; zero energy is something you proved. Read it aloud before any hands-on session.

items.text: ISOLATED is not ZERO. A locked disconnect means somebody cannot switch it on. It says nothing about the counterweight, the accumulator, the flywheel, the raised load, or the trapped fluid.
items.teaching_focus: The sentence the entire drill exists to install.

items.text: VERIFY BY TRYING TO OPERATE IT. After isolation and lockout, attempt to start the machine with the normal controls. If it moves, you were wrong about the isolation.
items.teaching_focus: The try-step. It is the cheapest verification in existence and it is routinely skipped.

items.text: RELIEVE, BLOCK, OR SUPPORT everything that is stored: bleed hydraulic and pneumatic pressure at a gauge you can read, let the flywheel stop, block or crib raised components mechanically, and secure suspended masses. A valve is not a block.
items.teaching_focus: Mechanical blocking, because hydraulics and controls fail and gravity does not.

items.text: USE THE BUILDING'S PEOPLE — AND VERIFY WHAT THEY TELL YOU. Maintenance staff and elevator technicians know where the energy is stored in THIS installation, and asking them is faster and safer than deducing it. Treat what they say as information to confirm, not as a verification you can skip: they may be describing how the system was built rather than how it is now, they may not know what a previous contractor changed, and they are not the ones who will be underneath it. Their word plus your own try-step and gauge reading, never their word alone.
items.teaching_focus: The resource crews forget because it is not on the apparatus — used properly, which means verified.

items.text: RE-VERIFY AFTER ANY CHANGE. New shift, new person, tool change, or anyone leaving the scene — verify again. Zero energy is a state, not a certificate.
items.teaching_focus: The state can change while nobody is looking at it.
